topics.t: Micro vs macro: thinking in aggregates
topics.h: One farmer in Punjab worries about the price of his wheat. The Finance Minister worries about the price of EVERYTHING at once. Welcome to macroeconomics!
p: Microeconomics studies individual units: one consumer, one firm, the market for one good like onions or cars.
Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole through aggregates: total output (GDP), total employment, the general price level, total saving and investment.

To keep things simple, macroeconomists often imagine all output as one representative good, so millions of separate markets are treated together (aggregate analysis instead of disaggregated analysis).
Economic agents are individuals or institutions that take economic decisions: households, firms, the government, and bodies like the RBI and SEBI.
Macroeconomic policy goals include higher growth, more employment, stable prices and better education and health for people.

ex.q: Classify: (i) the price of tomatoes in Nashik; (ii) India's inflation rate; (iii) a firm's demand for steel; (iv) total employment in India.
st: Ask: is it about one unit/market or the whole economy?
(i) one good's market → micro; (iii) one firm → micro
(ii) the general price level → macro; (iv) employment in the whole economy → macro
ex.a: (i) and (iii) are micro; (ii) and (iv) are macro

topics.rl: When the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee meets, it looks at aggregate inflation and GDP growth for all of India, not the price of one brand of biscuits.

rv.summary: Microeconomics studies individual units such as one consumer, firm or market, while macroeconomics studies the whole economy through aggregates like GDP, employment and the general price level.
focus: Classify a variable or question as micro or macro
Name economic agents and macro policy goals
Explain why macro uses aggregates
remember: Macro aggregates: total output (GDP), total employment, general price level, total saving and investment
Economic agents: households, firms, government, bodies like RBI and SEBI
Macro goals: growth, employment, stable prices, education and health
traps: The price of one good is micro, not macro
Macro adds up individual agents; it does not ignore them
A 'representative good' is a simplification, not a fact

topics.t: Classical economics and the Great Depression
topics.h: In 1929 the world's richest economy hit a wall: by 1933 one in every four American workers who wanted a job could not find one.
p: Adam Smith, author of 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776), is regarded as the founder of modern economics. Classical economists who followed him believed in free markets.
Classical view: if markets are left free, wages and prices adjust so that all who want work at the going wage find it; the economy tends to full employment by itself.
The Great Depression began in 1929. In the USA, output of goods and services fell sharply and the unemployment rate rose from about 3% to about 25% by 1933.
Unemployment rate = (number of people looking for work but jobless ÷ labour force) × 100, where the labour force = people working + people seeking work.
The long, deep slump showed that markets did not quickly correct themselves, which challenged the classical belief.

ex.q: In a town, 1,840 people have jobs and 160 people are actively looking for work but jobless. Find the unemployment rate.

topics.rl: During the COVID-19 lockdown in 2020, India's unemployment rate jumped sharply, reminding economists why the Great Depression made macroeconomics necessary.

rv.summary: Classical economists following Adam Smith believed free markets reach full employment by themselves. The Great Depression from 1929, when US unemployment rose from about 3% to about 25%, challenged this belief.
focus: Know Adam Smith and the classical view
Know the Great Depression's dates and unemployment figures
Compute the unemployment rate
remember: Adam Smith, 'The Wealth of Nations', 1776
Great Depression began 1929; US unemployment about 3% → about 25% by 1933
Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100
Labour force = employed + those seeking work
traps: Divide by the labour force, not by the employed
Don't confuse 1929 (Depression) with 1936 (General Theory)
The labour force excludes people not seeking work

topics.t: Keynes and the capitalist economy
topics.h: One book in 1936 split economics into two branches. Its author, John Maynard Keynes, also helped design the post-war world money system at Bretton Woods.
p: John Maynard Keynes, a British economist, published 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' in 1936.
Keynes argued that output and employment depend on aggregate (effective) demand, and that an economy can stay stuck with unemployment for a long time.
His approach studied the economy as a whole, so 1936 is taken as the birth of macroeconomics as a separate branch.
A capitalist economy has: (a) private ownership of the means of production, (b) production mainly for sale in the market, and (c) sale and purchase of labour services at a wage rate.
In a capitalist economy, firms run by capitalists hire wage workers and produce goods for profit.

ex.q: A village has a potter who makes pots only for his own family and a factory owner in Morbi who hires 200 workers on wages to make tiles for sale. Which shows capitalist production?
st: Check the three features: private ownership, production for market sale, wage labour
The potter: no market sale, no hired labour
The Morbi factory: private owner, tiles sold, workers paid wages

topics.rl: Modern India is a mixed economy, but large parts of it, such as private IT firms in Bengaluru hiring engineers for a salary to sell services worldwide, work on capitalist lines.

rv.summary: Keynes's General Theory (1936) said output and employment depend on aggregate demand and that unemployment can persist, giving birth to macroeconomics. A capitalist economy has private ownership, production for the market and wage labour.
focus: Know Keynes's book, year and main idea
Contrast Keynesian and classical views
List the features of a capitalist economy
remember: Keynes, 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money', 1936
Output and employment depend on aggregate (effective) demand
Capitalist economy: private ownership, production for sale, wage labour
traps: Don't give Keynes the classical belief in quick self-correction
Production for self-use is not capitalist production
The price of labour is the wage rate, not profit or rent

topics.t: Factors of production and the entrepreneur
topics.h: Every rupee of income in India ends up in one of four pockets: rent, wages, interest or profit. Which pocket is yours?
p: Four factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
Their rewards (factor payments): land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, entrepreneurship earns profit.
The entrepreneur organises the other factors, takes decisions and bears the risk of loss; profit is the reward for this risk-taking.
Investment expenditure is spending by firms on new machines, buildings and stocks; it adds to the productive capacity of the economy.

ex.q: Raghav runs a dhaba on a highway. He rents the plot for ₹20,000 a month, pays cooks ₹45,000, pays ₹5,000 interest on a bank loan, and keeps what is left. Name each factor payment.
st: Raghav (entrepreneur, bears the risk) → the remainder is profit
ex.a: Rent, wages, interest and profit respectively

topics.rl: Startup founders in Bengaluru are entrepreneurs: they combine venture capital, rented office space and hired coders, and they earn profit only if the risk pays off.

rv.summary: The four factors of production are land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship, rewarded by rent, wages, interest and profit. Profit is the entrepreneur's reward for bearing risk.
focus: Match each factor with its reward
Find profit as the remainder after other factor payments
Identify investment expenditure
remember: Land → rent; labour → wages; capital → interest; entrepreneurship → profit
Entrepreneur organises production and bears risk
Investment: spending on new machines, buildings and stocks
traps: Don't mix up rent (land) and interest (capital)
Buying vegetables or paying fees is consumption, not investment
Subtract every factor payment before calling the rest profit

topics.t: Four sectors of the macroeconomy
topics.h: Your chai purchase, a GST payment and an Infosys export bill to the USA all belong to different 'sectors' of the same economy.
p: Macroeconomics groups economic agents into four sectors: households, firms, government and the external sector (rest of the world).
Households supply factor services (labour, land, capital) and buy consumer goods; firms hire factors and produce goods and services.
Government makes laws, enforces contracts, taxes people and firms, spends on public services and infrastructure, and regulates economic activity.
External sector: exports (goods sold abroad), imports (goods bought from abroad) and capital flows (foreign investment and borrowing).
A closed economy has no external sector; an open economy trades and has capital flows with other countries.

ex.q: Assign each transaction to its sector: (i) Tata Motors hires workers; (ii) a family buys a fridge; (iii) the Centre collects income tax; (iv) India imports crude oil.
st: (i) a producing unit hiring factors → firms
(iv) trade with other countries → external sector

topics.rl: Remittances from Indians working in the Gulf and software exports to the USA connect India's households and firms with the external sector every day.

rv.summary: The macro model has four sectors: households, firms, government and the external sector. Households supply factors, firms produce, government taxes, spends and regulates, and the external sector covers trade and capital flows.
focus: Assign transactions to the right sector
Know the role of each sector
Tell open from closed economies
remember: Four sectors: households, firms, government, external sector
External sector: exports, imports, capital flows
Closed economy: no external sector; open economy: trades with the world
traps: Trade unions are not one of the four sectors
Foreign buying of Indian shares is a capital flow, not trade in goods
Firms pay factor incomes to households, not the other way round

topics.t: Final, intermediate, consumption and capital goods
topics.h: Milk poured on your cornflakes is a final good. The same milk poured into a chaiwala's kettle is an intermediate good. Same milk, different destiny!
p: Final goods are goods meant for final use (consumption or investment); they will not pass through any further stage of production in that year.
Intermediate goods are used up as inputs in producing other goods during the year, e.g. cotton bought by a textile mill.
Whether a good is final or intermediate depends on its use, not on what it is. Only final goods are counted in national income, to avoid double counting.
Consumption goods satisfy wants directly (food, clothes, haircuts). Consumer durables such as TVs, cars and fridges are consumption goods that last for years.
Capital goods (machines, tools, buildings) are durable goods used again and again in production; they are final goods but are not used up in one round.

ex.q: Classify: (i) wheat bought by a flour mill; (ii) a tractor bought by a farmer; (iii) a washing machine bought by a family; (iv) paper bought by a publisher.
st: (i) wheat is used up to make flour → intermediate
(ii) the tractor is used again and again to produce crops → capital good (final)
(iii) used by a household for years → consumer durable (final)
(iv) paper becomes part of books → intermediate
ex.a: (i) intermediate, (ii) capital good, (iii) consumer durable, (iv) intermediate

topics.rl: Steel sold by SAIL to Maruti Suzuki is intermediate, but the Swift car bought by a family is a final consumer durable. NSO counts only the car's value to avoid counting the steel twice.

rv.summary: Final goods are for final use and are counted in national income; intermediate goods are used up in producing other goods and are left out to avoid double counting. Whether a good is final depends on its use.
focus: Classify goods as final, intermediate, consumer durable or capital good
Explain why only final goods are counted
remember: Only final goods are counted, to avoid double counting
Final or intermediate depends on end use
Capital goods are final goods used again and again
traps: Milk or paint is not always final; check who uses it
Machines are final (capital) goods, not intermediate
A household car is a consumer durable, not a capital good

topics.t: Stocks, flows, investment and depreciation
topics.h: A water tank at a given moment holds 500 litres: that's a stock. Water flowing in at 10 litres a minute: that's a flow. The economy works the same way.
p: A stock is measured at a point of time (wealth, capital, money supply on 31 March). A flow is measured over a period of time (income, output, investment per year).
Water-tank analogy: the water in the tank is a stock; water entering per minute is a flow. Capital is a stock; investment is the flow that adds to it.
Gross investment = total addition to capital goods (and inventories) in a year.
Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) = fall in the value of fixed capital due to normal wear and tear and expected obsolescence.
Net investment = Gross investment − Depreciation. Only net investment adds to the capital stock.

ex.q: A firm buys a machine for ₹10,00,000 that lasts 20 years with no scrap value. In a year it also spends ₹2,00,000 on new equipment. Find annual depreciation of the first machine and the year's net investment, if the 2,00,000 is the year's gross investment.

topics.rl: Indian Railways adds new Vande Bharat trainsets (gross investment) while old coaches wear out (depreciation). Its fleet grows only by the difference.

rv.summary: A stock is measured at a point of time and a flow over a period. Gross investment adds to capital, depreciation wears it down, and net investment = gross investment − depreciation.
focus: Classify variables as stock or flow
Compute gross or net investment and depreciation
remember: Stock: capital, wealth, money supply; flow: income, output, investment
Net investment = Gross investment − Depreciation
Depreciation = consumption of fixed capital
traps: Investment is a flow, capital is a stock
Add depreciation to net investment to get gross
Only net investment adds to the capital stock

topics.t: Circular flow of income
topics.h: Every rupee a firm pays as wages comes back to it when workers shop. Money in an economy runs in a circle, like a lap around the Eden Gardens boundary.
p: Two-sector model: only households and firms. Households supply factor services; firms supply goods and services. This is the real flow.
The money flow runs the other way: firms pay factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) to households; households spend this money on firms' goods.
Simplifying assumptions: no government, no foreign trade, and households spend all their income (no saving), so there are no leakages.
Under these assumptions, aggregate output = aggregate factor income = aggregate expenditure. Each is a measurement point for national income.
This gives the three methods of measuring national income: product (value added), income and expenditure methods.

ex.q: In a two-sector economy with no saving, firms produce goods worth ₹500 crore. What are the aggregate factor incomes and aggregate expenditure?
st: The whole value of output is paid as factor incomes → ₹500 crore
With no saving, households spend all income on firms' output → ₹500 crore

topics.rl: When a Swiggy delivery partner earns wages and spends them at a kirana store, money moves from firm to household and back to a firm: the circular flow in action.

rv.summary: In the two-sector model, households supply factor services and firms supply goods (real flows), while money flows the opposite way. With no leakages, output = income = expenditure.
focus: Identify real and money flows
State the assumptions of the simple model
Link the three measurement points to the three methods
remember: Output = factor income = expenditure
Real flow: goods and factor services; money flow: payments
Leakages: saving, taxes, imports (assumed away)
traps: Wages are a money flow, not a real flow
The simple model assumes households save nothing
Don't confuse the direction of real and money flows

topics.t: Product method: value added
topics.h: If you add the value of wheat, flour and bread, you count the wheat three times. Value added fixes this classic trap.
p: Value added (gross) = value of output − intermediate consumption (inputs bought from other firms).
Farmer-baker idea: if a farmer grows wheat with no inputs and sells part to a baker who makes bread, adding both outputs counts the wheat twice; adding value added counts it once.
Gross value added (GVA) − depreciation = net value added (NVA).
GDP = sum of the gross value added of all producing units in the domestic territory.
Value added by a firm is the reward available for its factors of production (wages, rent, interest, profit).

ex.q: A farmer grows cotton worth ₹50 (no inputs) and sells it all to a weaver. The weaver makes cloth worth ₹120 and sells it to a tailor, who makes shirts worth ₹200. Find total value added and show the double counting.
st: Total value added = 50 + 70 + 80 = 200 (equals the final good's value)
ex.a: Value added = ₹200; summing outputs (₹370) double counts

topics.rl: Amul's value added is the value of its butter, cheese and milk powder minus the milk and packaging it buys; adding up such value added across all Indian producers gives GDP.

rv.summary: Value added = value of output − intermediate consumption, and GDP is the sum of gross value added of all producing units. Summing outputs double counts inputs.
focus: Compute GVA and NVA
Show double counting with a production chain
remember: GVA = Value of output − Intermediate consumption
NVA = GVA − Depreciation
GDP = Σ GVA of all producing units
traps: Deduct raw materials, not wages or profits
Don't add outputs of all firms
NVA, not GVA, excludes depreciation

topics.t: Inventories: planned and unplanned
topics.h: A Diwali sweet shop makes 500 kg of kaju katli but sells only 450 kg. The extra 50 kg is still part of what it produced this year.
p: Inventory (stock) = unsold finished goods, semi-finished goods and raw materials a firm carries from one year to the next.
Value of output = value of sales + change in inventories (stock).
Change in inventories during a year = closing stock − opening stock = production − sales. It can be positive (accumulation) or negative (decumulation).
Change in inventories is treated as investment, because it adds to the firm's stock of goods.
Planned inventory change is what the firm intended; unplanned change happens when sales differ from expectations (e.g. sales fall short → unplanned accumulation).

ex.q: A firm's sales in a year are ₹5,000. Its opening stock is ₹400 and closing stock ₹650. Find the change in stock and the value of output.
st: Value of output = sales + change in stock
ex.a: Change in stock ₹250; value of output ₹5,250

topics.rl: Car makers in India often see unplanned inventory pile up at dealers when festive-season sales are weaker than expected.

rv.summary: Inventories are unsold goods carried over; their change (closing − opening stock, or production − sales) counts as investment. Value of output = sales + change in stock.
focus: Compute change in stock and value of output
Tell planned from unplanned inventory changes
remember: Value of output = Sales + Change in stock
Change in stock = Closing − Opening = Production − Sales
Sales below expectation → unplanned accumulation
traps: Change in stock can be negative
Inventory is a stock; its change is a flow
Higher-than-expected sales cause decumulation, not accumulation

topics.t: Expenditure and income methods
topics.h: You can count India's GDP three ways and should get the same answer every time, like checking a sum by adding columns and then rows.
p: Expenditure method: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), where C = private final consumption, I = investment (including inventory change), G = government final consumption, X − M = net exports.
Imports are subtracted because C, I and G include spending on foreign goods that were not produced at home.

Income method: GDP = W + P + In + R in the simple model (wages, profits, interest, rent). In Indian accounts the components are compensation of employees, operating surplus (rent, interest, profit) and mixed income of the self-employed.
Strictly, adding factor incomes gives domestic income (NDP at factor cost); adding depreciation and net indirect taxes takes it to GDP at market prices.
Product, income and expenditure methods give the same GDP, because output = income = expenditure.

ex.q: C = 600, I = 200, G = 150, X = 80, M = 110 (₹ crore). Find GDP by the expenditure method.

topics.rl: India imports most of its crude oil; when petrol prices rise, spending on imports grows, which lowers net exports (X − M) in the GDP calculation.

rv.summary: By expenditure, GDP = C + I + G + (X − M); by income, add compensation of employees, operating surplus and mixed income. All three methods give the same GDP.
focus: Compute GDP from expenditure items
Compute domestic factor income
Know operating surplus and mixed income
remember: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)
Operating surplus = rent + interest + profit
Mixed income: income of the self-employed
traps: Subtract imports, don't add them
Compensation of employees is not part of operating surplus
Factor incomes give NDP at FC, not GDP at MP

topics.t: Factor cost, basic prices and market prices
topics.h: A packet of biscuits costs ₹30 in the shop, but the factors who made it earned less than that. The gap is mostly GST, a product tax.
p: Market price = what buyers pay. Factor cost = what the factors of production receive.
GDP at market prices − net indirect taxes = GDP at factor cost, where net indirect taxes = indirect taxes − subsidies.

Production taxes and subsidies are linked to production but not to the quantity produced (land revenue, stamp and registration fees, professional tax). Product taxes and subsidies are levied per unit of product (GST, excise duty, customs duty).
GVA at basic prices = GVA at factor cost + (production taxes − production subsidies). GVA at market prices = GVA at basic prices + (product taxes − product subsidies).
India's national accounts (NSO) report sector-wise GVA at basic prices, and GDP at market prices for the whole economy.

ex.q: GDP at market prices is ₹5,000 crore, indirect taxes are ₹600 crore and subsidies ₹100 crore. Find GDP at factor cost.
st: GDP at FC = GDP at MP − NIT

topics.rl: When the government cuts fertiliser prices through subsidies, the market price farmers pay falls below factor cost, so subsidies are added back when moving from market price to factor cost.

rv.summary: GDP at market prices − net indirect taxes = GDP at factor cost. Basic prices add net production taxes to factor cost, and market prices add net product taxes to basic prices.
focus: Convert between market prices, basic prices and factor cost
Classify production and product taxes
remember: GDP at FC = GDP at MP − (indirect taxes − subsidies)
GVA at basic prices = GVA at FC + production taxes − production subsidies
GVA at MP = GVA at basic prices + product taxes − product subsidies
Product taxes: GST, excise, customs
traps: Land revenue and stamp duty are production taxes, not product taxes
Add subsidies when going from MP to FC
India reports sector GVA at basic prices

topics.t: GNP, NNP and national income
topics.h: An Indian engineer working in Dubai adds to India's national income but not to India's domestic product. Domestic and national are not the same!
p: Domestic = produced within the country's territory. National = earned by the country's normal residents, wherever they work.
NFIA (net factor income from abroad) = factor income earned by residents from abroad − factor income earned by non-residents in the domestic territory.
GNP = GDP + NFIA. NDP = GDP − depreciation. NNP = GNP − depreciation.
National income (NI) = NNP at factor cost = NNP at market prices − net indirect taxes = NDP at factor cost + NFIA.
If NFIA is negative (as for India in recent years, due to large interest and profit payments abroad), GNP is less than GDP.

ex.q: GDP at market prices = 2,500, NFIA = −50, net indirect taxes = 200, national income = 2,000 (₹ crore). Find depreciation.
st: NNP at FC = GNP at MP − depreciation − NIT

topics.rl: Profits sent home by foreign companies operating in India are a factor income paid abroad, which is one reason India's NFIA is negative.

rv.summary: Domestic means produced within the territory; national means earned by normal residents. GNP = GDP + NFIA, and national income is NNP at factor cost.
focus: Compute GNP, NNP and national income
Use NFIA correctly
Classify incomes as domestic or national
remember: GNP = GDP + NFIA; NNP = GNP − Depreciation
NI = NNP at FC = NDP at FC + NFIA
NFIA negative ⇒ GNP < GDP
traps: NFIA is about factor income, not exports minus imports
Embassies are not part of the host country's domestic territory
Watch the sign of NFIA

topics.t: Personal income, disposable income and the saving gap
topics.h: National income is what the nation earns, but not all of it reaches your family's wallet. Companies keep some, the taxman takes some, and pensions add some back.
p: Personal income (PI) = NI − undistributed profits − net interest payments made by households − corporate tax + transfer payments to households (from government and firms).
Personal disposable income (PDI) = PI − personal tax payments − non-tax payments (such as fines). Households either consume or save PDI.
National disposable income = NNP at market prices + other current transfers from the rest of the world (gifts, aid, remittances).
Private income = factor income from NDP accruing to the private sector + national debt interest + NFIA + current transfers from government + other net transfers from the rest of the world.
From Y = C + I + G + X − M and Y = C + S + T: (S − I) = (G − T) + (X − M). Excess private saving over investment finances the budget deficit plus the trade surplus.

ex.q: NI = 5,000, undistributed profits = 300, net interest paid by households = 100, corporate tax = 400, transfers to households = 250, personal taxes = 500, non-tax payments = 50 (₹ crore). Find PI and PDI.
st: PDI = PI − personal taxes − non-tax payments

topics.rl: PM-KISAN payments to farmers and old-age pensions are transfers: they raise personal income without being payment for current production.

rv.summary: Personal income adjusts national income for undistributed profits, corporate tax, household interest and transfers; personal disposable income subtracts personal taxes and fines. The identity (S − I) = (G − T) + (X − M) links saving gaps.
focus: Compute PI and PDI
Know what is in private income but not NI
Use the saving-investment identity
remember: PI = NI − undistributed profits − net interest paid by households − corporate tax + transfers
PDI = PI − personal taxes − non-tax payments
traps: Transfers are added to get PI; corporate tax is subtracted
Interest on national debt is in private income, not NI
Fines are non-tax payments, subtracted for PDI

topics.t: Nominal GDP, real GDP and the GDP deflator
topics.h: If India's GDP doubles because every price doubled, are we any richer? Real GDP answers that by freezing prices.
p: Nominal GDP values each year's output at that year's (current) prices.
Real GDP values each year's output at the prices of a fixed base year (constant prices), so it changes only when quantities change.
GDP deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100. NCERT also writes it as the ratio itself (e.g. 1.2 instead of 120).
In the base year, nominal GDP = real GDP and the deflator is 100. A deflator above 100 means prices have risen since the base year.
Real GDP = Nominal GDP ÷ (deflator ÷ 100).

ex.q: Base year: 100 kg of rice at ₹10/kg. Current year: 110 kg at ₹12/kg. Find nominal GDP, real GDP and the deflator for the current year.

topics.rl: NSO publishes GDP 'at current prices' and 'at constant prices'; news headlines about India's growth rate use real GDP at constant prices.

rv.summary: Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP uses base-year prices, so it changes only with quantities. GDP deflator = nominal ÷ real × 100, and it is 100 in the base year.
focus: Compute nominal GDP, real GDP and the deflator
Interpret changes in nominal vs real GDP
remember: Real GDP = current quantity × base-year price
Deflator = Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP × 100
Real GDP = Nominal GDP ÷ (deflator ÷ 100)
traps: Divide by 1.2, not 120, when the deflator is 120
A rise in nominal GDP may be only a price rise
Use base-year prices for real GDP

topics.t: CPI, WPI and the deflator compared
topics.h: When your family's grocery bill jumps, that is CPI talking. When a factory's raw-material bill jumps, that is WPI.
p: Consumer Price Index (CPI) = (cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods at current prices ÷ its cost at base-year prices) × 100.
Wholesale Price Index (WPI) measures changes in prices of goods traded in bulk at the wholesale level; in many countries it is called the Producer Price Index (PPI).
Difference 1 (coverage): CPI covers goods bought by consumers; the GDP deflator covers all final goods and services produced in the economy.
Difference 2 (imports): CPI includes prices of imported consumer goods; the GDP deflator does not, since it covers only domestic output.
Difference 3 (weights): CPI uses fixed base-year quantities (weights); the deflator's weights change each year with the actual production.

ex.q: A basket of 10 kg rice and 5 kg dal cost ₹300 in the base year. Now rice is ₹40/kg and dal ₹100/kg. Find CPI.
st: Current cost of the same basket = 10 × 40 + 5 × 100 = 400 + 500 = 900

topics.rl: The RBI's inflation target is set in terms of CPI (combined) inflation, which tracks prices paid by ordinary households.

rv.summary: CPI prices a fixed basket of consumer goods, WPI tracks wholesale prices, and the GDP deflator covers all domestic final output. CPI includes imports and uses fixed weights; the deflator excludes imports and its weights change yearly.
focus: Compute CPI from a basket
List the differences between CPI and the GDP deflator
Know that WPI is called PPI in many countries
remember: CPI = current cost of basket ÷ base-year cost × 100
CPI includes imported consumer goods; deflator does not
Deflator weights change each year
Base-year index = 100
traps: Imported goods affect CPI, not the deflator directly
The deflator does not use a fixed basket
WPI is not the same as CPI

topics.t: GDP and welfare
topics.h: A city can post record GDP while its air becomes unbreathable. Is everyone really better off?
p: Higher GDP does not always mean higher welfare (well-being) of people; GDP is an incomplete index of welfare.
Distribution: if GDP rises but the increase goes to a few rich people, most people may be no better off or even worse off.
Non-monetary exchanges: housework, help within families and barter are not counted in GDP, so GDP understates real activity.
Externalities: benefits or harms to others that are not paid for. Pollution by a factory is a negative externality not deducted from GDP; a well-kept garden that neighbours enjoy is a positive one.
So per capita real GDP must be read alongside distribution, environment and non-market work when judging welfare.

ex.q: Village A's income rose from ₹100 lakh to ₹120 lakh, but the whole rise went to one landowner while 90% of families' incomes fell. Did welfare rise?
st: But the gain went to one person and most families became poorer
ex.a: Not necessarily: most people are worse off despite higher GDP

topics.rl: Delhi's winter smog shows a negative externality: vehicle and crop-burning pollution harms health, yet the harm is not subtracted from GDP.

rv.summary: Higher GDP does not always mean higher welfare. GDP ignores distribution, leaves out non-monetary exchanges like housework, and does not deduct externalities like pollution.
focus: Explain the three limits of GDP as a welfare index
Classify positive and negative externalities
remember: Limits: distribution, non-monetary exchanges, externalities
Negative externality: unpaid harm (pollution); positive: unpaid benefit (garden)
traps: A rise in GDP need not raise everyone's welfare
Paid domestic help is counted; own housework is not
Externalities are not deducted from GDP

topics.t: From barter to money
topics.h: Imagine paying for a movie ticket with two coconuts and a pencil, and the ticket seller wants rice. That is barter, and its headaches are why money was invented.
p: Barter = direct exchange of goods for goods (commodity for commodity) without money.

Drawbacks of barter: (1) need for a double coincidence of wants; (2) no common measure of value; (3) indivisibility of some goods (you cannot split a cow); (4) difficulty in storing wealth, since many goods perish or lose value.
Money is anything commonly accepted as a medium of exchange and a means of payment.
Medium of exchange: money separates buying from selling, removing the need for double coincidence of wants.
Unit of account (measure of value): values of all goods are expressed in money (₹), so relative prices are easy to compare. If a pen costs ₹20 and a notebook ₹60, one notebook = 3 pens.

ex.q: A farmer with wheat wants shoes, but the cobbler wants milk, not wheat. Explain the problem and how money solves it.
st: The farmer's want (shoes) and the cobbler's want (milk) do not match
This is the lack of double coincidence of wants
With money, the farmer sells wheat to anyone for ₹ and pays the cobbler in ₹
ex.a: Money as a medium of exchange removes the need for double coincidence of wants

topics.rl: When you scan a UPI QR code at a tea stall, rupees act as the medium of exchange and the menu prices (₹15 a cup) act as the unit of account.

rv.summary: Barter suffers from the need for a double coincidence of wants, no common measure of value, indivisibility and difficulty in storing wealth. Money, accepted by all, works as a medium of exchange and a unit of account.
focus: List the drawbacks of barter
Explain medium of exchange and unit of account
Compute relative prices in money terms
remember: Barter drawbacks: double coincidence of wants, no common measure of value, indivisibility, storing wealth
Money: anything commonly accepted as a medium of exchange
Relative price = price of one good ÷ price of another
traps: Money is defined by acceptance, not by being gold or paper
'Worth ₹X' is the unit of account, not medium of exchange
Medium of exchange removes the double coincidence problem

topics.t: Store of value, purchasing power and digital money
topics.h: ₹1,000 under your pillow keeps its number but not its power. If prices double, it buys only half as much.
p: Store of value: money lets people store wealth and spend it later. Money is the most liquid asset: it can be used for payment instantly without loss.
Other assets (land, gold, bonds, houses) may earn returns but are less liquid; converting them to money takes time and cost.
Purchasing power of money is the amount of goods one unit of money can buy. It falls when the general price level rises (purchasing power ∝ 1/price level).
Digital and cashless payments: Jan Dhan bank accounts, Aadhaar-enabled payment systems, e-wallets, UPI and the National Financial Switch (the network linking ATMs of different banks).

Demonetisation (8 November 2016): old ₹500 and ₹1000 notes ceased to be legal tender; aims included curbing black money, counterfeit notes and terror financing and promoting digital payments. New ₹500 and ₹2000 notes were issued.

ex.q: Prices in the economy double. What happens to the purchasing power of ₹500?
st: Purchasing power varies inversely with the price level
If the price level doubles, each rupee buys half as much

topics.rl: After demonetisation in 2016, many small shops in India began accepting UPI and wallet payments, and digital transactions grew rapidly.

rv.summary: Money is the most liquid store of value, but its purchasing power falls when prices rise. India promotes digital payments (UPI, Jan Dhan, NFS), and old ₹500 and ₹1000 notes were demonetised on 8 November 2016.
focus: Explain store of value and liquidity
Link purchasing power to the price level
Know digital payment systems and demonetisation facts
remember: Purchasing power ∝ 1/price level
Money is the most liquid asset
Demonetisation: 8 November 2016, old ₹500 and ₹1000 notes
NFS links ATMs of different banks
traps: Money does lose purchasing power with inflation
Land and gold are less liquid than money
Raising CRR was not an aim of demonetisation

topics.t: Demand for money
topics.h: Why keep cash in your wallet that earns nothing, when a fixed deposit pays interest? Because you need it to buy things, and sometimes to wait for a better chance.
p: Transaction demand: people hold money to make payments. It rises with income (more transactions) and is written M_T = kPY, where PY is nominal income and k is the fraction of income held as money.
k = 1/v, where v is the velocity of circulation (the number of times a unit of money changes hands in a year). If v = 4, k = 1/4.
Holding money has an opportunity cost: the interest given up. So a higher interest rate lowers the demand for money.
Speculative demand: bond prices and the interest rate move inversely. When the rate is high, people expect it to fall (bond prices to rise), so they buy bonds and hold less money.
Liquidity trap: at a very low interest rate everyone expects it to rise and bond prices to fall, so people hold any extra money and money demand becomes perfectly elastic.

ex.q: Nominal income in an economy is ₹2,400 crore and the velocity of money is 6. Find the transaction demand for money.

topics.rl: When FD rates rise, many Indian families shift money out of savings accounts into deposits, holding less idle money.

rv.summary: People demand money for transactions (M_T = kPY, with k = 1/v) and for speculation, which falls as the interest rate rises. At a very low rate the economy may be in a liquidity trap.
focus: Compute transaction demand and velocity
Explain why money demand falls with the interest rate
Explain the liquidity trap
remember: M_T = kPY; k = 1/v
Bond prices and interest rates move inversely
Liquidity trap: money demand perfectly elastic at a very low rate
traps: Divide nominal income by velocity, don't multiply
Higher interest rate → lower bond prices
In a liquidity trap people hold money, not bonds

topics.t: Supply of money: M1 to M4
topics.h: The rupee note in your pocket says 'I promise to pay the bearer...' and is signed by the RBI Governor. Yet it has almost no value as paper. So what makes it money?
p: Money supply is the total stock of money held by the public at a point of time. M1 = CU + DD (currency notes and coins held by the public + net demand deposits held by commercial banks).

M2 = M1 + savings deposits with Post Office savings banks. M3 = M1 + net time deposits of commercial banks. M4 = M3 + total deposits with Post Office savings organisations (excluding National Savings Certificates).
M1 and M2 are narrow money; M3 and M4 are broad money. Liquidity falls from M1 to M4. M3 is the most commonly used measure (aggregate monetary resources).
Currency notes are issued by the RBI; coins (and one-rupee notes) are issued by the Government of India. Currency is fiat money: it has no intrinsic value and is money by government order.
Currency is legal tender: it cannot be refused in settling payments. Cheques and demand deposits are not legal tender; a payee may refuse a cheque.

ex.q: The public holds currency of ₹30 lakh crore; net demand deposits are ₹25 lakh crore; net time deposits of banks are ₹150 lakh crore. Find M1 and M3.
ex.a: M1 = ₹55 lakh crore; M3 = ₹205 lakh crore

topics.rl: Your savings bank balance is a demand deposit counted in M1; a fixed deposit at SBI is a time deposit counted in M3.

rv.summary: Money supply is the stock of money held by the public. M1 = CU + DD, M2 adds Post Office savings deposits, M3 adds banks' net time deposits to M1, and M4 adds total Post Office deposits to M3.
focus: Define and compute M1 and M3
Order measures by liquidity
Know who issues notes and coins and what legal tender is
remember: M1 = CU + DD; M3 = M1 + net time deposits of banks
Narrow money: M1, M2; broad money: M3, M4
RBI issues notes; Government issues coins and one-rupee notes
Currency is fiat money and legal tender
traps: Cheques and demand deposits are not legal tender
M1 is the most liquid, not M4
Coins are not issued by the RBI

topics.t: The Reserve Bank of India and its functions
topics.h: During the 2008 global crisis and again in 2020, when banks feared a cash crunch, one institution in Mumbai stood ready to lend: the RBI.
p: The Reserve Bank of India was set up in 1935 as India's central bank. It is the apex monetary authority.
Bank of issue (currency authority): it has the sole right to issue currency notes (other than one-rupee notes), backed by assets such as foreign securities and gold.
Banker to the government: keeps government accounts, makes payments and receives deposits for it, manages its borrowing and advises it on financial matters.
Banker's bank and supervisor: commercial banks keep reserves with it; it lends to them as the lender of last resort in a crisis, and it regulates and supervises banks.
Custodian of foreign exchange reserves and controller of credit: manages India's forex reserves and controls money supply and credit through monetary policy.

ex.q: A bank faces a sudden rush of withdrawals and cannot borrow from other banks. Which RBI function helps, and how?
st: The bank has no other source of funds
The RBI can lend to it when no one else will
This is the lender of last resort function
ex.a: Lender of last resort, part of the RBI's role as banker's bank

topics.rl: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee announces the repo rate, while its banking supervision teams inspect banks like any regulator would.

rv.summary: The RBI, set up in 1935, is India's central bank: bank of issue, banker to the government, banker's bank and lender of last resort, custodian of forex reserves and controller of credit.
focus: Know the RBI's functions with examples
Explain lender of last resort
remember: RBI set up in 1935
Sole right to issue notes except one-rupee notes
Lender of last resort to banks in a crisis
Custodian of forex reserves; controls credit via monetary policy
traps: The RBI does not take deposits from the general public
1949 is nationalisation, not establishment
Coins are issued by the Government, not the RBI

topics.t: Commercial banks, balance sheets and the goldsmith's secret
topics.h: Centuries ago a goldsmith noticed something clever: people who left gold with him rarely all came back for it on the same day.
p: Commercial banks accept deposits from the public and lend to households and firms. They earn the spread: the difference between the interest rate on loans and the rate paid on deposits.
A bank's balance sheet: assets (reserves with itself and with the RBI, loans given, investments) and liabilities (deposits of the public, borrowings). Net worth = assets − liabilities.

Goldsmith story: people deposited gold for safety and received receipts; the receipts began to circulate as money. Since only a fraction of gold was withdrawn at a time, the goldsmith lent out the rest and earned interest.
This is fractional reserve banking: banks keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves and lend the rest.
By lending and creating new demand deposits, commercial banks create money; deposits are part of money supply.

ex.q: A bank pays 4% interest on deposits and charges 9% on loans. It has deposits of ₹10 crore and loans of ₹8 crore. Find its spread rate and simple annual interest margin (ignoring reserves' returns).
st: Interest earned on loans = 9% of 8 = ₹0.72 crore
Interest paid on deposits = 4% of 10 = ₹0.40 crore

topics.rl: When you deposit ₹10,000 in a savings account at a public sector bank, the bank keeps a part as reserves and lends much of the rest as home or business loans.

rv.summary: Commercial banks accept deposits and lend, earning the spread between loan and deposit rates. Like the goldsmiths, they keep only a fraction of deposits as reserves and, by lending, create money.
focus: Read a bank's balance sheet
Compute spread and net worth
Explain fractional reserve banking
remember: Deposits are liabilities; loans and reserves are assets
Net worth = assets − liabilities
Spread = lending rate − deposit rate
traps: Don't call deposits assets of the bank
Banks earn from the spread, not from printing money
Lending creates deposits, which are money

topics.t: Credit creation and the money multiplier
topics.h: Deposit ₹1,000 in a bank, and with a 10% reserve ratio the banking system can turn it into ₹10,000 of deposits. Magic? No, arithmetic.
p: With reserve ratio r, a bank keeps r of each new deposit as reserves and lends the rest. The loan is spent and redeposited, and the process repeats round after round.
Money multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio. With r = 20%, the multiplier is 1/0.2 = 5.
Total deposits created = initial deposit × money multiplier. Credit (loans) created = total deposits − initial deposit, since the initial deposit itself is kept as reserves in the end.
High powered money (reserve money) H = currency held by the public + reserves of banks (vault cash and deposits with the RBI). Money supply = money multiplier × H.
Limits: the reserve requirement, and leakages such as people holding cash instead of redepositing. A higher reserve ratio lowers the multiplier and the money supply.

ex.q: An initial deposit is ₹1,000 and the reserve ratio is 10%. Show the first two rounds and find total deposits and total credit created.

topics.rl: When the RBI cuts the CRR, banks such as SBI and HDFC can lend more out of each deposit, which raises the money multiplier.

rv.summary: With reserve ratio r, money multiplier = 1/r, and total deposits = initial deposit × multiplier. Money supply = multiplier × high powered money (currency with public + bank reserves).
focus: Compute multiplier, total deposits and credit created
Find the reserve ratio from given totals
Explain limits on credit creation
remember: Money multiplier = 1/r
Total deposits = initial deposit × 1/r
Credit created = total deposits − initial deposit
H = CU + R; money supply = multiplier × H
traps: A higher reserve ratio lowers the multiplier
Credit created excludes the initial deposit
Cash held by the public is a leakage

topics.t: Quantitative tools: CRR, SLR, repo and OMO
topics.h: Every two months, crores of rupees of home and car loans become cheaper or costlier depending on one number the RBI announces: the repo rate.
p: Quantitative instruments affect the total volume of credit; qualitative (selective) instruments affect its direction and use.

Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): the fraction of deposits banks must keep as cash reserves with the RBI. Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): the fraction of deposits banks must keep in liquid assets such as cash, gold and approved government securities.

Bank rate: the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks. Repo rate: the rate at which the RBI lends short-term to banks against government securities, with an agreement to repurchase them. Reverse repo rate: the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks.
Open market operations (OMO): outright purchase or sale of government securities by the RBI in the market. RBI buying securities injects money; selling absorbs money.
Raising CRR, SLR, bank rate or repo rate, or selling securities, contracts credit; lowering them or buying securities expands credit.

ex.q: To fight high inflation, what should the RBI do with (i) the repo rate and (ii) open market operations?
st: Inflation is a case of excess demand, so credit must be reduced
(i) Raise the repo rate so borrowing becomes costlier
(ii) Sell government securities to absorb money from banks
ex.a: Raise the repo rate and sell government securities

topics.rl: When the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee raises the repo rate, banks usually raise EMIs on loans linked to the repo rate.

rv.summary: Quantitative tools change the volume of credit: CRR, SLR, bank rate, repo and reverse repo rates, and open market operations. Raising rates or ratios or selling securities contracts credit; the opposite expands it.
focus: Define CRR, SLR, repo, reverse repo, bank rate and OMO
Choose tools for inflation or recession
Compute required CRR cash
remember: Repo: RBI lends to banks; reverse repo: RBI borrows from banks
CRR: cash with RBI; SLR: liquid assets kept by banks
RBI buys securities → money supply rises; sells → falls
traps: Don't swap repo and reverse repo
Selling securities reduces money supply
SLR assets are kept by banks, not with the RBI

topics.t: Qualitative tools, using the toolkit and sterilisation
topics.h: Sometimes the RBI doesn't change any rate at all. It simply 'requests' banks to go slow on certain loans, and they listen.
p: Margin requirement: the part of a security's value that a borrower must pay from own funds (loan = value − margin). Raising the margin reduces the loan available against that security.
Moral suasion: persuasion, requests and advice by the RBI to banks to follow its policy, e.g. to restrict or expand credit to certain sectors.
Excess demand (inflation): raise repo rate, bank rate, CRR, SLR and margin requirements; sell securities; use moral suasion to restrict credit.
Deficient demand (recession): lower repo rate, bank rate, CRR, SLR and margins; buy securities; encourage banks to lend.

Sterilisation: when large foreign capital inflows raise money supply (because the RBI buys foreign exchange), the RBI sells government securities to absorb the extra money and protect the economy from inflation.

ex.q: A borrower pledges shares worth ₹1,00,000 and the margin requirement is 40%. How much loan can he get? What happens if the margin rises to 60%?

topics.rl: When foreign portfolio investors pour dollars into Indian markets, the RBI buys dollars to steady the rupee and may sterilise the extra rupees by selling bonds.

rv.summary: Qualitative tools such as margin requirements and moral suasion steer credit to or away from uses. The RBI tightens all tools against inflation, loosens them in a recession, and sterilises large forex inflows by selling securities.
focus: Compute loans under margin requirements
Choose the right package for excess or deficient demand
Explain sterilisation
remember: Loan = value × (1 − margin)
Inflation: raise rates/ratios/margins, sell securities
Recession: lower them, buy securities
Sterilisation: sell securities to absorb money from forex inflows
traps: Sterilisation reduces, not increases, the extra money supply
Margin requirement is qualitative, not quantitative
Higher margin means a smaller loan

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment
topics.t: Ex ante, ex post and aggregate demand
topics.h: A biscuit factory PLANS to add ₹10 lakh to its stock this year. Sales flop and ₹25 lakh piles up. The plan was ex ante; what happened is ex post.
p: Ex ante = planned or intended values; ex post = actual or realised values. They can differ.
Example: a firm plans inventory investment of ₹100 but sales fall short, so actual inventory investment becomes ₹130. Unplanned inventory accumulation = ₹30.
Aggregate demand (AD) = total planned expenditure on final goods and services: C + I + G + (X − M). In the two-sector model, AD = C + I.
Investment is the addition to the stock of physical capital (machines, buildings) and to inventories. In the simple model investment is autonomous: I = Ī (fixed, not dependent on income).
Income determination is based on ex ante (planned) values, because plans decide how much people want to buy.

ex.q: A firm planned an inventory addition of ₹50 lakh. It produced goods worth ₹500 lakh, planned to sell ₹450 lakh, but sold only ₹420 lakh. Find ex post inventory investment and the unplanned part.
st: Actual (ex post) inventory change = production − sales = 500 − 420 = 80

topics.rl: Before Diwali, retailers in India plan large stocks (ex ante). Whether the festive season is strong decides the ex post stock left over in January.

rv.summary: Ex ante means planned and ex post means actual; the difference shows up as unplanned inventory change. Aggregate demand is total planned spending, C + I in two sectors, with investment taken as autonomous.
focus: Distinguish ex ante and ex post values
Compute unplanned inventory changes
List the components of AD
remember: AD = C + I + G + (X − M); two-sector AD = C + I
Unplanned inventory change = actual − planned
Autonomous investment I = Ī, independent of income
traps: Buying shares or an old house is not investment
Ex post S = I is an identity, not the equilibrium condition
Depreciation and taxes are not parts of AD

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment
topics.t: Consumption function, MPC and APC
topics.h: Even a family with zero income must eat. That minimum spending, borrowed or from savings, is autonomous consumption.
p: Consumption function: C = C̄ + cY. C̄ is autonomous consumption (spending even at zero income); cY is induced consumption, which depends on income.
Marginal propensity to consume (MPC) c = ΔC / ΔY: the share of extra income spent on consumption. 0 < MPC < 1 (MPC = 0 or 1 are extreme limits).
Average propensity to consume (APC) = C / Y: the share of total income consumed.
At low income APC can be greater than 1 (consumption exceeds income because of C̄). APC falls as income rises.

ex.q: Given C = 50 + 0.75Y, find C, APC and MPC when Y = 400.

topics.rl: When the Centre cuts income tax, economists ask how much of the extra take-home pay Indian families will spend: that is the MPC.

rv.summary: The consumption function C = C̄ + cY splits spending into autonomous C̄ and induced cY. MPC = ΔC/ΔY lies between 0 and 1, while APC = C/Y falls as income rises and can exceed 1 at low income.
focus: Compute C, APC and MPC from a consumption function
Explain why APC falls with income
remember: C = C̄ + cY
MPC = ΔC/ΔY, 0 < MPC < 1
APC = C/Y = C̄/Y + c
traps: APC can be greater than 1; MPC cannot
MPC is the slope, not C/Y
ΔC = MPC × ΔY, not MPC × Y

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment
topics.t: Saving function, MPS and APS
topics.h: Every rupee of income has only two destinies in this model: you spend it or you save it. So MPC + MPS must equal one.
p: Saving = income − consumption. From C = C̄ + cY, the saving function is S = −C̄ + (1 − c)Y.
Marginal propensity to save (MPS) s = ΔS/ΔY = 1 − c. Average propensity to save (APS) = S/Y.
Since ΔC + ΔS = ΔY, MPC + MPS = 1. Since C + S = Y, APC + APS = 1.
At low incomes saving is negative (dissaving), so APS can be negative while APC exceeds 1.
Break-even income: the level of Y at which C = Y and S = 0. For C = C̄ + cY, it is Y = C̄/(1 − c).

ex.q: Given C = 60 + 0.8Y, write the saving function and find S and APS at Y = 500. Also find the break-even income.

topics.rl: Household saving is the biggest source of India's investment funds, which is why policy-makers watch the MPS closely.

rv.summary: The saving function is S = −C̄ + (1 − c)Y, with MPS = 1 − MPC and APS = S/Y. MPC + MPS = 1 and APC + APS = 1, and break-even income is where S = 0.
focus: Derive the saving function
Compute APS, MPS and break-even income
Explain negative APS
remember: MPC + MPS = 1; APC + APS = 1
Break-even: S = 0, Y = C̄/(1 − c)
traps: MPC + MPS is exactly 1, never more
APS can be negative; MPS stays positive
Keep the minus sign on C̄ in the saving function

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment
topics.t: Equilibrium: AD = AS and S = I
topics.h: If shoppers plan to buy more than factories produce, shelves empty. If they plan to buy less, warehouses fill. Equilibrium is where plans match output.
p: Aggregate supply (AS) is the total output (and income) Y in the economy. Equilibrium income is where planned AD = AS.
In the two-sector model AD = C̄ + Ī + cY = Ā + cY, where Ā = C̄ + Ī is autonomous expenditure. Equilibrium: Y = Ā + cY.
Saving-investment approach: equilibrium is where planned saving = planned investment (S = I).
If AD > output, inventories fall unexpectedly (unplanned decumulation) and firms raise output. If AD < output, inventories pile up (unplanned accumulation) and firms cut output.
With a government that taxes T, consumption depends on disposable income: C = C̄ + c(Y − T).

ex.q: C̄ = 40, c = 0.8, Ī = 60. Output is 400. Is the economy in equilibrium? What will happen?
st: Unplanned inventory fall of 20; firms raise output
ex.a: Not in equilibrium; output will rise towards 500

topics.rl: When sales of two-wheelers beat expectations after a good monsoon, dealers' stocks fall and companies raise production: AD > AS pushing output up.

rv.summary: Equilibrium income is where planned AD = AS, or planned saving = planned investment. If AD exceeds output, inventories fall and output rises; if AD is below output, inventories pile up and output falls.
focus: Compute AD at a given output
Predict output changes when AD ≠ AS
Use C = C̄ + c(Y − T) with taxes
remember: AD = Ā + cY, Ā = C̄ + Ī
Equilibrium: AD = AS ⇔ planned S = planned I
AD > Y → output rises; AD < Y → output falls
traps: Use planned, not actual, values for equilibrium
With taxes, consume out of Y − T
I > S means income rises, not falls

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment
topics.t: Short-run equilibrium: the 45° line and algebra
topics.h: Draw one 45° line and one AD line on a graph, and the point where they cross tells you the income of a whole nation. That's the Keynesian cross.
p: Short-run assumption: the price level is fixed. This is reasonable when there is unused capacity and unemployment, so firms can raise output without raising prices.
Graph (described in words): income Y on the horizontal axis, expenditure on the vertical axis. The 45° line from the origin shows all points where expenditure = income; it represents AS.
The consumption line starts at C̄ on the vertical axis with slope c. The investment line is horizontal at Ī. Adding them vertically gives the AD line, starting at Ā = C̄ + Ī with slope c.
Equilibrium is where the AD line cuts the 45° line. Algebra: Y = Ā + cY, so Y* = Ā / (1 − c) = (C̄ + Ī) / (1 − c).
To test whether a given income is in equilibrium, compare AD at that income with the income itself.

ex.q: C̄ = 100, Ī = 50, c = 0.8. Find equilibrium income, and the consumption and saving at equilibrium.

topics.rl: In 2020-21, idle capacity in Indian factories meant that more demand could raise output without much inflation, the fixed-price case Keynes described.

rv.summary: With fixed prices in the short run, equilibrium is where the AD line (intercept Ā, slope c) cuts the 45° line. Algebraically Y* = Ā/(1 − c).
focus: Compute equilibrium income
Test whether a given income is equilibrium
Describe the 45° line diagram
remember: 45° line: expenditure = income (AS)
Fixed prices: valid with unused capacity
traps: Divide by MPS (1 − c), not by MPC
The AD intercept is C̄ + Ī, not c
Compare AD at the given income with that income

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment
topics.t: Shifts of AD: autonomous and parametric
topics.h: When the government announces a mega highway plan, the AD line jumps up. When people decide to spend a bigger share of every extra rupee, it tilts. Same graph, two very different moves.
p: A change in autonomous expenditure (C̄ or Ī) shifts the AD line parallel: up if Ā rises, down if it falls. The slope (c) does not change.
A parallel upward shift raises equilibrium income by more than the shift itself, through the multiplier.
A parametric shift is a change in a parameter of the function. A change in the MPC (c) changes the slope: the AD line swings (rotates) around its intercept Ā.
Higher c → steeper AD line → higher equilibrium income. Lower c → flatter AD line → lower equilibrium income.
A change in the intercept (C̄ or Ī) with the same c is also a parametric shift of the intercept, giving a parallel movement.

ex.q: Ā = 100 and c rises from 0.75 to 0.8. Describe the AD shift and find the new equilibrium income.
st: Change in c changes the slope: AD swings upward around Ā = 100
ex.a: AD becomes steeper; Y* rises from 400 to 500

topics.rl: A surge of private investment in renewable energy (higher Ī) shifts India's AD line up in parallel; a festive mood that makes families spend more of each extra rupee would tilt it.

rv.summary: A change in autonomous spending shifts AD parallel and changes income by a multiple of the change. A change in MPC changes the slope, swinging AD around its intercept.
focus: Tell parallel shifts from swings of AD
Compute the change in equilibrium income
remember: ΔY = ΔĀ/(1 − c)
Higher MPC → steeper AD → higher Y*
Higher MPS → flatter AD
traps: A change in MPC is not a parallel shift
ΔY is bigger than ΔĀ, not equal to it
Higher MPS lowers, not raises, the slope

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment
topics.t: The investment multiplier
topics.h: ₹100 crore spent on building a metro line becomes wages, which become spending at shops, which become more wages... The final rise in income can be several times ₹100 crore.
p: Investment multiplier k = ΔY / ΔI = 1 / (1 − MPC) = 1 / MPS.
Mechanism: an extra investment ΔI first raises income by ΔI. People spend c·ΔI, which becomes someone's income; they spend c²·ΔI, and so on.
Total ΔY = ΔI(1 + c + c² + c³ + ...) = ΔI / (1 − c), the sum of a geometric series with ratio c (0 < c < 1).
The larger the MPC (smaller the MPS), the larger the multiplier. Limits: k = 1 when MPC = 0; k → ∞ when MPC → 1.
ΔC = c·ΔY and ΔS = ΔI at the new equilibrium (saving rises to match the new investment).

ex.q: MPC = 0.8 and investment rises by ₹100 crore. Find the multiplier, rise in income, rise in consumption and rise in saving.

topics.rl: Government capital spending on roads and railways is defended partly by the multiplier: each rupee can raise total income by more than a rupee.

rv.summary: The investment multiplier k = ΔY/ΔI = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS works through rounds of induced consumption. A larger MPC gives a larger multiplier.
focus: Compute k, ΔY, ΔC and ΔS
Explain the multiplier process
remember: k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS
ΔY = k × ΔI; ΔC = MPC × ΔY; ΔS = ΔI
k = 1 when MPC = 0
traps: Don't use k = 1/MPC
The multiplier works through spending rounds, not printing money

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment
topics.t: Effective demand, full employment and the paradox of thrift
topics.h: Saving is good for a family. But if every family in India suddenly saves more, the nation's income could fall and total saving might not rise at all. Welcome to the paradox of thrift.
p: Full employment level of income: the output at which all who are willing and able to work at the prevailing wage are employed.
Involuntary unemployment: people willing to work at the going wage rate cannot find work.
Principle of effective demand: when prices are fixed, equilibrium output is decided by the level of AD. This equilibrium may be below full employment.
Paradox of thrift: if all people raise the proportion of income they save (MPS rises), total saving in the economy does not rise; it remains unchanged or falls, while income falls.
Reason: with investment autonomous, equilibrium needs S = Ī. A higher MPS lowers AD and income until total saving again equals the unchanged investment.

ex.q: C̄ = 40, Ī = 60, MPC falls from 0.8 to 0.75 (MPS rises from 0.2 to 0.25). Show the paradox of thrift.
st: Income falls by 100, total saving stays 60
ex.a: Income falls from 500 to 400; total saving unchanged at 60

topics.rl: During uncertain times, if all households cut spending to save more, businesses from Surat textile units to Delhi restaurants may see sales fall, lowering incomes for everyone.

rv.summary: By the principle of effective demand, output is set by AD and can settle below full employment with involuntary unemployment. In the paradox of thrift, a rise in everyone's MPS lowers income while total saving stays unchanged or falls.
focus: Define full employment and involuntary unemployment
Show the paradox of thrift numerically
remember: Full employment: all willing and able at the prevailing wage are employed
Equilibrium need not be at full employment
Paradox of thrift: higher MPS → lower Y, saving = Ī unchanged
traps: Equilibrium is not always full employment
Saving more as a whole does not raise total saving
Voluntary idleness is not involuntary unemployment

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Determination of Income and Employment
topics.t: Excess demand, deficient demand and their remedies
topics.h: Too little demand empties factories; too much demand empties wallets through inflation. Policy-makers try to keep AD just right at full employment.
p: Deficient demand: AD is less than the AD needed for full-employment output. The shortfall at full employment is the deflationary gap. Effects: unsold stock, falling output and employment, possible fall in prices.

Excess demand: AD is more than the AD needed for full-employment output. The excess at full employment is the inflationary gap. Effects: prices rise without any rise in output, since resources are fully used.
Fiscal remedies: for deficient demand, raise government spending and cut taxes; for excess demand, cut government spending and raise taxes.
Monetary remedies: for deficient demand, lower repo/bank rate, CRR and SLR, buy securities, lower margins; for excess demand, do the opposite.

Graph in words: draw the AD line and the 45° line. At the full-employment output Y_F, the vertical gap between the 45° line and a lower AD line is the deflationary gap; the gap above it to a higher AD line is the inflationary gap.

ex.q: Full-employment output is ₹1,000 crore. AD at full employment is ₹920 crore. Identify the situation and gap, and suggest one fiscal and one monetary measure.
st: AD (920) < AS at full employment (1,000) → deficient demand
Fiscal: raise government spending; monetary: cut repo rate
ex.a: Deficient demand with a deflationary gap of ₹80 crore

topics.rl: During the 2020 slowdown, the Indian government raised capital spending and the RBI cut the repo rate: remedies for deficient demand.

rv.summary: Deficient demand (deflationary gap) cuts output and jobs; excess demand (inflationary gap) raises prices at full employment. Fiscal and monetary tools raise AD in the first case and reduce it in the second.
focus: Measure inflationary and deflationary gaps
Choose fiscal and monetary remedies
Diagnose the situation from Y* and Y_F
remember: Inflationary gap = AD at Y_F − Y_F; deflationary gap = Y_F − AD at Y_F
Deficient demand: raise G, cut taxes, cut repo/CRR, buy securities
Excess demand: cut G, raise taxes, raise repo/CRR, sell securities
traps: Cutting repo worsens excess demand
Excess demand raises prices, not output, at full employment
Raising taxes is a cure for excess, not deficient, demand

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Government Budget and the Economy
topics.t: The budget and the allocation function
topics.h: Nobody sells tickets to street lights or national defence. If the market won't provide them, who will? Enter the government budget.
p: The government budget is an annual financial statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for a financial year (1 April to 31 March). Article 112 of the Constitution calls it the 'Annual Financial Statement'.
Allocation function: the government provides public goods that the market fails to supply in enough quantity, such as defence, roads, street lighting and public administration.
Public goods are non-rivalrous (one person's use does not reduce another's) and non-excludable (people who do not pay cannot easily be kept out).
Free-rider problem: since non-payers cannot be excluded, people avoid paying, so private firms cannot collect enough revenue. Hence the government provides public goods, financed by taxes.
Private goods (food, clothes, cars) are rivalrous and excludable and are supplied through markets.

ex.q: Classify as public or private goods: (i) a lighthouse; (ii) a pizza; (iii) national defence; (iv) a seat in a cinema hall.
st: Ask: is it non-rivalrous and non-excludable?
Lighthouse: ships cannot be kept from seeing it, and one ship's use doesn't reduce another's → public
Defence: protects everyone at once → public
Pizza and a cinema seat: one person's use excludes another's, and non-payers can be kept out → private

topics.rl: Every February, the Union Finance Minister presents the Union Budget in Parliament, setting out how much will be spent on defence, railways, health and more.

rv.summary: The budget is the government's annual statement of estimated receipts and expenditure (Article 112). Its allocation function provides public goods, which markets underprovide because they are non-rivalrous and non-excludable.
focus: Define the budget and the financial year
Classify public and private goods
Explain the free-rider problem
remember: Budget: 'Annual Financial Statement', Article 112, year 1 April–31 March
Public goods: non-rivalrous and non-excludable
Free-rider problem → government provides public goods
traps: Non-excludable is not the same as non-rivalrous
A cinema seat or bus ticket is a private good
The budget is an estimate, not actual figures

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Government Budget and the Economy
topics.t: Redistribution, stabilisation and the two budget accounts
topics.h: A tax on high incomes funding free school meals, and extra spending on highways during a slowdown: two different jobs done by the same budget.
p: Redistribution function: the government changes the distribution of income through taxes and transfers (pensions, subsidies, scholarships), so that disposable income is fairer.
Stabilisation function: the government uses its spending and taxes to reduce fluctuations in output and employment; raising AD in a slump and lowering it during inflation.
Other objectives: promoting economic growth (e.g. capital spending on infrastructure) and managing public enterprises.
The budget has two parts: the revenue budget (revenue receipts and revenue expenditure) and the capital budget (capital receipts and capital expenditure).
Fiscal policy means the use of government spending and taxation to achieve these objectives.

ex.q: Identify the budget function: (i) old-age pensions for poor elderly; (ii) extra spending on roads in a recession; (iii) building a defence radar system.
st: (i) a transfer to reduce inequality → redistribution
(ii) raising AD to fight a slump → stabilisation

topics.rl: Free foodgrain under the National Food Security Act and PM-KISAN transfers are examples of the redistribution function in India's budget.

rv.summary: Beyond allocation, the budget redistributes income through taxes and transfers, stabilises output and employment, and promotes growth. It has a revenue budget and a capital budget, and using it this way is fiscal policy.
focus: Identify the budget function in an example
Name the two parts of the budget
remember: Functions: allocation, redistribution, stabilisation (and growth)
Two parts: revenue budget and capital budget
Fiscal policy: use of government spending and taxes
traps: Stabilisation can mean cutting spending during inflation
A salary is not a transfer payment
Fiscal policy is not run by the RBI

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Government Budget and the Economy
topics.t: Revenue receipts: taxes and non-tax revenue
topics.h: When you pay GST on a cricket bat and your parent pays income tax, both rupees land in the same place: the government's revenue receipts.
p: Revenue receipts are receipts that neither create a liability nor reduce an asset of the government. They are non-redeemable.
Tax revenue: direct taxes are paid by the person on whom they are imposed (personal income tax, corporation tax); indirect taxes can be shifted to others (GST, customs duties, excise duties).
Progressive taxation: tax rate rises as income rises. It reduces inequality and supports the redistribution function.

Non-tax revenue: interest on loans given by the government, dividends and profits from public sector undertakings, fees, fines, and grants received from foreign governments and international organisations.
GST (introduced on 1 July 2017) replaced many indirect taxes of the Centre and States.

ex.q: Classify: (i) corporation tax; (ii) GST on a mobile phone; (iii) dividends from a PSU; (iv) a passport fee.
st: (i) paid by companies on their profits, cannot be shifted → direct tax
(ii) collected from buyers through prices → indirect tax
(iii) earnings from government investment → non-tax revenue
(iv) payment for a service → non-tax revenue (fee)
ex.a: (i) direct tax, (ii) indirect tax, (iii) and (iv) non-tax revenue

topics.rl: Profits that the RBI and PSUs such as Coal India pass to the Centre form a large part of non-tax revenue.

rv.summary: Revenue receipts neither create liabilities nor reduce assets. They are tax revenue (direct taxes like income and corporation tax; indirect taxes like GST and customs) and non-tax revenue (interest, dividends, fees, fines, grants).
focus: Classify direct and indirect taxes
Identify non-tax revenue items
Explain progressive taxation
remember: Revenue receipt: no liability, no reduction in assets
Direct: income tax, corporation tax; indirect: GST, customs, excise
Non-tax: interest, dividends, fees, fines, grants
GST from 1 July 2017
traps: Interest received is revenue, not capital
Grants received are revenue receipts
Borrowings and disinvestment are not revenue receipts

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Government Budget and the Economy
topics.t: Revenue expenditure vs capital expenditure
topics.h: Paying a teacher's salary keeps a school running this year. Building a new school building gives the country an asset for decades. The budget books them very differently.
p: Revenue expenditure neither creates assets nor reduces liabilities of the government: salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, and grants to state governments (even if the grants are used for creating assets).
Capital expenditure either creates assets or reduces liabilities: building roads, dams and schools, buying machinery and land, buying shares, loans given to states and PSUs, and repayment of loans.
Interest payment on debt is revenue expenditure, but repayment of the loan principal is capital expenditure.
Capital expenditure raises the economy's productive capacity; revenue expenditure maintains the normal functioning of government.

ex.q: Classify: (i) interest paid on public debt; (ii) repayment of a ₹1,000 crore loan; (iii) building a metro line; (iv) fertiliser subsidy.
st: (i) no asset, no reduction in liability → revenue expenditure
ex.a: (i) and (iv) revenue expenditure; (ii) and (iii) capital expenditure

topics.rl: The Union Budget's big push for capital expenditure on highways, railways and ports is meant to build assets that raise future growth.

rv.summary: Capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities (roads, shares, loans given, loan repayment); revenue expenditure does neither (salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies, grants to states).
focus: Classify spending items with the asset/liability test
Separate interest from loan repayment
remember: Capital expenditure: creates assets or reduces liabilities
Interest payment: revenue; repayment of principal: capital
Grants to states: revenue expenditure
traps: Grants to states are revenue even if used for assets
Subsidies are revenue expenditure
Loans given to states are capital expenditure

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Government Budget and the Economy
topics.t: Capital receipts: debt and non-debt
topics.h: When the government borrows ₹1 lakh crore, it gets cash today but owes it tomorrow. When it sells part of a PSU, it gets cash but owns less. Both are capital receipts.
p: Capital receipts either create a liability or reduce an asset of the government.

Debt-creating capital receipts: borrowings from the public (market loans), from the RBI and banks (treasury bills), loans from foreign governments and international bodies, and small savings such as post office deposits.
Non-debt-creating capital receipts: recovery of loans given earlier, and disinvestment proceeds (sale of shares in public sector undertakings).
Classification test: (1) Does it create a liability or reduce an asset? Then capital. (2) Neither? Then revenue.
Recovery of a loan is a capital receipt (reduces an asset), but interest on the loan is a revenue receipt.

ex.q: Classify: (i) borrowing ₹500 crore from the market; (ii) ₹200 crore from selling shares of a PSU; (iii) ₹50 crore interest from states; (iv) ₹100 crore loan repaid by a state.
st: (i) creates a liability → debt-creating capital receipt
(ii) reduces an asset → non-debt capital receipt
(iii) no liability, no asset reduction → revenue receipt
(iv) reduces an asset (the claim on the state) → non-debt capital receipt
ex.a: (i) debt capital receipt; (ii) and (iv) non-debt capital receipts; (iii) revenue receipt

topics.rl: Disinvestment, such as selling part of the government's stake in a company like LIC through an IPO, is a non-debt capital receipt.

rv.summary: Capital receipts create a liability or reduce an asset. Borrowings are debt-creating; loan recoveries and disinvestment are non-debt-creating capital receipts.
focus: Classify receipts as revenue, debt or non-debt capital
Compute non-debt capital receipts
remember: Capital receipt: creates liability or reduces asset
Debt-creating: borrowings, treasury bills, foreign loans, small savings
Non-debt: recovery of loans, disinvestment
traps: Disinvestment creates no debt
Interest received is a revenue receipt, but loan recovery is capital
Don't add borrowings into non-debt receipts

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Government Budget and the Economy
topics.t: Revenue, fiscal and primary deficits
topics.h: Each Budget Day, TV anchors quote one number above all: the fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP. Here's how it is calculated.
p: Balanced budget: estimated receipts = expenditure. Surplus budget: receipts > expenditure. Deficit budget: expenditure > receipts.
Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts. It shows government dissaving: borrowing to meet current (consumption) needs.
Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt-creating capital receipts). It equals the government's total borrowing requirement.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments. It shows borrowing needed for current needs apart from paying interest on past debt.
Fiscal deficit can also be written as: revenue deficit + capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts.

ex.q: Revenue receipts = 800, revenue expenditure = 1,000, capital expenditure = 200, non-debt capital receipts = 50, interest payments = 150 (₹ crore). Find RD, FD and PD.
ex.a: RD ₹200 crore; FD ₹350 crore; PD ₹200 crore

topics.rl: Union Budgets set fiscal deficit targets as a percentage of GDP, and rating agencies watch whether the government meets them.

rv.summary: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts; fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts); primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments.
