focus: Compute RD, FD and PD
Interpret what each deficit shows
remember: RD = RE − RR
FD = TE − (RR + non-debt capital receipts) = total borrowing
PD = FD − interest payments
FD = RD + capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts
traps: Don't include borrowings among receipts when computing FD
Zero PD means borrowing only for interest, not no debt
Expenditure > receipts is a deficit, not surplus, budget

topics.ch: Macroeconomics: Government Budget and the Economy
topics.t: Deficits, debt and the FRBM Act
topics.h: Borrowing to pay interest on old borrowing is like using one credit card to pay another. Governments worry about this debt trap too.
p: Fiscal deficit is financed by borrowing (from the public, banks, abroad) or, in deficit financing, by borrowing from the RBI, which creates new money and can be inflationary.
High fiscal deficits raise public debt and future interest payments. Higher interest payments raise revenue expenditure and the revenue deficit, which can lead to a debt trap.
Heavy government borrowing can push up interest rates and crowd out private investment.
The revenue deficit is a part of the fiscal deficit: FD = RD + (capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts). A high share of RD in FD means borrowing is used for consumption, not asset creation.

The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 set rules for fiscal discipline: reduce fiscal and revenue deficits over time (with a fiscal deficit target of 3% of GDP) and improve transparency.

ex.q: FD = 1,000, of which RD = 700 (₹ crore). What share of borrowing is used for current consumption? Is this a good sign?
st: Borrowing for consumption does not create assets to repay debt

topics.rl: When interest payments take a large share of the Centre's revenue receipts, less is left for health and education; this is why fiscal discipline laws like the FRBM Act exist.

rv.summary: Large deficits raise debt and interest burdens, can cause a debt trap, crowd out private investment, and become inflationary if financed by the RBI. The FRBM Act, 2003 set targets to reduce deficits.
focus: Explain the effects of high deficits
Compute the share of RD in FD
Know the FRBM Act's year and aims
remember: FRBM Act: 2003; aim: fiscal discipline
Deficit financing from RBI → new money → inflation
Crowding out: government borrowing reduces private investment
traps: A fiscal deficit is not always harmful if it builds assets
Deficit financing raises, not lowers, prices
RD is a part of FD, not bigger than it in general

topics.t: The open economy and the exchange rate
topics.h: Your phone was assembled in Noida from parts made in Taiwan, paid for in rupees that were swapped for dollars. Welcome to the open economy.
p: An open economy interacts with other countries through three linkages: output markets (trade in goods and services), financial markets (buying and selling of financial assets) and labour markets (workers moving across countries).
Imports are a leakage from the domestic circular flow: spending goes to foreign producers. Exports are an injection: foreign spending on domestic output adds to AD.
The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. In NCERT, e = rupees per unit of foreign currency, e.g. ₹83 per US dollar.
A rise in e means more rupees per dollar: the rupee has lost value. A fall in e means the rupee has gained value.
People accept a currency in international dealings only if they have confidence that it will keep its value.

ex.q: The exchange rate moves from ₹80/$ to ₹84/$. A US tourist has $100. How many more rupees does she get, and what happened to the rupee?
st: She gets ₹400 more; each dollar buys more rupees, so the rupee has lost value

topics.rl: Remittances sent home by Indian workers in the Gulf, foreign investment in Indian startups and the export of basmati rice all link India's economy to the world.

rv.summary: An open economy links with others through output, financial and labour markets; imports are a leakage and exports an injection. The exchange rate e is rupees per unit of foreign currency, and a rise in e means the rupee has lost value.
focus: Name the three linkages with examples
Convert prices using the exchange rate
Interpret a rise or fall in e
remember: Linkages: output, financial, labour markets
e = ₹ per unit of foreign currency
Rise in e: rupee loses value; fall in e: rupee gains value
traps: Imports are a leakage, exports an injection
A higher e means a weaker, not stronger, rupee
Buying foreign shares is a financial, not output, linkage

topics.t: Balance of payments: the current account
topics.h: India imports more goods than it exports, yet its current account deficit is much smaller than its trade deficit. The secret weapons: software exports and remittances.
p: Balance of payments (BoP): a systematic record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world during a year.

Current account records: trade in goods (visibles), trade in services, income flows (compensation of employees, investment income such as interest, profit and dividends) and transfer payments (gifts, remittances, grants).
Balance of trade (BoT) = exports of goods − imports of goods. A positive BoT is a trade surplus; negative is a trade deficit.
Net invisibles = net services (non-factor services like software, tourism, shipping, banking) + net income + net transfers.
Current account balance = balance of trade + net invisibles. Unlike BoT, it includes services, income and transfers.

ex.q: Exports of goods ₹3,000, imports of goods ₹4,200, net services +₹900, net income −₹200, net transfers +₹600 (₹ thousand crore). Find BoT and the current account balance.

topics.rl: India is one of the world's largest receivers of remittances, which appear as transfers in the current account and help offset its large trade deficit.

rv.summary: The BoP records all transactions with the rest of the world in a year. The current account covers goods, services, income and transfers; current account balance = balance of trade + net invisibles.
focus: Compute BoT and current account balance
Classify items as visible or invisible
Place items in the current account
remember: BoT = exports of goods − imports of goods
Net invisibles = net services + net income + net transfers
CA balance = BoT + net invisibles
traps: BoT covers only goods, not services
FDI and borrowings are capital account items
A trade deficit can still give a current account surplus

topics.t: Current account deficit and the capital account
topics.h: When a country spends more abroad than it earns, it must borrow or sell assets. The capital account shows exactly how.
p: Current account surplus: receipts exceed payments; the country is a net lender to the rest of the world. Current account deficit (CAD): the country is a net borrower.
Capital account records transactions in assets: foreign direct investment (FDI), foreign portfolio investment (FII/FPI), external commercial borrowings, and external assistance (aid loans).
Credit (inflow) entries: sale of domestic assets to foreigners and borrowing from abroad. Debit (outflow) entries: purchase of foreign assets and lending abroad.
Capital account surplus: inflows exceed outflows; deficit: outflows exceed inflows.
A CAD is not always alarming: if it finances investment that raises future exports and growth, it can be sustainable; if it finances consumption with short-term borrowing, it is risky.

ex.q: Classify as capital account credit or debit for India: (i) a US firm sets up a factory in Pune; (ii) Tata buys a company in the UK; (iii) an Indian company borrows from a Japanese bank.
st: (i) foreigners buy Indian assets → inflow → credit (FDI)
(ii) Indians buy foreign assets → outflow → debit
(iii) borrowing from abroad → inflow → credit (external borrowing)

topics.rl: Foreign portfolio investors buying Indian shares on the NSE bring capital inflows, which help finance India's current account deficit.

rv.summary: A current account deficit makes a country a net borrower; a surplus makes it a net lender. The capital account records asset transactions such as FDI, portfolio investment, commercial borrowings and external assistance.
focus: Classify capital account credits and debits
Compute capital account balance
Judge when a CAD is a concern
remember: Credit: sale of domestic assets to foreigners, borrowing from abroad
Debit: purchase of foreign assets, lending abroad
CA surplus = net lender; CAD = net borrower
traps: Indians buying foreign assets is a debit
A CAD is not always alarming
Remittances are current, not capital, account

topics.t: The BoP always balances: autonomous, accommodating and reserves
topics.h: Accountants say the balance of payments always balances. Newspapers say India has a BoP surplus. Both are right. Here's how.
p: BoP identity: current account balance + capital account balance (including changes in official reserves) = 0. In this accounting sense the BoP always balances.

Autonomous transactions are undertaken for their own sake, e.g. profit, trade or investment (above the line). Accommodating transactions are made to cover the gap left by autonomous ones (below the line).

Official reserve transactions: the central bank selling or buying foreign exchange. BoP surplus = autonomous receipts exceed autonomous payments, and official reserves rise; BoP deficit = reserves fall.
Errors and omissions: a balancing item for transactions that could not be recorded correctly.

BPM6 (IMF's sixth manual) presents the BoP as a current account, a capital account (capital transfers, non-produced non-financial assets) and a financial account (FDI, portfolio investment, other investment and reserve assets).

ex.q: Current account deficit = 40, capital account surplus (excluding reserves) = 55 ($ billion). What happens to official reserves? Is there a BoP surplus or deficit?
st: A surplus of 15 is added to official reserves
BoP surplus of $15 billion; reserves rise by 15
ex.a: BoP surplus of $15 billion; reserves rise by $15 billion

topics.rl: When the RBI's forex reserves climb to record levels, it usually means India's autonomous inflows exceeded autonomous outflows: a BoP surplus.

rv.summary: In accounting terms the BoP always balances, because gaps in autonomous transactions are filled by accommodating ones such as official reserve changes. A BoP surplus raises reserves and a deficit lowers them.
focus: Separate autonomous and accommodating transactions
Compute the change in reserves
Know BPM6's financial account
remember: BoP surplus → reserves rise; deficit → reserves fall
Errors and omissions: balancing item
BPM6: current, capital and financial accounts
traps: Rising reserves signal a surplus, not a deficit
Trade and remittances are autonomous, not accommodating
FDI is in the financial account under BPM6

topics.t: The foreign exchange market: demand and supply
topics.h: Every time an Indian student pays fees to a US university, someone in the forex market is buying dollars. Every time an Infosys client pays in dollars, someone is selling them.
p: The foreign exchange market is the market where national currencies are traded for one another. Participants: commercial banks, foreign exchange brokers, other authorised dealers and the central bank (RBI).
Demand for foreign exchange (say dollars) arises from: imports, travel and education abroad, gifts and remittances sent abroad, and purchase of foreign assets (investment abroad), plus speculation.
The demand curve for dollars slopes downward: when e (₹ per $) rises, imports become costlier in rupees, so fewer dollars are demanded.
Supply of foreign exchange comes from: exports, spending by foreign tourists, remittances from abroad, and foreign investment in India.
The supply curve slopes upward: when e rises, Indian goods become cheaper for foreigners, exports rise and more dollars are supplied.

ex.q: At ₹80/$ a $500 US textbook costs an Indian student ₹40,000. At ₹85/$ what does it cost, and how does this explain the slope of the demand curve?
st: The import is costlier in rupees
So fewer such imports (and dollars) are demanded at a higher e → downward slope
ex.a: ₹42,500; higher e reduces quantity of dollars demanded

topics.rl: During the IPL season, foreign broadcasters' payments and tourists add to the supply of dollars, while Indian fans travelling abroad for the T20 World Cup add to the demand.

rv.summary: In the forex market, demand for dollars comes from imports, travel, remittances out and investment abroad, and slopes downward; supply comes from exports, tourists, remittances in and foreign investment, and slopes upward.
focus: List sources of demand and supply of forex
Explain the slopes of the curves
Compute rupee costs at different rates
remember: Demand: imports, travel abroad, remittances out, investment abroad
Supply: exports, foreign tourists, remittances in, foreign investment
Higher e → imports dearer (less demand), exports cheaper (more supply)
traps: Indians buying foreign assets demand, not supply, forex
Foreign tourists in India supply forex
Higher e makes imports costlier, not cheaper

topics.t: Flexible exchange rates: depreciation and appreciation
topics.h: Headlines scream 'Rupee hits record low!' Nobody in the government decided that. Millions of buyers and sellers of dollars did.
p: Under a flexible (floating) exchange rate, e is determined by the market demand and supply of foreign exchange, without central bank intervention. Equilibrium e is where demand = supply.
Depreciation: a market-driven rise in e, so the domestic currency loses value (₹80/$ → ₹85/$). Appreciation: a market-driven fall in e, so the domestic currency gains value.

Rise in demand for dollars (e.g. more imports) shifts the demand curve right → e rises → rupee depreciates. Rise in supply of dollars (e.g. more exports or FDI) shifts supply right → e falls → rupee appreciates.
Speculation: if people expect the dollar to rise tomorrow, they buy dollars today, raising demand and e now.
Interest rates and income: higher interest rates in India attract capital inflows and appreciate the rupee; a rise in Indian income raises imports and the demand for dollars, depreciating the rupee.

ex.q: The rupee moves from ₹80/$ to ₹84/$ in a flexible system. Name this, find the % change in e and say who gains.
st: e rose because of market forces → depreciation of the rupee
Exporters gain (each dollar earns more rupees); importers lose

topics.rl: When foreign portfolio investors pull money out of Indian markets, the demand for dollars jumps and the rupee usually depreciates.

rv.summary: Under a flexible rate, e is set by forex demand and supply. A market rise in e is depreciation and a fall is appreciation; more imports depreciate the rupee, while more exports, FDI or higher interest rates appreciate it.
focus: Predict depreciation or appreciation from a shock
Compute % change in e
Say who gains from depreciation
remember: Depreciation: market rise in e; appreciation: market fall in e
Higher domestic interest rates → capital inflow → appreciation
Higher domestic income → more imports → depreciation
traps: Depreciation is not devaluation
A rise in income depreciates, not appreciates, the rupee
Exporters gain, importers lose from depreciation

topics.t: PPP, real exchange rates and the gold standard
topics.h: If a burger costs ₹400 in Mumbai and $5 in New York, what 'should' the rupee-dollar rate be? Purchasing power parity has an answer.
p: Purchasing power parity (PPP): in the long run, exchange rates move so that the same basket of goods costs the same in both countries. e = P / P_f (domestic price ÷ foreign price).
If Indian inflation is higher than US inflation, PPP predicts the rupee will depreciate in the long run.
Nominal exchange rate e = rupees per dollar. Real exchange rate = e × P_f / P: the relative price of foreign goods in terms of domestic goods. If PPP holds, the real exchange rate = 1.
Gold standard (roughly 1870s–1914): each currency was convertible into gold at a fixed price, so exchange rates were fixed by gold content.
Adjustment under the gold standard (price-specie-flow mechanism): a BoP deficit → gold flows out → money supply and prices fall → exports become cheaper and imports costlier → deficit corrects.

ex.q: A basket costs ₹4,000 in India and $50 in the USA. Find the PPP exchange rate. If the actual rate is ₹80/$, what is the real exchange rate?
st: Real exchange rate = e × P_f / P = 80 × 50 / 4,000

topics.rl: International bodies compare GDP of India and China at PPP, because ₹100 buys much more in Lucknow than its dollar value buys in London.

rv.summary: PPP says that in the long run e = P/P_f, so higher domestic inflation depreciates the currency. The real exchange rate is e × P_f/P, which equals 1 under PPP. Under the gold standard rates were fixed and gold flows corrected imbalances.
focus: Compute the PPP exchange rate
Compute and interpret the real exchange rate
Explain the price-specie-flow mechanism
remember: PPP: e = P/P_f
Real exchange rate = e × P_f / P (= 1 under PPP)
Gold standard: fixed rates by gold content; deficit → gold outflow → prices fall
traps: Higher home inflation depreciates, not appreciates, the rupee
Don't write the real exchange rate as P/P_f
Gold standard rates were fixed, not floating

topics.t: Fixed exchange rates: devaluation and intervention
topics.h: In July 1991, the Indian government deliberately made the rupee cheaper in two steps. That was devaluation, not depreciation. The difference matters in exams!
p: Under a fixed (pegged) exchange rate, the government or central bank fixes e at an official level.
Devaluation: the government raises e (makes the domestic currency cheaper) under a fixed system. Revaluation: the government lowers e (makes it dearer).
Devaluation vs depreciation: devaluation is a deliberate official act under a fixed system; depreciation is a market-driven fall in value under a flexible system.

To hold the peg when demand for dollars exceeds supply at the fixed rate, the central bank sells dollars from its reserves; when supply exceeds demand, it buys. If reserves run out, the peg breaks, and controls may create a black market.

Merits of fixed rates: stability and certainty for trade. Demerits: large reserves needed, loss of monetary independence, risk of speculative attacks. The Bretton Woods system (1944–1971) had fixed but adjustable rates with the US dollar convertible into gold.

ex.q: The official rate is ₹80/$. At this rate, demand for dollars is $120 million and supply $100 million. What must the RBI do to hold the peg?
st: RBI sells $20 million from its reserves at ₹80/$

topics.rl: The Bretton Woods conference of 1944 created the IMF and the World Bank, and set up the fixed-but-adjustable exchange rate system that lasted until 1971.

rv.summary: Under a fixed exchange rate, the government sets e and the central bank defends it with reserves. Devaluation (official rise in e) and revaluation (official fall) differ from market-driven depreciation and appreciation.
focus: Distinguish devaluation, revaluation, depreciation, appreciation
Compute intervention needed to hold a peg
List merits and demerits of fixed rates
remember: Devaluation: official rise in e under a fixed system
Excess demand at the peg → central bank sells dollars
Bretton Woods: 1944–1971
traps: Depreciation is not a government decision
Fixed rates need large reserves
Revaluation raises, not lowers, the currency's value

topics.t: Flexible vs managed floating and the open economy multiplier
topics.h: India's rupee is neither fully fixed nor fully free. The RBI lets it float but steps in to calm wild swings. That's a managed float.
p: Merits of flexible rates: automatic adjustment of BoP imbalances through exchange rate changes, no need for large reserves, and freedom for the central bank to use monetary policy for domestic goals.
Demerits of flexible rates: uncertainty and volatility in exchange rates can hurt trade and investment, and speculation can cause wide swings.
Managed floating (dirty floating): the exchange rate is mainly market-determined, but the central bank intervenes by buying or selling foreign exchange to smooth sharp movements. India follows this.

Open economy multiplier: with imports M = M̄ + mY (m = marginal propensity to import), ΔY/ΔĀ = 1 / (1 − c + m). It is smaller than the closed economy multiplier 1/(1 − c) because imports are a leakage.
Net exports NX = X − M̄ − mY. A rise in domestic income raises imports and lowers net exports.

ex.q: c = 0.8 and m = 0.3. Find the open economy multiplier and compare it with the closed economy multiplier. If autonomous spending rises by 100, how much do income and imports rise?

topics.rl: When the rupee swings sharply, the RBI often sells or buys dollars to calm the market, a classic managed float.

rv.summary: Flexible rates adjust BoP automatically but are volatile; India follows managed floating with RBI intervention. In an open economy the multiplier is 1/(1 − c + m), smaller than 1/(1 − c), because imports leak out.
focus: Compare flexible, fixed and managed floating systems
Compute the open economy multiplier
Explain why higher income lowers net exports
remember: Managed floating: market rate with RBI smoothing
Open economy multiplier = 1/(1 − c + m)
NX = X − M̄ − mY
traps: The open economy multiplier is smaller, not larger
Higher income lowers net exports
Large reserves are a need of fixed, not flexible, rates

topics.ch: IED: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
topics.t: Colonial rule and a stagnant economy
topics.h: Dhaka's muslin was so fine that legends claimed a whole length could pass through a finger ring. By 1947, India's famed handicrafts had faded and incomes barely grew. What happened?
p: Before colonial rule, India had an independent economy with agriculture plus a strong handicraft base: cotton and silk textiles (such as the fine muslin or malmal of Dhaka), metal work and precious-stone work, famous worldwide.
The colonial government's economic policies aimed to make India a supplier of raw materials for Britain's growing industries and a market for British manufactured goods, not to develop India.
In the first half of the twentieth century, India's aggregate real output grew at less than 2% a year and per capita output at only about 0.5% a year.

The British made no serious attempt to measure India's national income. Individual estimates were made by Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao and R.C. Desai; V.K.R.V. Rao's estimates are considered especially significant.

ex.q: Output grew at about 2% a year and per capita output at about 0.5% a year. Roughly how fast was population growing?
st: Per capita growth ≈ output growth − population growth

topics.rl: Today the Geographical Indication tag protects crafts like Banarasi silk, a reminder of the handicraft strength India had before colonial rule.

rv.summary: Before colonial rule India had agriculture and world-famous handicrafts. Colonial policies made India a raw-material supplier and a market for British goods, so output grew under 2% and per capita output only about 0.5% a year.
focus: State the aim of colonial economic policy
Know the growth figures of the early 20th century
Name the colonial-era national income estimators
remember: Aggregate output growth < 2%; per capita ≈ 0.5% a year
Estimators: Naoroji, Digby, Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao (most significant), R.C. Desai
Dhaka muslin (malmal) was world famous
traps: India was not only agricultural before colonial rule
Amartya Sen was not a colonial-era estimator
Don't swap the 2% (output) and 0.5% (per capita) figures

topics.ch: IED: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
topics.t: Agriculture under colonial rule
topics.h: In colonial Bengal, a farmer could toil all year and still lose his land if the zamindar missed a revenue deadline. No wonder farm output stagnated.
p: India's economy was basically agrarian: about 85% of the population lived in villages and depended directly or indirectly on agriculture.
Agriculture stagnated with low productivity, even though the area under cultivation expanded.

Land settlement systems, especially zamindari in the Bengal Presidency, meant profits went to zamindars, not cultivators. Zamindars collected high rents and did little to improve land; strict revenue deadlines made them squeeze tenants.
Other causes: low technology, lack of irrigation, negligible use of fertilisers, frequent famines.

Commercialisation of agriculture: some areas shifted to cash crops (like indigo, jute, cotton) needed by British industries, rather than food crops. This brought little gain to farmers and hurt food supply.

ex.q: Explain why zamindars had little interest in improving land.
st: Their main interest was collecting rent from cultivators
Revenue had to be paid to the government by fixed dates, or they lost their rights
So they squeezed tenants instead of investing in irrigation or better methods
ex.a: Rent collection and fixed revenue terms made investment unattractive

topics.rl: The Champaran movement of 1917, against forced indigo cultivation in Bihar, is a well-known example of the hardship caused by commercialised farming under colonial rule.

rv.summary: About 85% of Indians depended on agriculture, which stagnated because of zamindari, low technology, poor irrigation and few fertilisers. Commercialisation pushed cash crops for British industry with little gain to farmers.
focus: Explain the causes of agricultural stagnation
Explain zamindari and commercialisation
remember: About 85% depended on agriculture
Zamindari: profits to zamindars, high rents, no investment
Commercialisation: cash crops (indigo, jute, cotton) for Britain
traps: HYV seeds came after independence
Expansion of cultivated area does not explain stagnation
Commercialisation did not improve farmers' conditions

topics.ch: IED: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
topics.t: Industry: de-industrialisation and early factories
topics.h: India's handlooms once clothed the world. Then machine-made British cloth flooded in, and weavers lost their livelihoods. Historians call it de-industrialisation.
p: De-industrialisation: India's world-famous handicraft industries declined, but no modern industry grew to replace them.
The two-fold motive of colonial policy: (1) reduce India to an exporter of raw materials for British industries; (2) turn India into a market for British finished goods.
Modern industry began in the second half of the 19th century: cotton textile mills, mostly owned by Indians, in western India (Maharashtra and Gujarat); jute mills, mostly foreign-owned, in Bengal.
Iron and steel came early in the 20th century: TISCO (Tata Iron and Steel Company) was incorporated in 1907. Sugar, cement and paper industries came up after the Second World War.
Weaknesses: almost no capital goods industry, slow growth and a very small share in GDP, and a public sector limited to railways, power, communications, ports and a few departmental undertakings.

ex.q: Why did Indian handicrafts decline while modern industry did not grow fast enough to replace them?
st: Unequal tariffs and cheap machine-made British goods hurt handicrafts
Colonial policy wanted India as a raw-material supplier and a market
So there was little support for building modern Indian industry, especially capital goods
ex.a: De-industrialisation due to the two-fold colonial motive

topics.rl: Tata Steel at Jamshedpur, set up as TISCO in 1907, is still among India's biggest steel makers, a link between the colonial era and today.

rv.summary: Colonial India saw de-industrialisation: handicrafts declined without modern industry replacing them. A few industries arose (Indian-owned cotton mills in the west, foreign-owned jute mills in Bengal, TISCO in 1907), but there was almost no capital goods base.
focus: Explain de-industrialisation and the two-fold motive
Know where and when early industries started
List weaknesses of industry at independence
remember: Two-fold motive: raw-material supplier + market for British goods
Cotton mills: western India, Indian-owned; jute: Bengal, foreign-owned
TISCO incorporated 1907; sugar, cement, paper after World War II
traps: Jute mills were mostly foreign-owned
Sugar, cement and paper came after World War II, not before World War I
India had almost no capital goods industry

topics.ch: IED: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
topics.t: Foreign trade and the drain of wealth
topics.h: Under colonial rule India sold more abroad than it bought, yet the surplus never came home. Where did it go?
p: India exported primary products (raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo, jute) and imported finished consumer goods (cotton, silk, woollen cloth) and capital goods (light machinery) from Britain.
Britain kept monopoly control over India's foreign trade: more than half of it was with Britain; the rest was with China, Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and Persia (Iran).
The opening of the Suez Canal (1869) cut the cost and time of transport between Britain and India and tightened British control over Indian trade.

India had a large export surplus, but it was used to pay for the colonial administration's offices in Britain, British war expenses and invisible items, so no gold or silver flowed into India. This is called the drain of Indian wealth.

ex.q: Why did India's export surplus not benefit the Indian economy?
st: Exports exceeded imports, giving a surplus
The surplus paid for British administrative costs, wars and invisible imports
So wealth left India instead of being invested at home
ex.a: It was drained away to Britain

topics.rl: Dadabhai Naoroji's writings on the 'drain of wealth' became an important part of the national movement's economic critique of colonial rule.

rv.summary: India exported primary products and imported finished goods; Britain controlled over half its trade, helped by the Suez Canal (1869). The export surplus paid for British costs, causing a drain of wealth.
focus: Describe the pattern and direction of colonial trade
Explain the drain of wealth
Know the Suez Canal's effect
remember: Exports: raw silk, cotton, wool, sugar, indigo, jute
Over half of trade with Britain; rest with China, Ceylon, Persia
Suez Canal opened 1869
Drain: export surplus paid British administration, wars, invisibles
traps: India had an export surplus, not an import surplus
The surplus brought no gold or silver into India
The USA was not a listed trading partner

topics.ch: IED: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
topics.t: Demographic condition at independence
topics.h: In colonial India, a newborn could expect to live only about 32 years, and more than one in five babies died before turning one.
p: The first official census of British India was conducted in 1881. From then on, censuses were held every ten years (decennially).
1921 is called the year of the great divide: before 1921, India was in the first stage of demographic transition (high birth and death rates); the second stage began after 1921.
Social indicators were poor: overall literacy was less than 16%, female literacy only about 7%, the infant mortality rate about 218 per 1,000 live births, and life expectancy about 32 years.
Public health facilities were inadequate or unavailable, and water- and air-borne diseases were widespread. Extensive poverty and frequent famines added to the misery.

ex.q: The infant mortality rate was about 218 per 1,000. In a district with 50,000 live births in a year, about how many infants would die before age one?
st: IMR = infant deaths per 1,000 live births

topics.rl: India's Census, held every ten years since 1881, is one of the world's oldest continuous population counts; the 2021 round was postponed because of the pandemic.

rv.summary: The first census was in 1881, and 1921 marked the great divide in India's demographic transition. At independence literacy was under 16% (female about 7%), IMR about 218 per 1,000 and life expectancy about 32 years.
focus: Know the census and demographic transition dates
Recall the social indicators at independence
remember: First census 1881; decennial thereafter
1921: end of first stage of demographic transition
Literacy < 16%; female ≈ 7%; IMR ≈ 218 per 1,000; life expectancy ≈ 32 years
traps: 1921 was not the first census
Female literacy was about 7%, not 16%
Before 1921 India was in the first stage, not the second

topics.ch: IED: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
topics.t: Occupational structure at independence
topics.h: If you lined up 100 Indian workers in 1947, about 72 of them would be farmers, about 10 would work in industry and the rest in services.
p: Occupational structure means the distribution of the workforce across different occupations or sectors.
At independence, agriculture employed the largest share of the workforce, usually 70–75%; manufacturing about 10%; and services 15–20%.

Growing regional variation: parts of the Madras Presidency (areas of today's Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Karnataka), Bombay and Bengal saw a fall in the share of workers in agriculture and a rise in manufacturing and services.
But states such as Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab saw a rise in the share of the workforce in agriculture.
Shown as a pie chart in words: a big slice of about three-quarters for agriculture, a thin slice of about one-tenth for manufacturing, and the rest for services.

ex.q: Of 1,000 workers at independence, if agriculture had 72%, manufacturing 10%, how many were in services?

topics.rl: Even today agriculture employs the largest share of India's workers, though its share has fallen a lot since 1947.

rv.summary: At independence about 70–75% of workers were in agriculture, about 10% in manufacturing and 15–20% in services. Regional variation grew: agriculture's share fell in Madras, Bombay and Bengal but rose in Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab.
focus: Recall sector shares of the workforce
Name regions where agriculture's share fell or rose
remember: Agriculture 70–75%, manufacturing ≈ 10%, services 15–20%
Share in agriculture fell: Madras Presidency, Bombay, Bengal
Share in agriculture rose: Orissa, Rajasthan, Punjab
traps: Don't put Punjab or Rajasthan among regions where agriculture's share fell
Manufacturing was only about 10%
Occupational structure means distribution of the workforce, not wages

topics.ch: IED: Indian Economy on the Eve of Independence
topics.t: Colonial infrastructure and India's challenges at independence
topics.h: The British built thousands of kilometres of railway in India. Was it a gift to India or a tool for Britain? Economists still debate it.
p: Railways were introduced in 1850; the earliest line ran from Bombay to Thane. Railways enabled long-distance travel, broke geographical and cultural barriers, and promoted commercialisation of agriculture, which weakened the self-sufficiency of village economies.
Roads, inland waterways, ports, posts and the electric telegraph were developed mainly to serve colonial interests. Some waterways, such as the Coast Canal on the Orissa coast, proved uneconomical.
Main motives: moving the army within India and carrying raw materials to railway stations and ports for export.
Challenges at independence: stagnant agriculture, weak industry with no capital goods base, mass poverty, unemployment, poor health and literacy, and inadequate infrastructure.
Debate: some point to positive outcomes such as railways, ports, posts and telegraph; others argue these mainly served British interests and the costs to India outweighed the benefits.

ex.q: Give one benefit and one harmful effect of colonial railways on India.
st: Benefit: people could travel long distances; barriers between regions reduced
Harm: commercialisation of agriculture hurt village self-sufficiency
Exports grew, but the benefits rarely went to Indians
ex.a: Benefit: mobility; harm: loss of village self-sufficiency

topics.rl: Indian Railways today runs one of the world's largest networks, but its early layout, linking ports to the interior, reflects its colonial purpose.

rv.summary: Railways (from 1850), roads, ports, posts and the telegraph were built mainly to serve colonial interests: moving the army, carrying raw materials and keeping control. India began independence with stagnant agriculture, weak industry, poverty and poor infrastructure.
focus: Give benefits and harms of colonial infrastructure
List India's challenges at independence
remember: Railways introduced 1850 (Bombay–Thane)
Roads: army movement and raw materials to ports
Coast Canal (Orissa) was uneconomical
Telegraph: maintaining law and order
traps: Railways also hurt village self-sufficiency
India had no surplus of capital goods at independence
The British motive does not explain the travel benefit to Indians

topics.t: Choosing an economic system and planning
topics.h: In 1950, a newly independent India had to answer a giant question: should markets decide what to produce, or should the state? It chose a bit of both.
p: Every society must decide what, how and for whom to produce. A capitalist economy leaves this to market forces; a socialist economy lets the government decide; a mixed economy combines both.
Jawaharlal Nehru and most leaders preferred a mixed economy with a strong public sector alongside a private sector, guided by planning.
The Planning Commission was set up in 1950 with the Prime Minister as its chairperson. Five Year Plans began in 1951.
A plan spells out how a nation's resources should be used, with general goals and specific targets. Plans also have long-term goals spread over a 'perspective plan' of about 20 years.
P.C. Mahalanobis is regarded as the architect of Indian planning. The Second Five Year Plan was based on his ideas. He founded the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI) in Calcutta.

ex.q: Classify each decision: (i) the market decides how many phones to make; (ii) the government decides all production; (iii) the state runs steel plants while private firms make textiles.
st: (iii) state and private sectors side by side → mixed

topics.rl: The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015, but India's early steel plants, dams and IITs were built under the Five Year Plans.

rv.summary: India chose a mixed economy with a strong public sector guided by planning. The Planning Commission (1950), chaired by the Prime Minister, ran Five Year Plans from 1951, and P.C. Mahalanobis is the architect of Indian planning.
focus: Compare capitalist, socialist and mixed economies
Know planning institutions, dates and people
remember: Planning Commission 1950; First Five Year Plan 1951
Chairperson: Prime Minister
P.C. Mahalanobis: architect of planning; Second Plan; founded ISI
Perspective plan: about 20 years
traps: In capitalism the market, not the state, decides
The Planning Commission began in 1950, not 1951
Mahalanobis, not V.K.R.V. Rao, is the architect of planning

topics.t: Goals of the Five Year Plans
topics.h: Growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity: four goals that guided India for decades. But can you chase all four at once?
p: Growth: an increase in the country's capacity to produce goods and services, shown by steady growth in GDP.
Modernisation: adopting new technology (e.g. new seed varieties, new machines) and also social change, such as recognising that women should have the same rights as men.
Self-reliance: avoiding imports of goods that could be produced at home, especially food, to reduce dependence on other countries.
Equity: ensuring that the benefits of growth reach the poor, so that every Indian can meet basic needs like food, housing, education and health.

Goals can conflict, e.g. modern labour-saving technology can raise growth but reduce jobs. Also, India's service sector grew to the largest share of GDP while most workers stayed in agriculture, unlike the usual path through industry first.

ex.q: Identify the plan goal: (i) using HYV seeds; (ii) producing food at home to avoid imports; (iii) programmes to reduce poverty; (iv) raising GDP steadily.

topics.rl: Food self-reliance became a top goal after India had to import foodgrains in the 1960s; the green revolution was the answer.

rv.summary: The Five Year Plans aimed at growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity. These goals can conflict, and India's services grew to the largest share of GDP while most workers stayed in agriculture.
focus: Identify which goal a policy serves
Give an example of conflicting goals
remember: Growth: rise in productive capacity (GDP)
Modernisation: new technology + social change
Self-reliance: avoid imports, especially food
Equity: benefits reach the poor
traps: Equity does not mean equal incomes
The goals can conflict
Modernisation includes social change, not just machines

topics.t: Land reforms: land to the tiller
topics.h: Would you work harder on land you own or land a zamindar owns? Planners bet on ownership, and launched land reforms.
p: Ownership and incentives: when a cultivator owns the land, she gets the reward of extra effort and is more willing to invest and raise output.
Abolition of intermediaries (zamindars) made tillers the owners of land. About 200 lakh tenants came into direct contact with the government.
Land ceiling: fixing the maximum size of land an individual could own, to reduce concentration of land ownership. Surplus land was to be given to the landless.
Results were limited: big landlords used loopholes, filed court cases and transferred land to relatives or others (benami transfers) to escape the ceiling; some tenants were evicted.
Land reforms succeeded better in Kerala and West Bengal, where governments were committed to 'land to the tiller'.

ex.q: Why did land ceiling laws have limited success in many states?
st: Large landowners challenged the laws in courts, delaying them
They transferred land in the names of relatives and others
Loopholes let them keep land above the ceiling

topics.rl: Kerala's land reforms gave many tenants ownership of the land they tilled, and the state is often cited as a land reform success.

rv.summary: Land reforms abolished intermediaries so tillers became owners and fixed land ceilings to spread ownership. Loopholes and benami transfers limited results, except in Kerala and West Bengal.
focus: Explain abolition of intermediaries and land ceilings
Explain why ceilings had limited success
remember: Abolition of intermediaries: about 200 lakh tenants came into contact with government
Land ceiling: maximum land an individual can own
More success: Kerala and West Bengal
traps: Reforms were not equally successful everywhere
Benami transfers evaded ceilings
Ceilings aimed to reduce, not raise, land concentration

topics.t: The green revolution
topics.h: In the mid-1960s, India depended on food imports. Within two decades it was self-sufficient in foodgrains. The secret: tiny high-yielding seeds.
p: Green revolution: a large increase in foodgrain production from using high yielding variety (HYV) seeds, especially for wheat and rice.
HYV seeds needed the correct quantities of fertilisers and pesticides and a regular supply of water (assured irrigation).

First phase (about mid-1960s to mid-1970s): HYV seeds were used mainly in the more affluent states like Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, and mostly benefited wheat-growing regions. Second phase (mid-1970s to mid-1980s): the technology spread to more states and more crops.

Marketed surplus: the part of farm produce sold in the market by farmers. Because even small farmers sold a good share of the higher output, food prices fell relative to other goods, helping low-income groups; the government also built buffer stocks.

Risks: it might increase disparities between small and big farmers, and HYV crops were more prone to pests. The government gave small farmers cheap loans and subsidised inputs, and research institutes reduced pest risks.

ex.q: A farmer produces 100 quintals of wheat, keeps 30 quintals for family use and sells the rest. What is his marketed surplus?
st: Marketed surplus = produce sold in the market

topics.rl: Punjab became India's 'food bowl' during the green revolution; M.S. Swaminathan is widely remembered for his role in it.

rv.summary: The green revolution raised foodgrain output using HYV seeds with fertilisers, pesticides and assured irrigation, first in wheat in states like Punjab. Higher marketed surplus lowered relative food prices and allowed buffer stocks.
focus: Explain HYV technology and its phases
Compute and explain marketed surplus
Discuss its risks and how they were handled
remember: HYV seeds need fertilisers, pesticides and regular water
First phase: mid-1960s–mid-1970s, wheat, Punjab/AP/TN
Marketed surplus = produce sold in the market
traps: Marketed surplus is the amount sold, not the amount kept
Output rose, it did not fall
Government support kept small farmers from being left out

topics.t: Farm subsidies and the labour that stayed on the farm
topics.h: Cheap fertiliser helped farmers adopt new seeds. Decades later, people still argue: should the subsidy stay or go?
p: Arguments for subsidies: they encouraged farmers, especially small ones, to adopt new HYV technology; many argue subsidies are still needed because farming is risky and many farmers are poor.

Arguments against: once the technology is profitable and widely adopted, subsidies should be phased out; much of the subsidy benefits the fertiliser industry and farmers in prosperous regions; it is a large burden on the budget.
Prices as signals: in a market, prices indicate scarcity. Subsidies make inputs look cheaper than their true cost, which can encourage wasteful use (for example, of water or fertiliser).

Even as late as 1990, about 65% of India's population continued to be employed in agriculture, though agriculture's share in GDP had fallen. Planning failed to shift enough workers into industry and services.

ex.q: Agriculture's share of GDP fell a lot by 1990, but about 65% of people still worked in it. What does this imply about output per worker in agriculture?
st: A large share of workers produces a smaller share of output
So output per worker in agriculture is low compared with other sectors
Too many people remained dependent on farming
ex.a: Output per worker in agriculture is low

topics.rl: Free electricity for farm pumps in some states is linked to over-use of groundwater, a modern example of prices failing to act as signals.

rv.summary: Farm subsidies helped small farmers adopt HYV technology, but critics say they later mostly helped the fertiliser industry and rich farmers and weakened price signals. In 1990 about 65% of people still worked in agriculture.
focus: Give arguments for and against farm subsidies
Explain prices as signals
Explain the problem of labour staying in agriculture
remember: About 65% employed in agriculture even in 1990
Prices signal scarcity
Subsidies can encourage wasteful use of inputs
traps: Agriculture's GDP share fell but its job share stayed high
Budget burden is an argument against, not for, subsidies
Don't say most workers left agriculture by 1990

topics.t: Industrial policy: public sector, IPR 1956 and small industry
topics.h: In 1950, Indian industrialists lacked the money to build a steel plant and the market was too small to tempt them. So the state stepped in.
p: Why the public sector led: private industrialists lacked the capital needed for large industries, and the market was not big enough to encourage big investments. So the state controlled the 'commanding heights' of the economy.

Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) 1956: industries were classified into three categories. Category 1: exclusively owned by the state. Category 2: the private sector could supplement the state, which would start new units. Category 3: the remaining industries, open to the private sector.

Private industry was controlled through licences. Licences were also used to promote industry in backward regions (regional equality) and to prevent expansion that was not in the national interest. This came to be called the 'permit licence raj'.
Small-scale industry (SSI): the Karve Committee (1955) suggested using small industry to promote rural development. In 1950 an SSI was defined as one with a maximum investment of ₹5 lakh.
SSIs are labour-intensive and create employment. Many products were reserved for SSIs and they got concessions such as lower excise duty and bank loans at lower interest rates.

ex.q: Classify under IPR 1956: (i) a category where only the state can set up units; (ii) a category where the state starts new units but private firms may supplement it; (iii) all other industries.
st: (ii) Category 2: private sector supplements the state

topics.rl: SAIL's Bhilai and Rourkela steel plants, set up in the Second Plan era, are classic examples of public sector 'commanding heights'.

rv.summary: The state led industrialisation because private capital and markets were small. IPR 1956 set three categories of industries, licensing controlled private industry, and small-scale industry (₹5 lakh limit in 1950) got support for employment.
focus: Explain the role of the public sector
Describe the three categories of IPR 1956
Explain licensing and SSI support
remember: IPR 1956: three categories (state-only; state + private supplement; private)
Karve Committee 1955: SSI for rural development
SSI in 1950: maximum investment ₹5 lakh
traps: Licensing made industry harder, not easier, to start
IPR 1956 had three, not four, categories
SSI limit was ₹5 lakh, not ₹5 crore

topics.t: Import substitution and the 1950–1990 balance sheet
topics.h: For four decades, Indians waited months for a scooter or a phone connection, while factories at home were protected from foreign competition. Was it worth it?
p: Trade policy was inward looking: import substitution, i.e. producing at home goods that were earlier imported (e.g. making cars in India instead of importing them).
Protection used two tools: tariffs (taxes on imported goods, which make them costlier) and quotas (limits on the quantity of goods that can be imported).

Effects: industry's share of GDP rose from 11.8% in 1950-51 to 24.6% in 1990-91, and industry diversified widely. But protection led to inefficiency, poor quality, loss-making public enterprises, and weak exports since domestic firms faced no competition.

Debate: some argue public enterprises should be judged by their contribution to welfare, not just profit; others say losses wasted scarce resources and a sector could be privatised if it did not need the state.
Achievements and shortcomings of 1950–1990 (food self-sufficiency, diversified industry, but slow growth and inefficiency) set the stage for the 1991 reforms.

ex.q: A car costs $10,000 abroad. India imposes a 100% tariff. At ₹80/$, what is its landed price in India? How does this protect Indian car makers?
st: The higher price makes domestic cars more attractive

topics.rl: The long waiting lists for Bajaj scooters in the 1970s and 1980s are often quoted as a symptom of protection and licensing.

rv.summary: Inward-looking trade policy used tariffs and quotas for import substitution. Industry's GDP share rose from 11.8% (1950-51) to 24.6% (1990-91), but protection caused inefficiency, poor quality and weak exports.
focus: Define import substitution, tariff and quota
Evaluate the results of 1950–1990 policy
remember: Tariff: tax on imports; quota: quantity limit
Industry share of GDP: 11.8% → 24.6%
Protection → inefficiency, poor quality, weak exports
traps: A tariff is a tax, a quota is a quantity limit
Exports did not grow fast under import substitution
PSUs may be judged by welfare, not only profit

topics.ch: IED: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
topics.t: The 1991 crisis and the New Economic Policy
topics.h: In 1991, India's foreign exchange reserves could pay for barely two weeks of imports. The country was close to defaulting on its foreign payments.
p: The 1991 crisis: foreign exchange reserves fell to a level not enough to pay for imports for more than about two weeks; India could not pay interest on its foreign loans, and prices of essential goods rose sharply.
Roots: the government spent far more than it earned (large fiscal deficits), borrowed heavily at home and abroad, and imports grew much faster than exports.

India approached the World Bank (IBRD) and the IMF and received a loan of $7 billion. In return they expected India to liberalise the economy, reduce restrictions on the private sector and on trade, and reduce the role of government.
The New Economic Policy (NEP) was announced in 1991, based on liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation (LPG).

Stabilisation measures were short-term, to correct the BoP and control inflation (e.g. build forex reserves, restrain prices). Structural reform measures were long-term, to improve efficiency and competitiveness by removing rigidities.

ex.q: Classify: (i) building up forex reserves quickly in 1991; (ii) removing industrial licensing; (iii) controlling a sudden rise in prices; (iv) opening the economy to foreign competition.
st: Short-term correction of BoP or prices → stabilisation
Long-term efficiency and competitiveness → structural reform

topics.rl: In 1991 India even pledged part of its gold reserves to raise foreign currency, a sign of how serious the crisis was.

rv.summary: In 1991 India's reserves could pay for only about two weeks of imports, after years of high fiscal deficits and imports outpacing exports. With a $7 billion World Bank–IMF loan, India launched the New Economic Policy of liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.
focus: Explain the causes of the 1991 crisis
Distinguish stabilisation and structural reform measures
remember: Reserves ≈ two weeks of imports in 1991
Loan of $7 billion from World Bank (IBRD) and IMF
NEP 1991: LPG
Stabilisation: short-term (BoP, inflation); structural: long-term (efficiency)
traps: The loan had conditions
Stabilisation is short-term, not long-term
The crisis was caused by deficits and an import–export gap, not by an export surplus

topics.ch: IED: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
topics.t: Liberalisation of industry and finance
topics.h: Before 1991, you needed a government licence to expand a factory. After 1991, for most industries, you just needed customers.
p: Industrial licensing was abolished for almost all products except a few categories: alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, industrial explosives, electronics, aerospace, and drugs and pharmaceuticals.
Industries reserved for the public sector were cut drastically; today only a part of atomic energy generation and some core activities in railway transport remain reserved.
Many goods earlier reserved for small-scale industries were de-reserved, and markets were allowed to set prices in many industries.

Financial sector reforms: the RBI's role shifted from regulator to facilitator of the financial sector. Private sector banks (Indian and foreign) were allowed, and the limit on foreign investment in banks was raised.
Foreign institutional investors (FIIs) such as merchant bankers, mutual funds and pension funds were allowed to invest in Indian financial markets.

ex.q: A firm wants to start a cement plant in 1995 and another wants to make cigarettes. Who needs an industrial licence?
st: After 1991 licensing was abolished for most products
Cigarettes remained in the licensed list

topics.rl: Private banks such as HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank grew after the 1990s financial reforms opened banking to new players.

rv.summary: After 1991 licensing was abolished except for a few products, public sector reservation shrank to parts of atomic energy and railways, and SSI products were de-reserved. In finance, the RBI became a facilitator, private banks were allowed and FIIs could invest.
focus: List products still needing licences
Describe financial sector reforms
remember: Licences kept for alcohol, cigarettes, hazardous chemicals, explosives, electronics, aerospace, drugs
Reserved for public sector: part of atomic energy, some core railway activities
RBI: regulator → facilitator
traps: Public sector reservation was reduced, not expanded
Cement and textiles did not need licences after 1991
FIIs include mutual funds and pension funds

topics.ch: IED: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
topics.t: Tax, foreign exchange and trade reforms
topics.h: One nation, one tax: in July 2017, a single GST replaced a tangle of indirect taxes. It was part of a long line of reforms that began in 1991.
p: Tax reforms: income tax and corporation tax rates were reduced to encourage saving and voluntary disclosure, procedures were simplified, and indirect taxes were reformed to create a common national market.
GST came into effect from 1 July 2017, replacing many indirect taxes of the Centre and the States. Its idea: 'One Nation, One Tax, One Market'.
Foreign exchange reforms: in 1991 the rupee was devalued to resolve the BoP crisis and increase foreign exchange inflows. Later the exchange rate came to be determined largely by the market.

Trade and investment reforms: quantitative restrictions (QRs) on imports and exports were dismantled (fully removed for manufactured consumer goods and farm products from April 2001), tariff rates were reduced, import licensing was removed except for hazardous and environmentally sensitive industries, and export duties were removed.

ex.q: Before 1991, a TV import was limited to 1,000 sets a year and carried a 150% duty. After reforms, the quota is gone and the duty is cut. Which two reforms are these?
st: A limit on quantity is a quantitative restriction → removed
A tax on imports is a tariff → reduced
Both make imports easier and push domestic firms to compete
ex.a: Removal of QRs and reduction of tariffs

topics.rl: GST on a restaurant bill or a mobile phone is the same rate across states, making India more like a single market.

rv.summary: Reforms cut income and corporation tax rates, introduced GST from 1 July 2017, devalued the rupee in 1991 and later let the market set it, removed quantitative restrictions (fully by April 2001), cut tariffs and removed export duties.
focus: Explain tax reforms and GST
Explain forex and trade reforms
remember: GST from 1 July 2017: 'One Nation, One Tax, One Market'
Rupee devalued in 1991
QRs fully removed from April 2001
Export duties removed; tariffs reduced
traps: Export duties were removed, not raised
QRs are quantity limits, not taxes
Devaluation aimed to raise forex inflows, not to cheapen imports

topics.ch: IED: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
topics.t: Privatisation, disinvestment and the 'Ratna' PSUs
topics.h: Air India went back to the Tata group in 2022, almost 70 years after it was nationalised. That's privatisation in action.
p: Privatisation: shedding the ownership or management of a government-owned enterprise, either by withdrawing the government from ownership and management, or by outright sale to private buyers.

Disinvestment: privatisation by selling part of the equity (shares) of public sector undertakings (PSUs) to the public. Selling a majority stake with management control is a strategic sale; selling a small stake is a minority sale.
The main purposes were to improve financial discipline and efficiency of PSUs and to bring in private capital and managerial skills.

To improve efficiency and give autonomy, the government gives special status to profit-making PSUs: Maharatna, Navratna and Miniratna. These get greater freedom in managerial and investment decisions.
Examples of Maharatna companies include ONGC, NTPC, SAIL and Indian Oil Corporation.

ex.q: The government sells 10% of a PSU's shares in the stock market but keeps control. Is this privatisation? What kind?
st: Selling part of the equity to the public = disinvestment
Disinvestment is one form of privatisation
A small stake without control = minority sale
ex.a: Yes: disinvestment through a minority sale

topics.rl: Navratna and Maharatna PSUs like NTPC can approve large investments without seeking government approval for each one, which lets them compete with private firms.

rv.summary: Privatisation reduces government ownership or management of PSUs, often through disinvestment (selling shares). Profit-making PSUs get Maharatna, Navratna or Miniratna status for more autonomy.
focus: Define privatisation, disinvestment, strategic and minority sale
Know the Ratna categories and examples
remember: Disinvestment: sale of part of PSU equity to the public
Strategic sale: majority stake with control
Maharatnas include ONGC, NTPC, SAIL, IOC
traps: Navratnas have more, not less, freedom
Private firms like Infosys are not Maharatnas
Disinvestment is a form of privatisation

topics.ch: IED: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
topics.t: Globalisation, outsourcing and the WTO
topics.h: A bank in New York calls a customer, but the voice answering is in Gurugram. Outsourcing turned India into the world's back office.
p: Globalisation is the integration of a national economy with the world economy, through trade, investment, technology and people flows.

Outsourcing: a firm hires regular services from external sources, often from other countries. Examples: call centres (BPO), record keeping, accountancy, banking services, editing, transcription, medical advice, teaching. India is a favoured destination because of skilled, English-speaking workers at lower wages and good IT capacity.
Indian companies have also gone global, for example Tata Steel acquiring Corus (2007) and Tata Motors acquiring Jaguar Land Rover (2008).

The World Trade Organisation (WTO) was founded in 1995 as the successor to GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, 1948). It aims at a rule-based trading system, lower tariff and non-tariff barriers, and trade in services too. India is a founder member.
Bilateral trade is between two countries; multilateral trade involves many countries. Tariff barriers are taxes on trade; non-tariff barriers include quotas and other restrictions.

ex.q: Why is India a favoured destination for outsourcing?
st: Large pool of skilled, English-speaking workers
Lower wage costs than developed countries
ex.a: Skilled low-cost manpower and good IT capacity

topics.rl: Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune host global capability centres where Indian engineers work for firms across the world.

rv.summary: Globalisation integrates India with the world economy through trade, investment, technology and outsourcing, where India's skilled, low-cost workers attract services. The WTO (1995), successor to GATT (1948), promotes rule-based trade with lower barriers.
focus: Explain outsourcing and why India attracts it
Know the WTO's origin and aims
Tell bilateral from multilateral and tariff from non-tariff barriers
remember: WTO founded 1995; succeeded GATT (1948); India a founder member
Outsourcing: BPO, accounts, banking, transcription, teaching
Tata Steel–Corus (2007); Tata Motors–JLR (2008)
traps: Trade between two countries is bilateral
A quota is a non-tariff barrier
The WTO succeeded GATT, not the IMF

topics.ch: IED: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
topics.t: Assessing the reforms: growth, jobs and agriculture
topics.h: After 1991, India's GDP grew faster and forex reserves soared. Yet many asked: where are the jobs, and why are farmers struggling?
p: Positives: GDP growth increased, led by the service sector; foreign investment (FDI and FII) and foreign exchange reserves rose sharply, making India one of the largest holders of reserves; exports of auto parts, engineering goods, IT services and textiles grew.
Agriculture's growth slowed, and industrial growth fluctuated, while services grew fastest.
Criticism – growth and employment: GDP grew but did not generate enough good jobs (jobless growth).

Criticism – agriculture: public investment in farm infrastructure (irrigation, power, roads, market links, research and extension) fell; removal of fertiliser subsidies raised costs; lower import duties and removal of QRs exposed farmers to world competition.
Export-oriented policies shifted land from food crops to cash crops for export, putting pressure on food prices.

ex.q: Give one positive outcome of the reforms and one criticism related to agriculture.
st: Positive: forex reserves and foreign investment rose sharply
Criticism: public investment in irrigation and rural infrastructure declined
Also: cheaper imports put pressure on farmers
ex.a: Higher reserves; falling public investment in agriculture

topics.rl: India's forex reserves, which were tiny in 1991, have grown to among the largest in the world, a widely cited success of the reform era.

rv.summary: After reforms, growth rose led by services, and foreign investment and reserves rose sharply. Critics point to jobless growth and to agriculture, where public investment fell, subsidies were cut, imports competed and land shifted to cash crops.
focus: List positive outcomes of reforms
Explain criticisms on employment and agriculture
remember: Services grew fastest; agriculture slowed
Forex reserves and FDI/FII rose sharply
Jobless growth
Public investment in farm infrastructure declined
traps: Foreign investment rose, not fell
Fertiliser subsidies were cut, not raised
Import duties on farm goods were lowered, not raised

topics.ch: IED: Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal
topics.t: More criticisms and a balanced verdict
topics.h: Cheaper imported toys and gadgets delight shoppers but can worry small Indian manufacturers. Every reform has winners and losers.
p: Criticism – industry: cheaper imports replaced demand for domestic goods; poor infrastructure (power, ports, roads) kept costs high; developed countries kept some non-tariff barriers (for example, quota restrictions on textiles and clothing).
Criticism – disinvestment: PSU assets were said to be undervalued and sold cheaply; proceeds were often used to cover revenue shortfalls instead of building assets.
Criticism – fiscal policy: tax rate cuts did not raise revenue much, and pressure to cut deficits reduced social sector spending.

Case: in Siricilla (then Andhra Pradesh, now Telangana), power-sector reforms raised electricity tariffs for power looms, causing severe distress among weavers, showing how reforms can hurt vulnerable groups without safeguards.
A balanced view: reforms opened markets, brought technology and raised growth, but critics argue benefits were uneven, widening inequality and leaving out sectors like agriculture and small industry.

ex.q: Why was the use of disinvestment proceeds criticised?
st: Proceeds were often used to meet current revenue shortfalls
They were not used to build new assets or improve PSUs
So national assets were sold without lasting gain
ex.a: They financed revenue gaps rather than asset creation

topics.rl: Debates on selling stakes in PSUs at the 'right price' recur in Parliament whenever a big disinvestment is announced.

rv.summary: Other criticisms: cheap imports and poor infrastructure hurt industry, PSU assets were undervalued and proceeds spent on revenue gaps, and tax cuts squeezed social spending. The Siricilla weavers' distress shows reforms can hurt vulnerable groups.
focus: Explain industry, disinvestment and fiscal criticisms
Give the Siricilla example
Give a balanced verdict on reforms
remember: Industry: cheap imports, poor infrastructure, foreign non-tariff barriers
Disinvestment: undervalued assets, proceeds used for revenue shortfalls
Siricilla: higher power tariffs hurt power-loom weavers
traps: Benefits were not equal for all sections
Disinvestment proceeds were not mainly used to build assets
Cash crops and fertilisers are agricultural, not industrial, criticisms

topics.ch: IED: Human Capital Formation in India
topics.t: Human capital and economic growth
topics.h: Land becomes a factory, and a factory becomes physical capital. A curious student becomes an AIIMS doctor or an ISRO engineer, and that is human capital.
p: Human capital is the stock of skill and expertise of a nation at a point of time. Just as land can be turned into physical capital, human resources (like students) can be turned into human capital (like engineers and doctors) through investment.
Human capital raises growth: an educated, healthy worker is more productive; skilled people innovate and can absorb new technology quickly.
Causality runs both ways: higher income allows more spending on education and health, and more human capital raises income. So it is hard to prove which causes which.
Measurement is difficult: education is often measured in years of schooling and health by life expectancy, which do not fully capture quality.

Since 1951, India has seen big improvements in literacy, life expectancy, infant mortality and per capita income. With its skilled workforce in IT, India is often described as moving towards a knowledge economy.

ex.q: Explain the two-way link between human capital and economic growth with an example.
st: Growth → human capital: a richer family or state can spend more on schools and hospitals
Human capital → growth: better educated workers raise productivity and innovate
Each feeds the other, which makes the cause hard to isolate
ex.a: Higher income funds education and health, which in turn raise income

topics.rl: India's software and IT services exports show how a skilled workforce can drive growth in a knowledge economy.

rv.summary: Human capital is the stock of skill and expertise of a nation, created by investing in people. It raises productivity and innovation, and the link with growth runs both ways.
focus: Define human capital
Explain how it raises growth and the two-way link
Explain why measurement is hard
remember: Human capital: stock of skill and expertise at a point of time
Two-way causality: income ↔ human capital
Years of schooling and life expectancy miss quality
traps: Human capital is not machines or population size
The link with growth is two-way, not one-way
India's indicators have improved since 1951

topics.ch: IED: Human Capital Formation in India
topics.t: Sources of human capital: education, health and training
topics.h: A vaccine at a primary health centre, a diploma from an ITI, and a week of training at a factory: all three are investments in human capital.
p: Investment in education is the main source of human capital. Spending on education by individuals and governments is like a firm's investment: it raises future income.

Investment in health: a sick worker cannot work well. Health spending includes preventive medicine (vaccination), curative medicine (treating illness), social medicine (spreading health literacy) and providing clean drinking water and good sanitation.
On-the-job training: firms train workers at the workplace, under skilled workers, or send them for off-campus courses, and expect higher productivity in return.
Firms may insist that trained workers stay for a period so that the firm recovers the cost of training.

ex.q: Classify the health spending: (i) polio drops for children; (ii) surgery after an accident; (iii) a campaign on handwashing; (iv) piped clean water to a village.
st: (iv) basic health infrastructure → clean water and sanitation
ex.a: (i) preventive, (ii) curative, (iii) social medicine, (iv) clean water/sanitation

topics.rl: India's Pulse Polio campaign, a preventive health programme, helped the country get certified polio-free by the WHO in 2014.

rv.summary: Main sources of human capital are spending on education, health (preventive, curative, social medicine, clean water and sanitation) and on-the-job training.
focus: Classify types of health spending
Explain why firms train workers
remember: Preventive: vaccination; curative: treatment; social: health literacy
On-the-job training raises productivity; firms may require workers to stay
Education spending is an investment
traps: Education is not pure consumption
A factory machine is physical, not human, capital
Vaccination is preventive, not curative

topics.ch: IED: Human Capital Formation in India
topics.t: Migration, information and physical vs human capital
topics.h: A nurse from Kerala moves to Dubai for higher pay; a young engineer in Bihar checks an online job portal before choosing a course. Both are investing in human capital.
p: Migration: people move from rural to urban areas or abroad in search of better jobs and wages. Costs include transport, higher living costs and the psychological cost of living in a new place; migration happens when expected higher earnings exceed these costs.
Expenditure on information about the labour market (jobs, wages) and the education market (courses, colleges) helps people make better decisions, so it is also a source of human capital.
Physical vs human capital: physical capital is tangible and can be sold; human capital is intangible and embodied in its owner, who sells only its services.
Physical capital can be separated from its owner; human capital cannot. Both depreciate: machines wear out; human capital declines with ageing but can be renewed through education and health.
Physical capital gives mainly private benefits; human capital gives private benefits and also social benefits (e.g. an educated person spreads knowledge and improves the community).

ex.q: A worker earns ₹15,000 a month in a village. A city job pays ₹25,000, but extra rent and travel cost ₹6,000 a month. Is migration worthwhile in money terms?
st: Net gain = ₹4,000 a month > 0, so yes (ignoring psychological costs)
ex.a: Yes, net gain of ₹4,000 a month

topics.rl: Online portals like the government's National Career Service help job-seekers find information about vacancies and training.

rv.summary: Migration and spending on information are also sources of human capital. Unlike physical capital, human capital is intangible, inseparable from its owner, and gives social as well as private benefits.
focus: Weigh the costs and gains of migration
Compare physical and human capital
remember: Migrate when expected extra earnings > costs
Human capital: intangible, inseparable, only its services sold
Human capital has social benefits
traps: Human capital cannot be sold like a machine
Both kinds of capital depreciate
Psychological cost is also a cost of migration

topics.ch: IED: Human Capital Formation in India
topics.t: Human development and the role of government
topics.h: Is education worth it only if it raises your salary? Human capital says 'mostly yes'. Human development says 'learning is valuable in itself'.
p: Human capital treats education and health as means to increase labour productivity. Human development treats them as ends in themselves, part of human well-being.

Human development is a broader idea: even if education or health does not raise productivity, it is valuable because it enhances well-being. Every individual has a right to basic education and health care.

Why government intervenes: education and health have external benefits for society, their benefits are long-term, and individuals often lack full information about quality; private providers may charge high fees.
Regulatory bodies in education: Ministry of Education, NCERT, UGC (University Grants Commission), AICTE (All India Council for Technical Education).
In health: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, ICMR (Indian Council of Medical Research) and the National Medical Commission (NMC).

ex.q: A grandmother learns to read at 70. Her productivity at work does not change. Is this human capital formation, human development, or both?
st: Human capital looks at productivity gains: none here
Human development values education as an end in itself
So it counts as human development

topics.rl: Adult literacy drives under programmes for neo-literates show the human development view: literacy matters even when it doesn't change someone's income.

rv.summary: Human capital sees education and health as means to productivity; human development sees them as ends in themselves. Government regulates these sectors because of externalities and information gaps, through bodies like NCERT, UGC, AICTE, ICMR and NMC.
focus: Distinguish human capital from human development
Explain why government intervenes
Match regulatory bodies to fields
remember: Human development: education and health as ends
Education bodies: Ministry of Education, NCERT, UGC, AICTE
Health bodies: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, ICMR, NMC
traps: Human capital does not treat education as an end in itself
AICTE is for technical education, ICMR for medical research
UGC deals with universities, not primary schools

topics.ch: IED: Human Capital Formation in India
topics.t: India's education sector: spending, RTE and achievements
topics.h: Free schooling for every child from 6 to 14 is now a legal right in India. Getting there took decades of debate and spending.
p: Government spending on education is measured as (a) a share of total government expenditure and (b) a share of GDP. Both have risen over time but remain below targets.
Elementary education takes the largest share of education spending; per-student spending on higher (tertiary) education is much higher than on elementary.
The Education Commission (1964–66) recommended that at least 6% of GDP be spent on education; actual spending has stayed below this.

The Right to Education Act, 2009 made free and compulsory education a right of all children aged 6–14. The government also levies an education cess (an extra levy on Union taxes) earmarked for education.
Achievements: adult literacy, youth literacy and primary completion rates have improved, and the gender gap is narrowing, though female rates still lag behind male rates.

ex.q: A state's GDP is ₹10,00,000 crore and it spends ₹40,000 crore on education. What % of GDP is this, and how far is it from the 6% target?
ex.a: 4% of GDP, 2 percentage points below the target

topics.rl: Under the RTE Act, private unaided schools must reserve 25% of entry-level seats for children from economically weaker and disadvantaged groups.

rv.summary: Education spending is below the 6% of GDP recommended by the Education Commission (1964–66). The RTE Act, 2009 gives free, compulsory education to ages 6–14, and literacy and completion rates are improving.
focus: Compute education spending as % of GDP
Know the RTE Act and the 6% target
Compare elementary and higher education spending
remember: Target: at least 6% of GDP (Education Commission 1964–66)
RTE Act 2009: ages 6–14
Elementary education gets the largest share; higher education costs more per student
Education cess is earmarked for education
traps: India's spending is below 6%, not above
RTE covers 6–14, not 3–10 or 14–18
Largest share ≠ highest per-student spending

topics.ch: IED: Human Capital Formation in India
topics.t: Future prospects and challenges
topics.h: India has one of the world's largest young populations. Turning that crowd into a skilled workforce is the big challenge of the century.
p: Education for all is still a distant dream: although literacy has risen, many adults remain illiterate and many children drop out.
Gender equity is improving: the gap between male and female literacy is narrowing. Women's education matters because it improves fertility choices, child health and women's economic independence.
Higher education has few takers relative to the population, and unemployment among educated youth (graduates) is high, partly because skills do not match job needs.
