Problems in human capital formation: a large and growing population, brain drain, poor quality of many institutions, low spending on education and health, and weak links between education and employment.
Fee regulation is debated: many argue the government should regulate fees in private schools and hospitals so that services stay affordable.

ex.q: Give two reasons why women's education is especially important.
st: It improves fertility choices and family health care
It increases women's economic independence and social status
Benefits pass on to children's education and health
ex.a: Better health and fertility outcomes, and economic independence

topics.rl: Programmes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao aim to improve girls' education and the child sex ratio.

rv.summary: India still has not achieved education for all; the gender gap is narrowing, educated unemployment shows a skill mismatch, and brain drain and low spending hold back human capital formation.
focus: List problems of human capital formation
Explain why women's education matters
Explain educated unemployment and brain drain
remember: Problems: population, brain drain, low quality, low spending, weak education–job link
Women's education: fertility, health, economic independence
Brain drain: skilled people migrating abroad
traps: The gender gap in literacy is narrowing, not widening
Educated unemployment is a skill mismatch, not too few graduates
Buying land or gold is not human capital

topics.t: What is rural development?
topics.h: About two-thirds of Indians live in villages. If rural India doesn't progress, India can't. Rural development is the plan to make sure it does.
p: Rural development is a comprehensive term: it focuses on action for the development of areas that are lagging behind in the overall development of the village economy.

Key areas: developing human resources (literacy, especially female literacy, education and skills; health, including sanitation and public health), land reforms, and developing the productive resources of each locality.

More key areas: infrastructure (electricity, irrigation, credit, marketing, transport including village roads and highways, and agricultural research and extension) and special measures for poverty alleviation and better opportunities for weaker sections.

After 1991, agricultural growth slowed: public investment in agriculture fell, rural infrastructure stayed weak, and alternative jobs in industry and services did not grow enough in rural areas, causing farm distress.

ex.q: Classify each programme by the key area of rural development: (i) a village toilet drive; (ii) a new cold storage; (iii) a literacy camp for women; (iv) a farm road.

topics.rl: Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, which builds all-weather roads to villages, is an example of rural infrastructure development.

rv.summary: Rural development is action to develop lagging village areas through human resources (literacy, health), land reforms, local resources, infrastructure and poverty alleviation. After 1991 falling public investment slowed agriculture and caused farm distress.
focus: List the key areas of rural development
Explain the post-1991 slowdown in agriculture
remember: Key areas: human resources, land reforms, local productive resources, infrastructure, poverty alleviation
Post-1991: fall in public investment in agriculture → farm distress
traps: Rural development is not only higher farm output
Urban malls are not part of rural development
Infrastructure includes credit and marketing, not just roads

topics.t: Rural credit: from moneylenders to NABARD
topics.h: A farmer sows in June but harvests in October. Who pays for the seeds and family needs in between? For centuries, the answer was a moneylender at crippling interest.
p: Need for credit: farming has a long gestation period between sowing and selling; farmers need money for seeds, fertilisers, implements, and family needs such as marriages, deaths and religious ceremonies.
Before independence, moneylenders and traders exploited small farmers with very high interest rates and manipulated accounts, trapping them in debt.

After 1969 (bank nationalisation), India adopted social banking and a multi-agency approach to rural credit. NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) was set up in 1982 as the apex body to coordinate all institutions involved in rural financing.
Institutional sources: commercial banks, regional rural banks (RRBs), cooperative credit societies, and land development banks.

ex.q: A moneylender lends ₹10,000 at 5% per month simple interest; a cooperative lends at 9% per year. Compare the interest for one year.

topics.rl: Kisan Credit Cards issued by banks give farmers short-term crop loans at lower interest, part of institutional rural credit.

rv.summary: Farmers need credit because of the long gap between sowing and income. Moneylenders exploited them, so after 1969 India built institutional credit, with NABARD (1982) as the apex body.
focus: Explain why farmers need credit
List institutional and non-institutional sources
Compare interest costs
remember: NABARD set up 1982; apex body for rural credit
Social banking after 1969 bank nationalisation
Institutional: commercial banks, RRBs, cooperatives, land development banks
traps: Moneylenders are not institutional lenders
Land development banks give long-term loans
Monthly interest × 12 gives the yearly rate

topics.t: Self-help groups, micro-credit and Jan Dhan
topics.h: Twelve women in a Kerala village each save ₹100 a month. A year later they're lending to each other and running a pickle business. That's the power of a self-help group.
p: Self-help groups (SHGs): small groups, mostly of women, that pool regular small savings (thrift) and give small loans to members at reasonable interest; many are linked to banks for larger loans.

Micro-credit programmes give small loans to poor people who lack collateral. SHGs help women become financially independent and empowered. Limitation: loans are often used for consumption rather than productive purposes, and amounts are small.
Kudumbashree, a Kerala government programme, is a women-oriented, community-based poverty reduction programme built on thrift and credit societies.
Appraisal of rural banking: institutional credit expanded and reduced dependence on moneylenders, but recovery of loans has been poor, defaults are common, and informal lenders still matter.
Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (2014): bank accounts for all, including zero-balance accounts, RuPay debit cards, accident insurance cover and overdraft facility, to promote financial inclusion.

ex.q: An SHG has 15 members, each saving ₹200 a month. How much is pooled in a year? If it lends 60% of it, how much is lent?

topics.rl: Jan Dhan accounts have also been used for direct benefit transfers, so subsidies and support reach people's bank accounts directly.

rv.summary: Self-help groups pool small savings and give small loans, empowering women; Kudumbashree in Kerala is an example. Rural banking expanded but suffers from defaults, and Jan Dhan (2014) aims at financial inclusion.
focus: Explain how SHGs work and their limits
Know Kudumbashree and Jan Dhan features
remember: SHGs: thrift + small loans, mostly women
Kudumbashree: Kerala
PMJDY 2014: zero-balance account, RuPay card, insurance, overdraft
traps: Institutional credit has not fully replaced moneylenders
Micro-credit loans are often used for consumption
Jan Dhan accounts need no minimum balance

topics.t: Agricultural marketing and regulated markets
topics.h: A farmer grows perfect tomatoes but sells them at a throwaway price because she doesn't know the mandi rate and has no cold storage. Marketing matters as much as farming.
p: Agricultural marketing is the process of assembling, storing, processing, transporting, packaging, grading and distributing farm products across the country.
Before regulation, farmers faced faulty weights, manipulated accounts, no information on market prices, and poor storage, so they often sold at low prices right after harvest.
Measure 1: regulation of markets to create orderly and transparent marketing conditions; this benefits both farmers and consumers.
Measure 2: building physical infrastructure such as roads, railways, warehouses, godowns, cold storages and processing units, which are still inadequate for growing demand.

ex.q: A farmer sells 20 quintals at ₹1,500 per quintal to a trader just after harvest. With storage, she could sell 3 months later at ₹1,800. Ignoring storage cost, how much more would she earn?

topics.rl: Electronic platforms like e-NAM give farmers price information from many mandis, attacking the old problem of no price information.

rv.summary: Agricultural marketing covers every step from farm to consumer. Farmers faced faulty weights, manipulated accounts and no storage or price information, so the government regulated markets and built physical infrastructure.
focus: Define agricultural marketing
List problems farmers faced
Explain regulated markets and infrastructure
remember: Marketing: assembling, storing, processing, transporting, packaging, grading, distributing
Regulated markets: orderly, transparent conditions
Infrastructure: warehouses, godowns, cold storages, processing units
traps: Marketing infrastructure is still inadequate
Prices are not highest just after harvest
Regulation helps both farmers and consumers

topics.t: Cooperatives, MSP and alternate marketing channels
topics.h: A dairy farmer in Anand gets a fair price for milk because she co-owns the cooperative that buys it. That simple idea built Amul.
p: Measure 3: cooperative marketing helps farmers get fair prices. The milk cooperatives of Gujarat transformed the social and economic life of rural Gujarat.

Measure 4: policy instruments: minimum support prices (MSP) for agricultural products, buffer stocks of wheat and rice maintained by the Food Corporation of India (FCI), and distribution of foodgrains and sugar through the public distribution system (PDS).
MSP protects farmers' income; buffer stocks and PDS protect poor consumers' access to food.

Alternate marketing channels let farmers sell directly to consumers: Apni Mandi (Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan), Hadaspar Mandi (Pune), Rythu Bazars (vegetable and fruit markets in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana) and Uzhavar Sandies (farmers' markets in Tamil Nadu).
Contract farming: national and international fast-food chains enter into contracts with farmers to grow produce of a desired quality at pre-announced prices.

ex.q: A trader buys onions from a farmer at ₹15/kg and sells to consumers at ₹30/kg. At a Rythu Bazar the farmer sells directly at ₹24/kg. Who gains and by how much per kg?

topics.rl: Amul, built on Gujarat's milk cooperatives, is a well-known example of cooperative marketing.

rv.summary: Cooperatives (like Gujarat's milk cooperatives), MSP, FCI buffer stocks and PDS support farmers and consumers. Alternate channels such as Apni Mandi, Rythu Bazars and Uzhavar Sandies, and contract farming, connect farmers directly to buyers.
focus: Explain MSP, buffer stocks and PDS
Match alternate marketing channels to states
Explain contract farming
remember: MSP protects farmers; PDS protects poor consumers
FCI keeps buffer stocks
Rythu Bazars: AP and Telangana; Uzhavar Sandies: Tamil Nadu; Apni Mandi: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan; Hadaspar: Pune
traps: PDS mainly protects consumers, not farmers
Don't swap Rythu Bazars and Uzhavar Sandies
MSP is a floor price, not a maximum price

topics.t: Diversification: animal husbandry and fisheries
topics.h: If the monsoon fails, a farmer with only paddy loses everything. A farmer with paddy, two buffaloes and a fish pond still has an income.
p: Diversification has two parts: (1) change in cropping pattern (crop diversification) and (2) shifting part of the workforce from agriculture to allied activities (livestock, poultry, fisheries) and non-farm sectors.
It reduces the risk from depending only on farming and gives productive jobs in the long non-farm season, especially where irrigation is lacking.
Non-farm activities include agro-processing, food processing, leather industry, tourism, and traditional crafts like pottery and handicrafts.

Animal husbandry (cattle, goats, poultry) gives stable income, food security and transport. Operation Flood (launched 1970) organised milk cooperatives, pooling milk from farmers and marketing it; India is the world's largest milk producer.

Fisheries: inland (rivers, lakes, ponds, reservoirs) and marine sources. Problems of fishing communities include low literacy, indebtedness and lack of capital; women play a large role in fish marketing and processing.

ex.q: A farmer earns ₹60,000 a year from crops and ₹40,000 from dairy. A drought cuts crop income by half. What is his total income now, and what fraction came from dairy?

topics.rl: The 'White Revolution' through Operation Flood, led by Verghese Kurien, made India the world's largest milk producer.

rv.summary: Diversification means changing the cropping pattern and shifting part of the workforce to allied activities (livestock, poultry, fisheries) and non-farm work, reducing risk. Operation Flood built milk cooperatives.
focus: Explain the two parts of diversification and why it matters
Classify allied and non-farm activities
Know Operation Flood and fishing problems
remember: Diversification: crops + workforce shift
Operation Flood (1970): milk cooperatives
Fisheries: inland and marine; problems: low literacy, debt, no capital
traps: Diversification shifts part, not all, of the workforce
Food processing is non-farm; sowing is farm work
Operation Flood is about milk, not flood control

topics.t: Horticulture, IT and women in agriculture
topics.h: India grows more mangoes and bananas than any other country, and flowers from Indian farms reach markets abroad. Horticulture is a quiet success story.
p: Horticulture includes fruits, vegetables, tuber crops, flowers, medicinal and aromatic plants, spices and plantation crops.
India has emerged as a world leader in a variety of fruits like mangoes, bananas, coconuts and cashew nuts and a number of spices, and is the second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables.
Horticulture raises incomes and gives employment, especially to women, in floriculture, nursery maintenance, hybrid seed production, tissue culture and food processing.
Information technology helps rural development by giving information on weather, crop practices, prices and government schemes, and can support food security and new jobs in rural areas.

Tamil Nadu Women in Agriculture (TANWA), started in 1986, trains women farmers in the latest agricultural techniques and encourages them to use the knowledge in farming and set up farm women's groups.

ex.q: A farmer shifts 1 acre from wheat (net income ₹20,000/acre) to flowers (net income ₹50,000/acre). How much does her income rise, and by what %?

topics.rl: Ratnagiri's Alphonso mangoes and Kerala's spices are famous horticulture products sold across the world.

rv.summary: Horticulture (fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, plantation crops) raises incomes and employs many women; India is the second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables. IT spreads farm information, and TANWA (1986) trains women farmers.
focus: List horticulture products and benefits
Explain IT's role
Know TANWA
remember: India: second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables
Women's jobs: floriculture, nurseries, hybrid seeds, tissue culture
TANWA: Tamil Nadu Women in Agriculture, 1986
traps: Milk is not a horticulture product
TANWA trains women farmers, not industrial workers
India is second, not first, in fruits and vegetables

topics.t: Organic farming and sustainable rural development
topics.h: Chemical fertilisers boosted yields for decades, but now soils are tired and groundwater is polluted. Organic farming asks: can we grow food the way nature does?
p: Chemical fertilisers and pesticides have harmful effects: they can contaminate soil, water and food, and harm health and the environment.
Organic farming is a whole system of farming that restores, maintains and enhances the ecological balance. It avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides.

Benefits: it replaces costly inputs (HYV seeds, chemical fertilisers, pesticides) with locally produced organic inputs, generates income through exports (there is international demand), gives healthier food, and is more labour-intensive, so it creates jobs.

Limitations: yields can be lower in the initial years, small and marginal farmers may find it hard to adopt, organic produce may have a shorter shelf life, choice in off-season is limited, and awareness and marketing are problems.
Boxes: organic cotton farming in Maharashtra showed it can be viable; the Saansad Adarsh Gram Yojana (2014) asks MPs to develop model villages with better infrastructure and social development.

ex.q: Organic yield is 15 quintals/acre at ₹3,000/quintal; chemical farming yields 20 quintals at ₹2,000/quintal. Ignoring costs, which gives more revenue per acre?
st: Organic gives ₹5,000 more despite lower yield

topics.rl: Sikkim became India's first fully organic state in 2016, a striking example of sustainable rural development.

rv.summary: Organic farming restores ecological balance without synthetic chemicals. It cuts input costs, creates jobs and has export demand, but early yields may be lower and small farmers may struggle to adopt it.
focus: Explain the benefits and limitations of organic farming
Compare revenue from organic and chemical farming
remember: Organic farming: restores, maintains, enhances ecological balance
Benefits: cheaper local inputs, exports, healthy food, more jobs
Limits: lower early yields, shorter shelf life, marketing problems
Saansad Adarsh Gram Yojana (2014): model villages
traps: Chemical fertilisers do harm soil and health
Organic yields may be lower at first
Organic farming is labour-intensive, not labour-saving

topics.ch: IED: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
topics.t: Who is a worker?
topics.h: A farmer's teenage son who helps at harvest is a worker. A mother who cooks for the family all day, without pay, is not counted as one. Why?
p: People work to earn a living, but work also gives a sense of self-worth and dignity and lets people contribute to national income.
A worker is anyone engaged in an economic activity (any activity that contributes to GDP), in whatever capacity, high or low. This includes the self-employed and those who help the main workers.
People temporarily away from work due to illness, injury, bad weather, festivals or social or religious functions are also counted as workers.
India's workforce is large and mostly rural: about two-thirds of workers live in rural areas, and men form the majority of the workforce.
Unpaid household work (cooking, fetching water and fuel, caring for children), mostly done by women, is not counted as economic activity, so many women are not counted as workers.

ex.q: Who are workers? (i) a girl helping her father sell vegetables; (ii) a college student who does not work; (iii) a factory worker on sick leave; (iv) a homemaker cooking for her family.
st: (i) helps in a market activity → worker
(ii) no economic activity → not a worker
(iii) temporarily absent due to illness → worker

topics.rl: A Swiggy rider, a weaver in Varanasi and an ISRO scientist are all workers because each contributes to India's GDP.

rv.summary: A worker is anyone engaged in an economic activity that contributes to GDP, including the self-employed, helpers and those temporarily absent. Unpaid household work is not counted, so many women are left out.
focus: Decide who counts as a worker
Explain why many women are not counted
remember: Worker: anyone in economic activity contributing to GDP
Temporarily absent (illness, festivals) still counted
About two-thirds of workers are rural
traps: Unpaid helpers in a family business are workers
Unpaid household work is not counted
Salary is not required to be a worker

topics.ch: IED: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
topics.t: Worker-population ratio
topics.h: If 35 out of every 100 Indians are working, who is feeding and supporting the other 65? The worker-population ratio tells this story.
p: Worker-population ratio (WPR) = (total number of workers ÷ total population) × 100. It shows what share of the population is actively contributing to production.
A higher WPR means more people are engaged in economic activity; it is an indicator of the employment situation.
In India, WPR is higher for men than for women, and slightly higher in rural areas than in urban areas.
Rural WPR is higher partly because rural people have limited resources and many must work to survive, while many urban youths are in education. Rural women's WPR is higher than urban women's.
Reasons for low female WPR (especially in cities): when men earn higher incomes, families may discourage women from working; much of women's work is unpaid household work, which is not counted.

ex.q: A town has a population of 50,000 and 17,500 workers. Find its WPR. If the population grows to 60,000 with the same WPR, how many workers will there be?

topics.rl: PLFS surveys by the National Statistical Office track India's WPR, and one major policy concern is the low participation of women.

rv.summary: Worker-population ratio = workers ÷ population × 100. In India it is higher for men than women and in rural than urban areas; urban women have the lowest WPR.
focus: Compute WPR and number of workers
Explain rural–urban and male–female differences
remember: WPR = (workers ÷ population) × 100
WPR: men > women; rural > urban
Lowest WPR: urban women
traps: Divide by total population, not the labour force
Women's WPR is lower, not higher, than men's
Low female WPR partly reflects uncounted home work

topics.ch: IED: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
topics.t: Self-employed, regular and casual workers
topics.h: A kirana owner, a bank clerk and a construction labourer all work, but in very different ways: one owns the business, one has a monthly salary, one is paid by the day.
p: Self-employed workers own and operate an enterprise to earn their livelihood: farmers on their own land, shopkeepers, tailors, doctors with their own clinics. This is the largest category in India, about half the workforce.
Hired workers are of two kinds. Regular salaried employees are engaged by someone on a regular basis and paid wages or salaries, often with social security benefits.
Casual wage labourers are not hired regularly, get no social security benefits, and are paid daily or for a task. They are the most vulnerable workers.
Self-employment is larger in rural areas; regular salaried jobs are a much larger share in urban areas. Women are more likely to be self-employed or casual workers than in regular jobs.
Classifying jobs: a fruit seller with his own cart is self-employed; a nurse in a government hospital is a regular salaried employee; a construction labourer hired daily is a casual wage labourer.

ex.q: Classify: (i) a doctor running her own clinic; (ii) an IT engineer with a monthly salary; (iii) a farm labourer paid ₹400 a day at harvest; (iv) a weaver working at his own loom.
st: (ii) hired on a regular basis → regular salaried
(iii) hired daily, no security → casual wage labourer

topics.rl: Construction sites in Indian cities employ many casual wage labourers, often migrants paid by the day.

rv.summary: Workers are self-employed (about half the workforce), regular salaried employees or casual wage labourers. Casual workers are the most vulnerable, and regular jobs are a larger share in cities.
focus: Classify workers by status
Explain why casual workers are vulnerable
remember: Self-employed: own and run an enterprise (largest group)
Hired workers: regular salaried + casual wage labourers
Casual: daily or task pay, no social security
traps: A farmer on his own land is self-employed
Self-employed are not hired workers
Regular jobs are more common in urban than rural areas

topics.ch: IED: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
topics.t: Workers across sectors
topics.h: Most Indian workers still earn a living from the land, even though services now produce the biggest share of GDP.
p: Primary sector: agriculture, forestry and fishing, and mining and quarrying.
Secondary sector: manufacturing, electricity, gas and water supply, and construction.
Tertiary (service) sector: trade, transport and storage, and services such as banking, education, health and IT.
The primary sector is the main source of employment for most workers, especially in rural areas.
In urban areas the tertiary sector employs the largest share of workers. Women in rural areas are concentrated in the primary sector.

ex.q: Classify by sector: (i) a coal miner; (ii) a bricklayer on a construction site; (iii) a bank teller; (iv) a fisherman.

topics.rl: Bengaluru's IT workers belong to the tertiary sector, while Jharkhand's coal miners belong to the primary sector.

rv.summary: The primary sector (agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining) employs most Indian workers; the secondary sector covers manufacturing, utilities and construction; the tertiary sector covers trade, transport and services and dominates urban jobs.
focus: Classify occupations by sector
Know which sector employs most workers
remember: Primary: agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining and quarrying
Secondary: manufacturing, electricity–gas–water, construction
Tertiary: trade, transport, storage, services
traps: Mining is primary, not secondary
Construction and utilities are secondary
Services have the largest GDP share but not the largest workforce share

topics.ch: IED: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
topics.t: Growth, jobless growth and casualisation
topics.h: India's GDP has multiplied many times since 1950, but jobs have not kept pace. Economists call it jobless growth.
p: During 1950–2010, India's GDP grew positively and faster than employment. Employment growth stayed modest (around 2% a year) while output grew much faster.
Jobless growth: the economy produces more goods and services without a matching increase in employment opportunities.
Trends from 1972-73 to 2017-18: the share of the workforce in the primary sector fell and the shares of secondary and tertiary sectors rose; self-employment remained the largest status category.
Casualisation: the process by which workers move from self-employment and regular salaried jobs to casual wage work. It makes workers more vulnerable.
Since growth did not create enough good jobs, many workers moved into casual and informal work.

ex.q: GDP grows by 6% a year and employment by 2% a year. Roughly how fast is output per worker growing? What does this suggest?
st: Output per worker growth ≈ GDP growth − employment growth
Output is growing much faster than jobs → jobless growth tendency
ex.a: About 4% a year; jobs lag output

topics.rl: Rapid growth in capital-intensive and IT-based sectors raised GDP but created relatively few jobs, a key reason for the jobless growth debate.

rv.summary: India's GDP grew faster than employment, a tendency called jobless growth. The primary sector's share of workers fell, and casualisation pushed many into insecure casual work.
focus: Explain jobless growth and casualisation
Estimate output per worker growth
remember: Jobless growth: output rises without matching jobs
Casualisation: shift to casual wage work
Output per worker growth ≈ GDP growth − employment growth
traps: Casualisation reduces, not improves, security
GDP grew faster than employment, not slower
The primary sector's share fell over time

topics.ch: IED: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
topics.t: Formal and informal sectors
topics.h: A clerk at a public sector bank gets a pension and paid leave. A street vendor outside the bank gets neither. One is formal, the other informal.
p: Formal (organised) sector: all public sector establishments and private sector establishments that employ 10 or more hired workers.
Informal (unorganised) sector: farmers, agricultural labourers, owners of small enterprises and people working in them, and self-employed people without hired workers.
Features of informal work: no regular income, no social security (pension, provident fund, gratuity), no protection by labour laws, little ability to form trade unions, and often unsafe conditions.
Only a small share of India's workforce is in the formal sector; most work in the informal sector, and informalisation has increased.
Box: when many Ahmedabad textile mills closed, thousands of permanent workers lost formal jobs and had to take up informal work (like vending and casual labour) at lower, irregular incomes.

ex.q: Classify: (i) a private firm with 25 hired workers; (ii) a family-run sweet shop with 3 helpers; (iii) a government hospital; (iv) a farm labourer.

topics.rl: e-Shram, a national database of unorganised workers, aims to extend social security schemes to informal workers.

rv.summary: The formal sector covers all public establishments and private ones with 10 or more hired workers; everyone else is informal. Most Indian workers are informal and lack social security and legal protection.
focus: Classify establishments as formal or informal
List features of informal work
remember: Formal: public sector + private with 10+ hired workers
Informal: no social security, irregular income, little legal protection
Most workers are informal
traps: Not all private firms are formal
Laid-off formal workers often move to informal work
Informal workers rarely have pensions or unions

topics.ch: IED: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
topics.t: Unemployment and its types
topics.h: Five brothers work on a small farm that needs only three. Remove two, and output stays the same. Those two are 'employed', yet not really. That's disguised unemployment.
p: NSO definition: unemployment is a situation in which people who, owing to lack of work, are not working but either seek work (through employment exchanges, intermediaries, friends or relatives, or applications) or express willingness to work at prevailing conditions of work and wages.
Sources of data: Census reports, NSO's reports (Periodic Labour Force Survey) and employment exchange data (DGET).
Open unemployment: people willing and able to work are without any job; common in urban and industrial areas.
Disguised unemployment: more people are working than needed; their marginal product is zero, so removing them does not reduce output. Common in agriculture.

Seasonal unemployment: people are unemployed during certain months of the year, e.g. farm workers between harvest and sowing. Educated unemployment: educated people cannot find jobs matching their qualifications.

ex.q: A farm produces 100 quintals with 5 workers. With 3 workers it still produces 100 quintals. How many are disguisedly unemployed? What is their marginal product?
st: Output does not change when 2 workers are removed

topics.rl: MGNREGA work demand often rises in the lean agricultural season, reflecting seasonal unemployment in rural India.

rv.summary: Unemployment means people seeking or willing to work cannot find work. Types include open, disguised (zero marginal product, common in agriculture), seasonal and educated unemployment, measured through Census, NSO's PLFS and employment exchanges.
focus: Identify types of unemployment
Compute disguised unemployment
Know the data sources
remember: Disguised: extra workers with zero marginal product
Seasonal: idle between harvest and sowing
Data: Census, NSO (PLFS), employment exchanges
traps: Disguised unemployed workers add nothing to output
SEBI is not a source of unemployment data
Open unemployment is mostly urban

topics.ch: IED: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
topics.t: Government and employment generation
topics.h: In 2005, India made a promise to rural households: if you want unskilled manual work, the government will provide at least 100 days a year.
p: Direct employment: the government employs people in its departments for administrative purposes and runs industries, hotels and transport companies, providing jobs directly.
Indirect employment: when output from government enterprises increases, private firms that buy their output or supply them also expand and hire more workers.
Employment generation and poverty alleviation programmes provide jobs and also infrastructure like roads, irrigation and housing.

MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act), 2005: it guarantees 100 days of wage employment in a year to rural households whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work.

ex.q: A rural household has two adults willing to do unskilled work. Under MGNREGA, how many days of guaranteed employment does the household get in a year? If the wage is ₹250 a day, what can it earn?
st: The guarantee is per household, not per person: 100 days

topics.rl: MGNREGA works such as farm ponds, check dams and village roads create rural assets while giving wage employment.

rv.summary: The government creates jobs directly in its departments and enterprises, and indirectly through linked private firms. MGNREGA (2005) guarantees 100 days of wage work a year to rural households doing unskilled manual work, while also building infrastructure.
focus: Distinguish direct and indirect employment generation
Know MGNREGA's provisions
remember: MGNREGA 2005: 100 days per rural household per year
For adult members volunteering unskilled manual work
Direct: government hires; indirect: linked private firms expand
traps: The 100 days are per household, not per individual
MGNREGA is rural, not urban
Indirect employment is through private firms, not government hiring

topics.t: Environment and its four functions
topics.h: The air you breathe, the river that carries away a city's waste, the forest full of species, and the Himalayan view from a hill station: the environment does all of this for free.
p: Environment is the total planetary inheritance and the totality of all resources. It includes biotic factors (living things: plants, animals, birds) and abiotic factors (non-living things: air, water, land, rocks, sunlight).

Function 1: it supplies resources, both renewable (trees, fish, which can be used without exhaustion if extraction stays within regeneration) and non-renewable (fossil fuels, minerals, which get exhausted with use).
Function 2: it assimilates waste produced by human activity.
Function 3: it sustains life by providing genetic diversity and biodiversity.
Function 4: it provides aesthetic services such as scenery and natural beauty.

ex.q: Identify the environmental function: (i) a river diluting and carrying away waste; (ii) coal used in a power plant; (iii) tourists enjoying the Valley of Flowers; (iv) a forest rich in many species.
st: (iv) many species → sustains life through biodiversity
ex.a: (i) waste assimilation, (ii) resource supply, (iii) aesthetic, (iv) biodiversity

topics.rl: Kaziranga's rhinos (biodiversity), the Ganga absorbing waste (assimilation) and Kashmir's valleys (aesthetics) show the environment's many roles in India.

rv.summary: The environment is the total planetary inheritance of biotic and abiotic resources. It supplies renewable and non-renewable resources, assimilates waste, sustains life through biodiversity and provides aesthetic services.
focus: Name the four functions of the environment with examples
Classify renewable and non-renewable, biotic and abiotic
remember: Functions: supply resources, assimilate waste, sustain life, aesthetic services
Renewable: regenerates if extraction ≤ regeneration
Non-renewable: fossil fuels, minerals
traps: Coal and natural gas are non-renewable
Water and air are abiotic
Renewables can run out if over-extracted

topics.t: Carrying capacity and the environmental crisis
topics.h: A pond can support a few fishermen forever. Add a hundred trawlers and it collapses. That limit is called carrying capacity.
p: The environment can perform its functions only if it stays within its carrying capacity: resource extraction must not exceed the rate of regeneration, and wastes generated must stay within the environment's assimilating capacity.
Absorptive capacity is the ability of the environment to absorb degradation.
An environmental crisis arises when the demand for environmental resources and services exceeds their supply (for example, when pollution and extraction outrun the environment's capacity).
Today, with population and affluence growing, the demand for environmental services is much higher than in the past, while supply is limited and falling.
Opportunity costs of environmental damage are high: polluted air and water raise health costs; water, once free, has become an economic good that people must pay for (bottled water, purifiers).

ex.q: A forest regenerates 500 tonnes of wood a year. A village extracts 650 tonnes a year. Is this within carrying capacity? What happens over time?
st: The stock falls by 150 tonnes a year
The forest shrinks: carrying capacity is exceeded
ex.a: No; the forest will be depleted

topics.rl: Families in Delhi buying air purifiers and households across India buying bottled water show the rising opportunity cost of a degraded environment.

rv.summary: The environment works within its carrying capacity only if extraction stays below regeneration and wastes stay within assimilative capacity. When demand for its services exceeds supply there is an environmental crisis, with high opportunity costs.
focus: State the conditions of carrying capacity
Explain the environmental crisis and its costs
remember: Carrying capacity: extraction < regeneration and waste < assimilative capacity
Crisis: demand for environmental services > supply
Absorptive capacity: ability to absorb degradation
traps: Degradation has economic costs (health, water)
Over-extraction shrinks the stock year after year
Water is now an economic good, not free

topics.t: Global warming and ozone depletion
topics.h: Two global problems, two global treaties: Kyoto for greenhouse gases, Montreal for the ozone layer.
p: Global warming is the gradual increase in the average temperature of the earth's lower atmosphere, due to a rise in greenhouse gases (like carbon dioxide and methane) since the Industrial Revolution.
Causes: burning fossil fuels, deforestation, and other human activities. Effects: melting of polar ice, rising sea levels, coastal flooding, changes in rainfall and disruption of ecosystems.
The Kyoto Protocol (1997, Kyoto, Japan) was an international agreement under which industrialised countries agreed to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

Ozone depletion is the thinning of the ozone layer in the stratosphere, which protects us from ultraviolet (UV) radiation. It is caused mainly by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs, used as coolants and in aerosols) and halons (used in fire extinguishers).
UV radiation can cause skin cancer and harm crops and marine life. The Montreal Protocol (1987) was adopted to phase out CFCs and other ozone-depleting chemicals.

ex.q: Match each cause to its problem: (i) CFCs from old refrigerators; (ii) burning coal in power plants; (iii) cutting down forests.
st: Burning coal adds CO₂ → global warming
Deforestation reduces CO₂ absorption → global warming

topics.rl: Rising sea levels threaten low-lying coastal areas like the Sundarbans, a reminder of how global warming affects India.

rv.summary: Global warming is the rising average temperature of the lower atmosphere due to greenhouse gases; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) set emission cuts for industrialised countries. Ozone depletion by CFCs and halons lets in UV radiation; the Montreal Protocol (1987) phases them out.
focus: Explain the causes and effects of global warming
Explain ozone depletion
Match protocols to problems and years
remember: Kyoto Protocol 1997: greenhouse gas cuts
Montreal Protocol 1987: phase out CFCs
CFCs and halons deplete ozone; UV causes skin cancer
traps: Don't swap Kyoto (1997) and Montreal (1987)
Deforestation worsens warming
Ozone depletion and global warming are different problems

topics.t: State of India's environment
topics.h: India supports about 17% of the world's people and 20% of its livestock on just 2.5% of the world's land. Imagine the pressure on every hectare!
p: India has a rich natural resource base: fertile soils (e.g. Indo-Gangetic plains, black soil of the Deccan), many rivers, forests, and mineral deposits like iron ore, coal and natural gas.
Twin threats: poverty-induced environmental degradation (poor people depending on fragile resources) and pollution from affluence and a rapidly growing industrial sector.
Priority environmental issues: land degradation, biodiversity loss, air pollution (especially vehicular pollution in cities), management of fresh water, and solid waste management.

Causes of land degradation: deforestation, unsustainable fuelwood and fodder extraction, shifting cultivation, encroachment of forest land, forest fires and overgrazing, poor soil conservation, improper crop rotation, indiscriminate use of agro-chemicals, poor irrigation planning, over-extraction of groundwater, open access resources and poverty.

Pressure figures: India has about 17% of the world's population and 20% of its livestock on 2.5% of the world's geographical area; per capita forest land is only about 0.08 hectare against about 0.47 hectare needed for basic needs. The number of vehicles has grown sharply, worsening urban air pollution.

ex.q: Per capita forest land in India is about 0.08 hectare, while about 0.47 hectare is needed. What is the shortfall per person?

topics.rl: Delhi's winter smog, groundwater depletion in Punjab and mountains of urban garbage are examples of India's priority environmental issues.

rv.summary: India has rich natural resources but faces twin threats: poverty-induced degradation and pollution from affluence and industry. Its land is under pressure, with 17% of the world's people and 20% of its livestock on 2.5% of the area.
focus: List priority environmental issues
Explain causes of land degradation
Recall the pressure figures
remember: 17% of population, 20% of livestock, 2.5% of area
Per capita forest land ≈ 0.08 ha vs 0.47 ha needed
Priorities: land degradation, biodiversity, air pollution, fresh water, solid waste
traps: Overgrazing causes, not prevents, degradation
Vehicular pollution is mainly urban
Per capita forest land is 0.08 ha, not 0.47 ha

topics.t: People's movements and pollution control boards
topics.h: In the Himalayan villages of the 1970s, people hugged trees to stop them being felled. A decade later, villagers in Karnataka did the same. Both became symbols of conservation.
p: Chipko movement: started in the Himalayas (in today's Uttarakhand) in the 1970s; villagers, especially women, hugged trees to prevent felling.
Appiko movement: a similar movement in Karnataka (from 1983, in the Western Ghats region); 'appiko' means to hug.
Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) was set up in 1974; State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) work in the states.

Their functions include: investigating, collecting and sharing information on water, air and land pollution; laying down standards for sewage and industrial effluent and emissions; giving technical help to governments; promoting research; and planning programmes to prevent and control pollution.
They also monitor air quality in cities and water quality in rivers, wells and lakes.

ex.q: Which body would set standards for effluents released by a factory into a river, and which movement is known for hugging trees in Karnataka?
st: Standards for effluents → Central/State Pollution Control Boards

topics.rl: The CPCB publishes the National Air Quality Index, which tells city residents how polluted their air is each day.

rv.summary: People's movements like Chipko (Himalayas, 1970s) and Appiko (Karnataka, 1983) protected forests by hugging trees. The CPCB (1974) and state boards set pollution standards and monitor air and water quality.
focus: Know Chipko and Appiko
List functions of pollution control boards
remember: Chipko: Himalayas (Uttarakhand), 1970s
Appiko: Karnataka, 1983; means 'to hug'
CPCB set up 1974
traps: Appiko is in Karnataka, not Uttarakhand
Pollution boards set standards; they don't collect taxes
Both movements aimed to save forests

topics.t: Sustainable development: meaning and ideas
topics.h: Use the planet today in a way that your grandchildren can use it too. That simple idea is sustainable development.
p: The UN Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) defined sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present generation without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. The idea was popularised by the Brundtland Commission.
This implies intergenerational equity: we should hand over to the next generation at least as good a quality of life and stock of resources as we inherited.

Edward Barbier: sustainable development is directly concerned with raising the material standard of living of the poor at the grassroots level (more food, real income, education, health care, sanitation and water supply).

Herman Daly's requirements: (1) limit population to the environment's carrying capacity; (2) technological progress should be input-efficient, not input-consuming; (3) renewable resources should be extracted sustainably (not above regeneration); (4) depletion of non-renewables should not exceed the rate of creating renewable substitutes; (5) inefficiencies from pollution should be corrected.
The UN's Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): 17 goals adopted in 2015, to be achieved by 2030.

ex.q: A town uses up 100 units of a non-renewable fuel a year and creates renewable substitutes (like solar) of 60 units a year. Does it meet Daly's rule?
st: Daly: depletion of non-renewables ≤ creation of renewable substitutes
So the rule is not met; it must expand renewables or cut depletion
ex.a: No, depletion exceeds substitute creation by 40 units

topics.rl: India's commitments under the SDGs, from clean water to clean energy, are tracked by NITI Aayog's SDG India Index.

rv.summary: Sustainable development meets present needs without compromising future generations, implying intergenerational equity. Barbier stresses raising the poor's living standards, Daly gives rules for staying within environmental limits, and the UN adopted 17 SDGs in 2015.
focus: Define sustainable development and intergenerational equity
List Herman Daly's requirements
Know Barbier's view and the SDGs
remember: UNCED definition: present needs without compromising future generations
Daly: population within carrying capacity, input-efficient technology, sustainable extraction, substitutes, correct pollution
17 SDGs adopted 2015, for 2030
traps: It does not sacrifice present needs
Technology should be input-efficient, not input-consuming
Barbier, not Daly, focused on the poor at the grassroots

topics.t: Clean energy strategies for sustainable development
topics.h: Rooftop solar in Gujarat, windmills in Tamil Nadu, CNG buses in Delhi, gobar gas in villages: India's energy shift is already visible.
p: Use non-conventional (renewable) sources instead of thermal power (which pollutes) and large hydro power (which can flood land and disturb ecosystems).

LPG and gobar gas in rural areas: replace fuelwood and dung cakes that cause indoor air pollution and deforestation. Gobar gas (biogas) is made from cattle dung, and the slurry left over is a good manure.
CNG in urban transport: Delhi shifted public transport to CNG, which helped reduce air pollution.
Wind power uses wind to turn turbines; solar power uses photovoltaic (PV) cells to turn sunlight into electricity. India and France launched the International Solar Alliance in 2015.
Mini-hydel plants: small hydro plants on mountain streams generate electricity for local areas without the environmental damage of large dams.

ex.q: A village family burns fuelwood for cooking. Suggest two cleaner options and one benefit of each.
st: Gobar gas: uses cattle dung, gives fuel and the slurry is good manure

topics.rl: The Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana provides LPG connections to poor households, cutting indoor smoke from traditional fuels.

rv.summary: Clean energy strategies replace thermal and large hydro power with renewables: LPG and gobar gas in villages, CNG in city transport (as in Delhi), wind, solar PV and mini-hydel plants. India and France launched the International Solar Alliance in 2015.
focus: Name clean energy options and their benefits
Explain why thermal power is discouraged
remember: Gobar gas from cattle dung; slurry is manure
Delhi shifted public transport to CNG
Solar PV turns sunlight into electricity
International Solar Alliance 2015: India and France
traps: Wind is renewable
Mini-hydel avoids big-dam damage
Thermal power pollutes

topics.t: Traditional knowledge, composting and biopest control
topics.h: Long before chemical pesticides, Indian farmers used neem leaves and let owls and snakes guard their fields. Old wisdom, new relevance.
p: Traditional knowledge and practices: Indians have long lived close to nature; systems like Ayurveda, Unani, Tibetan and folk medicine use plants. Herbal products and cosmetics are regaining popularity.
Biocomposting: converting organic waste into compost. Vermicomposting uses earthworms to turn organic matter into compost quickly, replacing chemical fertilisers.

Biopest control: using natural methods instead of chemical pesticides, such as neem-based pesticides, mixed cropping and crop rotation, and natural predators like birds, lizards, snakes and owls that eat pests.
Classification practice: renewable vs non-renewable resources; functions of the environment; causes of land degradation.
Every local community can adopt sustainable strategies, such as composting kitchen waste, rainwater harvesting and using solar lamps.

ex.q: A farmer wants to cut pesticide costs. Suggest three biopest control methods.
st: Practise crop rotation and mixed cropping
Protect birds, owls, snakes and lizards that eat pests

topics.rl: Many Indian cities now encourage households to compost kitchen waste, turning garbage into manure for gardens.

rv.summary: Traditional knowledge (Ayurveda, Unani, folk medicine), biocomposting and vermicomposting, and biopest control with neem, crop rotation and natural predators offer sustainable alternatives to chemicals.
focus: Explain composting and vermicomposting
List biopest control methods
remember: Vermicomposting uses earthworms
Biopest control: neem, mixed cropping, crop rotation, natural predators
Traditional medicine: Ayurveda, Unani, Tibetan, folk
traps: Biopest control avoids synthetic pesticides
Natural gas is non-renewable
Crop rotation breaks pest cycles

topics.ch: IED: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
topics.t: Neighbours on similar paths
topics.h: India, China and Pakistan started their modern journeys within a few years of each other. Seventy years later, their economies look very different. Comparing them is a great way to learn what works.
p: Countries form regional and economic groupings to strengthen their economies and understand their neighbours: SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation), the European Union (EU), ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations), G-20 and BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa).
Comparing development paths helps a country learn from the strengths and weaknesses of its neighbours.
India and Pakistan became independent in 1947; the People's Republic of China was established in 1949.

All three began planned development at similar times: India announced its First Five Year Plan for 1951–56, China its first Five Year Plan in 1953, and Pakistan its first Five Year Plan in 1956 (now called the Medium Term Development Plan).
Until the late 1970s, all three had similar growth rates and per capita incomes.

ex.q: Arrange the start of the first Five Year Plans of India, China and Pakistan in time order.

topics.rl: India hosted the G-20 summit in New Delhi in 2023 and is a founding member of BRICS and SAARC.

rv.summary: Countries form groupings like SAARC, EU, ASEAN, G-20 and BRICS and compare development with neighbours. India (1947), Pakistan (1947) and China (1949) began planning at similar times and had similar development until the late 1970s.
focus: Know regional groupings
Recall the start years of the first plans
remember: First plans: India 1951, China 1953, Pakistan 1956
PRC established 1949
BRICS: Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa
traps: SAARC is South Asian; ASEAN is Southeast Asian
Don't mix up the 1951, 1953 and 1956 plan years
China's founding year does not explain similar development

topics.ch: IED: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
topics.t: China: from the Great Leap Forward to the 1978 reforms
topics.h: In 1958 China tried to industrialise overnight with steel furnaces in backyards. It failed badly. Twenty years later, a gentler, step-by-step approach transformed the country.
p: Great Leap Forward (GLF), 1958: aimed at industrialising the country on a massive scale. People were encouraged to set up industries in their backyards. In rural areas, communes were started for collective farming.
The GLF faced many problems: a severe drought caused huge loss of life (about 3 crore people died), and a conflict with Russia led it to withdraw its professionals.
Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution (1966–76): students and professionals were sent to work and learn in the countryside.

1978 reforms were introduced in phases. Initial phase: agriculture, foreign trade and investment. Commune land was divided into small plots allotted (for use, not ownership) to households, who could keep income after paying taxes (household responsibility system). Later phase: industry; private firms and township and village enterprises (TVEs), owned and run by local collectives, could produce goods.
Dual pricing: farmers and firms bought and sold fixed quantities at government-fixed prices and the rest at market prices. Special Economic Zones (SEZs) were set up to attract foreign investors.

ex.q: Under dual pricing, a farmer must sell 60 tonnes to the state at ¥2,000/tonne and sells 40 tonnes in the market at ¥3,000/tonne. Find total revenue.

topics.rl: Shenzhen, once a fishing town, grew into a huge manufacturing city after becoming one of China's first SEZs.

rv.summary: China's Great Leap Forward (1958) pushed massive industrialisation and communes but failed; the Cultural Revolution ran 1966–76. Reforms from 1978 brought the household responsibility system, TVEs, dual pricing and SEZs.
focus: Know the GLF and Cultural Revolution
Explain the 1978 reforms
remember: GLF 1958: backyard industries, communes
Cultural Revolution 1966–76
Reforms 1978: household responsibility, TVEs, dual pricing, SEZs
traps: The GLF was not a success
Commune land was allotted for use, not ownership
TVEs were owned by local collectives

topics.ch: IED: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
topics.t: Pakistan's development path
topics.h: Pakistan started with a mixed economy like India's, swung towards nationalisation, then swung back. Its growth story is tied to remittances from workers in the Gulf.
p: Pakistan followed a mixed economy model with both public and private sectors.
In the late 1950s and 1960s it introduced import substitution industrialisation, combining tariff protection for consumer goods industries with direct import controls on competing imports.
The green revolution brought mechanisation and more public investment in infrastructure in select areas, raising foodgrain output and changing the agrarian structure.
In the 1970s, capital goods industries were nationalised. In the late 1970s and 1980s, policy shifted to denationalisation and encouraging the private sector.
During this period Pakistan received financial support from Western nations and remittances from emigrants working in the Middle East. Economic reforms were initiated in 1988.

ex.q: Put Pakistan's policy phases in order and name one feature of each.
st: 1950s–60s: import substitution with tariffs and import controls
Late 1970s–80s: denationalisation and private sector push

topics.rl: Remittances from Pakistani workers in the Gulf remain one of the country's major sources of foreign exchange.

rv.summary: Pakistan followed a mixed economy: import substitution with tariffs and import controls (1950s–60s), green revolution, nationalisation of capital goods (1970s), then denationalisation (late 1970s–80s), with reforms from 1988.
focus: Order Pakistan's policy phases
Know its sources of external support
remember: Import substitution: tariffs + direct import controls
1970s nationalisation; late 1970s–80s denationalisation
Reforms 1988; remittances from the Middle East
traps: Pakistan was mixed, not purely socialist
Pakistan's reforms began in 1988, not 1978 or 1991
Don't give Pakistan China's SEZs or TVEs

topics.ch: IED: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
topics.t: Demographic indicators compared
topics.h: China's one-child norm slowed population growth dramatically, but created a new problem: too few young people to care for a growing elderly population.
p: Demographic indicators compared: population size, annual population growth rate, density (people per sq km), sex ratio, fertility rate and urbanisation.
Among the three, Pakistan has the highest population growth rate and fertility rate; China has the lowest fertility rate and the highest urbanisation; India has the highest population density.

China introduced the one-child norm in the late 1970s. It sharply reduced population growth, but led to a falling sex ratio and, a few decades later, a larger share of elderly people relative to young workers. (China has since relaxed the policy.)
The sex ratio is low and biased against females in all three countries, which NCERT attributes to son preference.
Population growth rate = (change in population ÷ base population) × 100 per year.

ex.q: A country's population grows from 200 million to 204 million in a year. Find the growth rate. What would the population be after another year at the same rate?

topics.rl: India's own family planning efforts and rising female education have brought its fertility rate down sharply over recent decades.

rv.summary: Pakistan has the highest population growth and fertility, China the lowest fertility and highest urbanisation, and India the highest density. China's one-child norm slowed growth but led to an ageing population, and son preference lowers sex ratios in all three.
focus: Compare demographic indicators
Explain effects of the one-child norm
Compute population growth rates
remember: One-child norm: China, late 1970s
Highest density: India; highest urbanisation: China; highest fertility: Pakistan
Low sex ratio due to son preference
traps: Pakistan has the highest, not lowest, growth rate
The one-child norm led to more elderly, not more young people
India, not China, has the highest density

topics.ch: IED: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
topics.t: GDP and sectoral structure compared
topics.h: China went from farms to factories to offices. India and Pakistan skipped the factory stage and jumped straight to services. That one difference explains a lot.
p: GDP (measured at purchasing power parity) is largest for China, followed by India, with Pakistan far behind.
In the 1980s China grew at close to double digits, far faster than India and Pakistan, and Pakistan grew faster than India in that decade. Later, growth slowed (decelerated) in Pakistan and in China.

In all three countries, agriculture's share of the workforce is much larger than its share of GVA, meaning low output per worker in farming. China's share of workforce in agriculture is the lowest of the three.
China's industry (manufacturing) has a large share of GVA. In India and Pakistan, the service sector contributes the largest share of GVA.
Structural change: China moved from agriculture to manufacturing and then to services; India and Pakistan moved largely from agriculture directly to services.

ex.q: Agriculture employs 43% of a country's workers but gives 16% of GVA. What does this say about productivity in agriculture compared with the rest of the economy?
st: Output share (16%) is far below workforce share (43%)
Output per worker in agriculture ≈ 16/43 of the average
So productivity in farming is low compared with other sectors

topics.rl: China is often called the 'factory of the world', while India's growth has been led by services like IT and finance.

rv.summary: China has the largest GDP (PPP) and grew fastest in the 1980s, with Pakistan ahead of India then; growth later slowed in China and Pakistan. China moved through manufacturing to services, while India and Pakistan moved largely from agriculture to services.
focus: Compare GDP and growth rates
Compare sectoral structure and paths of change
remember: Largest GDP (PPP): China
1980s: China fastest; Pakistan faster than India
China: agriculture → manufacturing → services; India, Pakistan: agriculture → services
Agriculture: workforce share ≫ GVA share
traps: India did not follow China's manufacturing-first path
Services, not manufacturing, lead GVA in India and Pakistan
Growth decelerated later in China and Pakistan

topics.ch: IED: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
topics.t: Human development and liberty compared
topics.h: Growth figures tell one story; life expectancy, child survival and freedom tell another. Here's how the three neighbours compare on people's lives.
p: Human Development Index (HDI) combines life expectancy, education (schooling) and per capita income. Among the three, China ranks highest on HDI, India comes next and Pakistan is lowest.
China performs better than India and Pakistan on most human development indicators: higher life expectancy and per capita income, and much lower infant and maternal mortality.
Other indicators compared include access to improved sanitation, drinking water and malnutrition among children.

Liberty indicators are a missing dimension of the HDI: the extent of democratic participation in social and political decision-making, protection of civil rights and the rule of law, including an independent judiciary.
If liberty indicators were included, the ranking of countries might change, because countries differ widely in democratic participation, civil rights and the rule of law.

ex.q: Infant mortality is the number of infants dying before age one per 1,000 live births. A district has 25,000 live births and 700 infant deaths. Find its IMR.

topics.rl: Indian voters choosing their governments in elections is an example of the liberty indicators that the HDI does not capture.

rv.summary: On HDI (life expectancy, education, per capita income) China ranks highest, India next and Pakistan lowest. Liberty indicators such as democratic participation and the rule of law are missing from the HDI and could change rankings.
focus: Rank the three countries on HDI
Explain liberty indicators
Compute IMR
remember: HDI: life expectancy, education, per capita income
HDI ranking: China > India > Pakistan
Liberty indicators: democratic participation, civil rights, rule of law
traps: Liberty indicators are not part of the HDI
Including liberty could change rankings
IMR is per 1,000 live births

topics.ch: IED: Comparative Development Experiences of India and its Neighbours
topics.t: Appraising development strategies
topics.h: Why did China race ahead while Pakistan slowed down and India moved at a steady pace? The answers lie in when, why and how each country reformed.
p: China's reforms were self-initiated, not forced by a crisis or by IMF and World Bank conditions. Earlier investments in education, health, land reforms and decentralised planning had built strong social infrastructure that helped growth take off.
China tried reforms on a small scale first and expanded them when they succeeded (experimental scaling). This allowed growth with relatively low risk.
Pakistan's slowdown: political instability, over-dependence on remittances and foreign aid, and volatile agricultural performance (dependent on good harvests). Many reforms were not sustained.
India began wide reforms after the 1991 BoP crisis. India still needs to raise sustainable growth in manufacturing and manufactured exports, and to create more jobs.

Data activity: exports as a percentage of imports = (exports ÷ imports) × 100. A value below 100 means imports exceed exports (a trade deficit). Since the late 1970s, the three countries' outcomes have diverged sharply.

ex.q: A country's exports are $300 billion and imports $400 billion. Find exports as a percentage of imports. What does it show?
st: Below 100% → imports exceed exports: a trade deficit

topics.rl: China's pilot SEZs before nationwide reforms are a well-known case of experimenting small before scaling up.

rv.summary: China's self-initiated reforms built on strong social infrastructure and experimental scaling; Pakistan's growth slowed due to political instability, dependence on remittances and aid, and volatile farming; India reformed after the 1991 crisis and still needs manufacturing growth and jobs.
focus: Explain why China succeeded and Pakistan slowed
Compute exports as a percentage of imports
remember: China: self-initiated reforms, prior social investment, experimental scaling
Pakistan: instability, remittances and aid dependence, volatile agriculture
Exports ÷ imports × 100 < 100% ⇒ trade deficit
traps: India's reforms followed a crisis
China's reforms were not forced by the IMF
A ratio above 100% is a surplus, not a deficit

qa.q: Which of the following is a macroeconomic variable?
qa.a: The general price level
qa.e: Macroeconomics deals with aggregates for the whole economy; the general price level is an aggregate.

qa.q: Macroeconomic analysis often treats all goods as a single 'representative good' mainly because
qa.a: it simplifies the study of the whole economy by aggregating many markets
qa.e: Aggregation lets economists talk about total output and the general price level without studying each market separately.

qa.q: Which of these is an economic agent?
qa.a: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
qa.e: Economic agents are individuals or institutions that take economic decisions. SEBI takes decisions regulating the share market.

qa.q: Which pair correctly shows a micro and a macro question?
qa.a: Micro: price of cotton; Macro: rate of inflation
qa.e: Price of one good is micro; the overall inflation rate is macro.

qa.q: Which is NOT usually listed as a macroeconomic policy goal?
qa.a: Maximising the profit of one particular firm
qa.e: Macro policy aims at goals for the economy as a whole; one firm's profit is a micro concern.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Macroeconomics studies the determination of national income and employment. Reason (R): Macroeconomics deals with aggregates of the whole economy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: National income and employment are aggregates, which is exactly why macroeconomics studies them.

qa.q: A study of how a rise in the price of petrol affects the demand for scooters is an example of
qa.a: microeconomics
qa.e: It examines individual markets (petrol and scooters), so it is a micro study.

qa.q: Why do macroeconomists study aggregate rather than disaggregated data?
qa.a: To understand how the economy as a whole behaves, such as total output and the price level
qa.e: Aggregates show the overall picture (growth, inflation, jobs) that policy-makers need.

qa.q: Who wrote 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776) and is regarded as the founder of modern economics?
qa.a: Adam Smith
qa.e: Adam Smith published 'The Wealth of Nations' in 1776; the classical tradition grew from his ideas.

qa.q: According to the classical economists, an economy left to free markets would
qa.a: tend to full employment automatically as wages and prices adjust
qa.e: Classical economists believed flexible wages and prices would clear the labour and goods markets.

qa.q: During the Great Depression the unemployment rate in the USA rose from about 3% to about
qa.e: From 1929 to 1933 the US unemployment rate rose from about 3% to about 25%.

qa.q: In an economy 9,500 people are employed and 500 are seeking work but unemployed. What is the unemployment rate?
qa.e: Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100 = 500 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = 5%.

qa.q: Which people are counted in the labour force?
qa.a: Those who are working and those who are looking for work
qa.e: The labour force includes the employed plus the unemployed who are actively seeking work.

qa.q: The labour force of a district is 80,000 and its unemployment rate is 6%. How many people are unemployed?
Assertion (A): The Great Depression weakened faith in the classical theory. Reason (R): Output and employment stayed low for years instead of recovering quickly on their own.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Classical theory predicted quick self-correction; the long slump contradicted that, so R explains A.

qa.q: When did the Great Depression begin?
qa.e: The Great Depression started in 1929; 1936 is the year Keynes's General Theory appeared.

qa.q: 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' was written by
qa.a: John Maynard Keynes
qa.e: Keynes published the General Theory in 1936.

qa.q: In which year was Keynes's General Theory published?
qa.e: It was published in 1936, seven years after the Depression began.

qa.q: Keynes's main idea was that the level of output and employment is determined by
qa.a: aggregate (effective) demand
qa.e: Keynes said aggregate demand decides how much is produced and how many people are employed.

qa.q: Which is NOT a feature of a capitalist economy?
qa.a: Production mainly for self-consumption
qa.e: Capitalist production is for the market, not for one's own use.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Macroeconomics emerged as a separate branch after Keynes. Reason (R): Keynes analysed the working of the economy as a whole, focusing on aggregate demand.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Keynes's whole-economy approach is exactly why his work founded macroeconomics.

qa.q: A capitalist in NCERT's sense is a person who
qa.a: owns a firm, hires workers and sells output for profit
qa.e: Capitalists own the means of production and hire wage labour to produce for the market.

qa.q: Which statement best describes the Keynesian view compared with the classical view?
qa.a: Unemployment can persist for a long time unless demand increases
qa.e: Keynes rejected automatic quick self-correction and stressed demand.

qa.q: In a capitalist economy, the price paid for labour services is called the
qa.a: wage rate
qa.e: Labour is bought and sold at the wage rate; rent, interest and profit go to other factors.

qa.q: The reward for entrepreneurship is
qa.a: profit
qa.e: The entrepreneur bears risk and earns the residual surplus called profit.

qa.q: Interest is the reward paid for the use of
qa.a: capital
qa.e: Capital earns interest; land earns rent.

qa.q: Which role is unique to the entrepreneur?
qa.a: Bearing the risk of loss while organising production
qa.e: Risk-bearing and decision-making mark the entrepreneur; profit rewards it.

qa.q: Investment expenditure by firms on new machines
qa.a: adds to the productive capacity of the economy
qa.e: New capital goods raise the economy's ability to produce in future.

qa.q: A firm pays ₹3 lakh as wages, ₹1 lakh as rent and ₹50,000 as interest. Its revenue is ₹6 lakh and it has no other costs. What is the profit (in ₹)?
Assertion (A): The entrepreneur earns profit. Reason (R): Profit is the reward for bearing risk and uncertainty in production.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Profit exists because the entrepreneur bears risk, so R explains A.

qa.q: Rent is the reward for
qa.a: land
qa.e: Land (natural resources) earns rent.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of investment expenditure?
qa.a: A textile mill buying new looms
qa.e: Buying capital goods like looms is investment; the others are consumption or transfers.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the four sectors in the simple macro model?
qa.a: Trade unions
qa.e: The four sectors are households, firms, government and the external sector.

qa.q: Which sector supplies factor services such as labour?
qa.a: Households
qa.e: Households own factors of production and supply their services to firms.

qa.q: Imports, exports and capital flows belong to the
qa.a: external sector
qa.e: The external sector covers dealings with the rest of the world.

qa.q: Which of these is a function of the government sector?
qa.a: Imposing taxes and spending on public services
qa.e: Government makes laws, taxes and spends, and regulates the economy.

qa.q: An economy that has no dealings with the rest of the world is called a
qa.a: closed economy
qa.e: A closed economy has no external sector.

qa.q: A foreign company buying shares of an Indian firm is an example of
qa.a: a capital flow in the external sector
qa.e: Purchase of Indian assets by foreigners is a capital inflow.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In the four-sector model, firms make payments to households. Reason (R): Households supply factor services to firms.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Firms pay wages, rent, interest and profit because households provide the factors.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.a: Government: enforcing laws and contracts
qa.e: Enforcing laws and contracts is a government role; the others are wrongly paired.

qa.q: Why are only final goods included in national income?
qa.a: To avoid double counting of intermediate goods
qa.e: The value of intermediate goods is already included in the value of final goods; adding them again would count them twice.

qa.q: Which of these is a final good?
qa.a: A mobile phone bought by a college student
qa.e: The phone is for final use; the others are inputs for further production.

qa.q: A machine bought by a factory is
qa.a: a final (capital) good
qa.e: Machines are used repeatedly in production and are not used up in one year, so they are final capital goods.

qa.q: A car bought by a household is classified as a
qa.a: consumer durable
qa.e: It is used for consumption over many years, so it is a consumer durable.

qa.q: Whether a good is final or intermediate depends on
qa.a: its end use
qa.e: The same good, like milk or sugar, can be final or intermediate depending on who uses it and for what.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Capital goods are final goods. Reason (R): Capital goods are not used up or transformed in the production process within the year.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: They are used repeatedly and not merged into other goods, which is why they are final goods.

qa.q: Which is an intermediate good?
qa.a: Paint bought by a car manufacturer
qa.e: Paint used by a car maker becomes part of the car, so it is an intermediate good.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Milk is always a final good. Reason (R): Final goods are goods meant for final consumption or investment.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Milk bought by a tea stall is intermediate, so A is false; R correctly defines final goods.

qa.q: Which of the following is a flow variable?
qa.a: National income
qa.e: National income is measured over a period, usually a year.

qa.q: Which of the following is a stock variable?
qa.a: Capital
qa.e: Capital is measured at a point of time; investment is the flow that changes it.

qa.q: Gross investment in an economy is ₹900 crore and depreciation is ₹150 crore. What is net investment (₹ crore)?
qa.e: Net investment = gross investment − depreciation = 900 − 150 = 750.

qa.q: Depreciation is also called
qa.a: consumption of fixed capital
qa.e: Depreciation measures the fixed capital used up through wear and tear.

qa.q: A bus costing ₹40,00,000 has a useful life of 8 years and no scrap value. What is its annual depreciation (in ₹)?
qa.e: Straight-line depreciation = cost ÷ life = 40,00,000 ÷ 8 = 5,00,000.

qa.q: Net investment is ₹400 crore and depreciation is ₹60 crore. Gross investment (₹ crore) is
qa.e: Gross investment = net investment + depreciation = 400 + 60 = 460.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Investment is a flow variable. Reason (R): Investment is measured over a period of time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Investment is the addition to capital during a period, so it is a flow; R gives the reason.

qa.q: In the water-tank analogy, the water flowing in per minute corresponds to
qa.a: investment
qa.e: The inflow per period is like investment, which adds to the stock of capital (the water in the tank).

qa.q: In a two-sector circular flow, which flows from households to firms?
qa.a: Factor services and consumption expenditure
qa.e: Households provide factor services (real flow) and spend money on goods (money flow) to firms.

qa.q: Which assumption is made in the simplest circular flow model?
qa.a: Households spend all their income
qa.e: No saving, no government and no foreign trade means no leakages.

qa.q: Factor payments by firms to households form the
qa.a: money flow
qa.e: Payments of wages, rent, interest and profit are money flows.

qa.q: Aggregate expenditure on final goods equals aggregate factor payments because
qa.a: the money spent on goods is paid out by firms as factor incomes
qa.e: Revenue received by firms from sales is distributed as rewards to the factors that produced the goods.

qa.q: Which is a real flow in the two-sector model?
qa.a: Labour services supplied by households to firms
qa.e: Real flows are flows of goods and factor services; the others are money payments.

qa.q: If aggregate output in a simple two-sector economy is ₹1,200 crore, aggregate factor income (₹ crore) is
qa.e: In the simple model, output = income = expenditure, so factor income is ₹1,200 crore.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In the simplest two-sector model, there are no leakages from the circular flow. Reason (R): The model assumes no saving, no taxes and no imports.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Saving, taxes and imports are the leakages, and all are assumed away.

qa.q: The three methods of measuring national income are based on
qa.a: production, income and expenditure points of the circular flow
qa.e: National income can be measured at the production point, the income point or the expenditure point.

qa.q: A firm's value of output is ₹800 and it buys raw materials worth ₹350. What is its gross value added (in ₹)?
qa.e: GVA = value of output − intermediate consumption = 800 − 350 = 450.

qa.q: A farmer grows wheat worth ₹100 without buying inputs and sells it to a baker, who makes bread worth ₹250. The GDP contribution of the two is (₹)
qa.e: Value added: farmer 100, baker 250 − 100 = 150; total = 250, equal to the final good (bread).

qa.q: Gross value added of a firm is ₹600 and depreciation is ₹45. Net value added (₹) is
qa.e: NVA = GVA − depreciation = 600 − 45 = 555.

qa.q: GDP by the product method is the sum of
qa.a: gross value added of all producing units
qa.e: GDP adds up GVA across all firms; summing outputs double counts.
