qa.q: Which item is deducted from the value of output to find a firm's value added?
qa.a: Raw materials bought from other firms
qa.e: Intermediate inputs are deducted. Wages, interest and profit are paid out of value added.

qa.q: Three firms have outputs of ₹100 (no inputs), ₹180 (inputs ₹100) and ₹300 (inputs ₹180). Total value added (₹) is
qa.e: Value added = 100 + 80 + 120 = 300, equal to the value of the final output.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Adding the value of output of all firms overstates GDP. Reason (R): The value of intermediate goods gets counted more than once.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Intermediate inputs are included in each buyer's output again, which is double counting.

qa.q: Value added by a firm is distributed as
qa.a: wages, rent, interest and profit to factors
qa.e: Value added is the income created by the firm, paid to its factors of production.

qa.q: Sales of a firm are ₹2,000 and change in stock is ₹150. The value of output (₹) is
qa.e: Value of output = sales + change in stock = 2,000 + 150 = 2,150.

qa.q: A firm's opening stock is ₹600 and closing stock ₹450. Its sales are ₹3,000. Value of output (₹) is
Change in inventories is included in national income accounts as part of
qa.a: investment
qa.e: Additions to stock are treated as inventory investment.

qa.q: A firm expected to sell goods worth ₹1,000 but sold only ₹900, having produced ₹1,000. The unplanned inventory change (₹) is
qa.e: Unsold goods of ₹100 piled up unexpectedly: an unplanned accumulation of +100.

qa.q: Unplanned decumulation of inventories happens when
qa.a: sales turn out higher than expected
qa.e: If buyers buy more than expected, stocks fall below plan.

qa.q: Production of a firm is ₹700 and its sales are ₹760. The change in inventories (₹) is
qa.e: Change in inventories = production − sales = 700 − 760 = −60 (stocks fell).

qa.q: Assertion (A): Inventory is a stock while change in inventory is a flow. Reason (R): Change in inventory is measured over a period of time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Inventory is measured at a point of time; its change over the year is a flow.

qa.q: Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Value of output = sales + change in stock
qa.e: Goods produced but not sold are still output, so the change in stock is added to sales.

qa.q: GDP by the expenditure method equals
qa.a: C + I + G + (X − M)
qa.e: Final expenditure on domestic output = consumption + investment + government spending + net exports.

qa.q: Private consumption 1,200, investment 400, government consumption 300, exports 200, imports 250 (₹ crore). GDP (₹ crore) is
Why are imports subtracted in the expenditure method?
qa.a: Spending on imports buys goods produced abroad, not domestic output
qa.e: C, I and G include spending on foreign goods; subtracting M leaves only spending on domestic production.

qa.q: Compensation of employees ₹500 crore, rent ₹60 crore, interest ₹40 crore, profit ₹200 crore, mixed income ₹100 crore. Domestic factor income (₹ crore) is
Operating surplus is the sum of
qa.a: rent, interest and profit
qa.e: Operating surplus = rent + interest + profit; compensation of employees is separate.

qa.q: The income of a self-employed tailor who uses her own shop and machine is recorded as
qa.a: mixed income
qa.e: Self-employed people earn a mix of wages, rent, interest and profit that cannot be separated, called mixed income.

qa.q: Assertion (A): GDP measured by the product, income and expenditure methods is the same. Reason (R): Value of output is fully paid out as factor incomes and is fully bought as final expenditure.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because output = income = expenditure in the circular flow, the three methods agree.

qa.q: In an economy GDP is ₹2,000 crore, C = 1,300, I = 400 and G = 250 (₹ crore). Net exports (₹ crore) are
GDP at market prices is ₹8,000 crore, indirect taxes ₹900 crore and subsidies ₹200 crore. GDP at factor cost (₹ crore) is
qa.e: GDP at FC = GDP at MP − (indirect taxes − subsidies) = 8,000 − 700 = 7,300.

qa.q: Which of these is a product tax?
qa.a: Goods and Services Tax (GST)
qa.e: GST is levied per unit of the product sold; the others are production taxes not tied to quantity.

qa.q: GVA at basic prices equals
qa.a: GVA at factor cost + production taxes − production subsidies
qa.e: Basic prices add net production taxes to factor cost; product taxes come in only at market prices.

qa.q: GVA at basic prices is ₹2,000 crore, product taxes are ₹300 crore and product subsidies ₹50 crore. GVA at market prices (₹ crore) is
Subsidies are added when moving from GDP at market prices to GDP at factor cost because
qa.a: subsidies make market prices lower than what factors receive
qa.e: With a subsidy, buyers pay less than factor cost, so it must be added back.

qa.q: In India's national accounts, industry-wise output is reported as
qa.a: GVA at basic prices
qa.e: NSO reports sector-wise GVA at basic prices and GDP at market prices.

qa.q: GDP at factor cost is ₹4,200 crore and net indirect taxes are ₹350 crore. GDP at market prices (₹ crore) is
qa.e: GDP at MP = GDP at FC + NIT = 4,200 + 350 = 4,550.

qa.q: Assertion (A): GDP at market prices is usually greater than GDP at factor cost. Reason (R): Indirect taxes usually exceed subsidies.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: When net indirect taxes are positive, market price value exceeds factor cost value.

qa.q: Net factor income from abroad is defined as
qa.a: factor income earned by residents abroad minus factor income earned by non-residents in the domestic territory
qa.e: NFIA is about factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit), not trade in goods.

qa.q: GDP at market prices is ₹10,000 crore and NFIA is −₹200 crore. GNP at market prices (₹ crore) is
NNP at market prices is ₹6,500 crore, indirect taxes ₹700 crore and subsidies ₹150 crore. National income (₹ crore) is
NDP at factor cost is ₹3,000 crore and NFIA is ₹40 crore. National income (₹ crore) is
qa.e: NI = NDP at FC + NFIA = 3,000 + 40 = 3,040.

qa.q: GDP at market prices = ₹1,800 crore, NFIA = ₹20 crore, net indirect taxes = ₹150 crore, national income = ₹1,500 crore. Depreciation (₹ crore) is
When will GNP be less than GDP?
qa.a: When net factor income from abroad is negative
qa.e: GNP = GDP + NFIA, so a negative NFIA makes GNP smaller.

qa.q: Wages earned by an Indian resident working temporarily at a US embassy in New Delhi are
qa.a: part of India's national income but not its domestic product
qa.e: Embassies are not part of the domestic territory of the host country, so the income is earned outside India's domestic territory by an Indian resident: it is factor income from abroad.

qa.q: Assertion (A): National income can be greater than domestic income. Reason (R): NFIA can be positive.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: NI = domestic income (NDP FC) + NFIA, so a positive NFIA makes national income larger.

qa.q: NI ₹8,000 crore, undistributed profits ₹500 crore, corporate tax ₹700 crore, net interest paid by households ₹200 crore, transfers to households ₹400 crore. Personal income (₹ crore) is
Personal income is ₹3,600 crore, personal taxes ₹450 crore and fines and fees ₹30 crore. PDI (₹ crore) is
Which item is ADDED to national income to get personal income?
qa.a: Transfer payments to households
qa.e: Transfers reach households without current production, so they are added; the others are subtracted.

qa.q: National disposable income is NNP at market prices plus
qa.a: other current transfers from the rest of the world
qa.e: It shows the total goods and services a nation can use from its income and receipts from abroad.

qa.q: Which is included in private income but NOT in national income?
qa.a: Interest on national debt
qa.e: National debt interest is a transfer (the debt mostly financed non-productive needs), so it enters private income but not NI.

qa.q: Private saving is ₹500 crore, investment ₹400 crore and the budget deficit (G − T) is ₹150 crore. Using (S − I) = (G − T) + (X − M), net exports (₹ crore) are
qa.e: S − I = 100 = 150 + (X − M), so X − M = −50: a trade deficit of 50.

qa.q: Private saving exceeds investment by ₹80 crore and the trade surplus (X − M) is ₹30 crore. The budget deficit (₹ crore) is
Assertion (A): Personal disposable income is smaller than personal income. Reason (R): Households must pay personal taxes and non-tax payments such as fines out of personal income.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: PDI = PI − personal taxes − non-tax payments, so it is smaller whenever these are positive.

qa.q: Real GDP is calculated using
qa.a: base-year (constant) prices
qa.e: Real GDP holds prices fixed at base-year levels to isolate changes in output.

qa.q: Nominal GDP is ₹4,500 crore and real GDP is ₹3,600 crore. The GDP deflator is
Nominal GDP is ₹2,400 crore and the GDP deflator is 120. Real GDP (₹ crore) is
An economy produces 50 cycles. Base-year price ₹4,000; current price ₹5,000. Real GDP of the current year (₹) is
qa.e: Real GDP = current quantity × base price = 50 × 4,000 = 2,00,000.

qa.q: Nominal GDP rose from ₹1,000 crore to ₹1,100 crore while real GDP stayed at ₹1,000 crore. This means
qa.a: only prices rose, by 10%
qa.e: Real GDP unchanged means no change in quantity; the deflator went from 100 to 110.

qa.q: Current year: 200 units at ₹15; base year price ₹12. The GDP deflator for the current year is
Assertion (A): Real GDP is a better measure of growth in output than nominal GDP. Reason (R): Real GDP removes the effect of price changes by using constant prices.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Because prices are held fixed, real GDP changes only when quantities change.

qa.q: If the GDP deflator is 100 in a given year, that year is most likely
qa.a: the base year
qa.e: In the base year nominal and real GDP are equal, so the deflator is 100.

qa.q: A consumer basket cost ₹2,000 in the base year and costs ₹2,300 now. The CPI is
Which index includes prices of imported goods bought by consumers?
qa.a: Consumer Price Index
qa.e: CPI covers all consumer goods, including imported ones; the deflator covers only domestic output.

qa.q: Which statement about the GDP deflator is correct?
qa.a: Its weights change according to each year's production
qa.e: The deflator compares current output at current and base prices, so its 'basket' is each year's own output.

qa.q: In many countries the wholesale price index is replaced by the
qa.a: Producer Price Index
qa.e: WPI is also called the PPI in many countries; it tracks prices at the producer or wholesale level.

qa.q: CPI was 160 last year and 168 this year. The rate of inflation (%) is
A rise in the price of imported smartphones bought by Indian households would
qa.a: raise CPI but not directly affect the GDP deflator
qa.e: Imported goods are in the consumer basket but are not part of domestic production.

qa.q: Assertion (A): CPI and GDP deflator can give different measures of inflation. Reason (R): They differ in the goods they cover and in how they are weighted.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Different coverage (consumer vs all domestic goods, imports) and weights cause the gap.

qa.q: The base-year value of any price index is
qa.e: Indices are scaled so that the base year equals 100.

qa.q: Which is a reason why GDP is not a perfect measure of welfare?
qa.a: It ignores how income is distributed among people
qa.e: Average GDP can rise while most people's incomes fall.

qa.q: A factory pollutes a river and fishermen lose their catch without compensation. This is
qa.a: a negative externality
qa.e: Harm to others that is not paid for is a negative externality.

qa.q: Which activity is NOT included in India's GDP?
qa.a: Services of a homemaker for her own family
qa.e: Own-household services are non-monetary and are left out, while paid services are counted.

qa.q: A beautiful garden kept by a family that neighbours also enjoy is an example of
qa.a: a positive externality
qa.e: Others benefit without paying, so it is a positive externality.

qa.q: Assertion (A): GDP may underestimate the actual economic activity in a country. Reason (R): Non-monetary exchanges such as housework and barter are not counted.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Leaving out non-market work makes measured GDP smaller than real activity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A rise in GDP always increases the welfare of all people. Reason (R): GDP is an incomplete index of welfare.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false because distribution and externalities matter; R is true.

qa.q: Which situation shows that GDP growth may not improve welfare?
qa.a: GDP rises, but traffic and air pollution sharply worsen health
qa.e: Negative externalities can reduce welfare even as GDP grows.

qa.q: Per capita GDP of a town rose 10%, but the incomes of the poorest 80% fell. This mainly shows the problem of
qa.a: distribution of GDP
qa.e: The gain was unequally distributed, so most people were worse off.

qa.q: The main drawback of the barter system that money removes as a medium of exchange is
qa.a: the need for a double coincidence of wants
qa.e: Money lets people sell to one person and buy from another, so wants need not match.

qa.q: When we say a laptop is worth ₹50,000, money is acting as a
qa.a: unit of account
qa.e: Expressing value in rupees is the unit of account (measure of value) function.

qa.q: A pen costs ₹25 and a notebook ₹75. The relative price of a notebook in terms of pens is
qa.e: Relative price = 75 ÷ 25 = 3 pens per notebook.

qa.q: Which is a drawback of barter that relates to goods like cattle?
qa.a: Indivisibility
qa.e: A cow cannot be divided to pay for small purchases.

qa.q: Money is best defined as
qa.a: anything that is commonly accepted as a medium of exchange
qa.e: Money is defined by general acceptability, not by its material.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Barter makes it hard to compare the values of many goods. Reason (R): Under barter there is no common unit in which all values can be expressed.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: With n goods there are many separate exchange ratios; no common measure exists.

qa.q: Under barter, a person who holds tomatoes as wealth faces the problem of
qa.a: storing wealth, since tomatoes perish
qa.e: Perishable goods cannot hold value over time, unlike money.

qa.q: Which function of money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants?
qa.a: Medium of exchange
qa.e: As a medium of exchange, money is accepted by everyone in return for goods.

qa.q: Money is said to be the most liquid asset because
qa.a: it can be used for payments immediately without any loss of value
qa.e: Liquidity means easy, costless conversion into a means of payment; money already is one.

qa.q: If the general price level rises by 25%, the purchasing power of money
qa.a: falls
qa.e: Each rupee buys fewer goods when prices rise.

qa.q: The price index rises from 100 to 125. A rupee now buys what ₹ ___ bought earlier.
qa.e: Purchasing power = 100 ÷ 125 = 0.8 of its earlier value.

qa.q: Which asset is the least liquid?
qa.a: A residential plot of land
qa.e: Land takes time and cost to sell; the others are money already.

qa.q: The old ₹500 and ₹1000 notes were demonetised in
qa.a: November 2016
qa.e: The announcement was made on 8 November 2016.

qa.q: The National Financial Switch in India mainly
qa.a: links ATMs of different banks so cards work across banks
qa.e: NFS is the shared ATM network that lets a customer of one bank use another bank's ATM.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Money works as a store of value. Reason (R): Money never loses purchasing power.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Money stores value, but inflation reduces its purchasing power, so R is false.

qa.q: Which was NOT one of the stated aims of demonetisation in 2016?
qa.a: Raising the CRR of banks
qa.e: The CRR is a monetary policy tool unrelated to demonetisation's stated aims.

qa.q: Transaction demand for money mainly depends on
qa.a: the level of income
qa.e: More income means more transactions, so people hold more money for payments.

qa.q: If nominal income is ₹5,000 crore and velocity of money is 5, transaction demand for money (₹ crore) is
Why does the demand for money fall when the interest rate rises?
qa.a: The opportunity cost of holding money rises
qa.e: Money earns no interest, so a higher rate makes holding it costlier.

qa.q: When the market interest rate rises, the price of existing bonds
qa.a: falls
qa.e: Bond prices and interest rates are inversely related.

qa.q: A liquidity trap is a situation where
qa.a: at a very low interest rate people hold all extra money and none buy bonds
qa.e: Expecting the rate to rise, people avoid bonds and hold money; money demand becomes perfectly elastic.

qa.q: If k = 0.2, the velocity of circulation of money is
Assertion (A): When the interest rate is very high, speculative demand for money is low. Reason (R): People expect the interest rate to fall and bond prices to rise, so they buy bonds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Expecting capital gains on bonds, people hold bonds instead of money.

qa.q: Nominal GDP is ₹3,000 crore and the money held for transactions is ₹750 crore. The velocity of money is
M1 is defined as
qa.a: currency held by the public + net demand deposits of banks
qa.e: M1 = CU + DD.

qa.q: Currency with the public ₹40, net demand deposits ₹35 and net time deposits of banks ₹120 (₹ lakh crore). M3 (₹ lakh crore) is
qa.e: M3 = M1 + time deposits = (40 + 35) + 120 = 195.

qa.q: Which measure of money supply is the most liquid?
qa.a: M1
qa.e: Liquidity falls as we move from M1 to M4; M1 contains only currency and demand deposits.

qa.q: In India, coins are issued by
qa.a: the Government of India
qa.e: Coins and one-rupee notes are issued by the Government of India; other currency notes by the RBI.

qa.q: Money that has no intrinsic value and is accepted because the government declares it so is called
qa.a: fiat money
qa.e: Fiat money derives its value from government authority, not its material.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT legal tender?
qa.a: A cheque
qa.e: A cheque can be refused; currency notes and coins cannot be refused in settling debts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): M3 is called broad money. Reason (R): M3 includes the net time deposits of commercial banks.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Adding the large, less liquid time deposits makes M3 a broad measure.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Demand deposits are legal tender. Reason (R): Demand deposits can be withdrawn by cheque on demand.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Demand deposits are money (part of M1) but not legal tender, since a cheque can be refused; R is true.

qa.q: The Reserve Bank of India was established in
qa.e: The RBI was set up in 1935; it was nationalised later, in 1949.

qa.q: 'Lender of last resort' means the RBI
qa.a: lends to commercial banks in a crisis when they cannot get funds elsewhere
qa.e: It supports banks facing liquidity shortages to protect the banking system.

qa.q: Which is a function of the RBI as banker to the government?
qa.a: Managing the public debt of the government
qa.e: The RBI handles government accounts and borrowing.

qa.q: The RBI is called the 'bank of issue' because
qa.a: it has the sole right to issue currency notes (except one-rupee notes)
qa.e: Note issue is the RBI's monopoly; coins and one-rupee notes come from the government.

qa.q: Commercial banks keep a part of their deposits as reserves with the RBI. This shows the RBI's role as
qa.a: banker's bank
qa.e: Holding banks' reserves and lending to them makes the RBI the banker's bank.

qa.q: Which institution acts as the custodian of India's foreign exchange reserves?
qa.a: Reserve Bank of India
qa.e: The RBI holds and manages the forex reserves.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The RBI can control the volume of credit in the economy. Reason (R): The RBI uses tools such as the repo rate, CRR and open market operations.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: These monetary tools change banks' ability and cost of lending.

qa.q: Which is NOT a function of the RBI?
qa.a: Accepting savings deposits from individual customers
qa.e: The RBI does not deal with the general public like a commercial bank.

qa.q: A commercial bank's profit mainly comes from
qa.a: the spread between lending and deposit interest rates
qa.e: Banks charge more on loans than they pay on deposits.

qa.q: On a bank's balance sheet, deposits of the public are
qa.a: liabilities
qa.e: Deposits are owed to depositors, so they are liabilities.

qa.q: A bank has assets of ₹500 crore and liabilities of ₹460 crore. Its net worth (₹ crore) is
qa.e: Net worth = assets − liabilities = 500 − 460 = 40.

qa.q: The goldsmith story explains the origin of
qa.a: fractional reserve banking
qa.e: Keeping a fraction of deposits and lending the rest is what goldsmiths discovered.

qa.q: Loans given by a bank appear in its balance sheet as
qa.a: assets
qa.e: Loans are claims of the bank on borrowers, so they are assets.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Commercial banks are creators of money. Reason (R): When banks lend, they create new demand deposits, which are a part of money supply.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since deposits are money, lending that creates deposits creates money.

qa.q: A bank pays 3.5% on deposits and charges 10% on loans. Its spread (percentage points) is
qa.e: Spread = 10 − 3.5 = 6.5 percentage points.

qa.q: Why could the goldsmith lend out part of the gold?
qa.a: Only a small fraction of depositors came to withdraw at any one time
qa.e: Since withdrawals were partial, the rest of the gold lay idle and could be lent.

qa.q: If the reserve ratio is 25%, the money multiplier is
qa.e: Money multiplier = 1/0.25 = 4.

qa.q: An initial deposit of ₹5,000 is made and the reserve ratio is 20%. Total deposits created (₹) are
Initial deposit ₹2,000; reserve ratio 10%. The total credit (loans) created (₹) is
A banking system creates total deposits of ₹40,000 from an initial deposit of ₹8,000. The reserve ratio (%) is
High powered money consists of
qa.a: currency held by the public and reserves of commercial banks
qa.e: H = CU + R; it is the base on which banks create deposits.

qa.q: If the RBI raises the reserve ratio from 10% to 20%, the money multiplier
qa.a: falls from 10 to 5
qa.e: Multiplier = 1/r: 1/0.1 = 10 and 1/0.2 = 5.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The money multiplier would be smaller if people held more cash instead of depositing it. Reason (R): Cash held by the public is a leakage that is not redeposited and lent again.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Leakages reduce the rounds of redepositing and lending.

qa.q: Reserve money H is ₹100 crore and the money multiplier is 4. Money supply (₹ crore) is
qa.e: Money supply = multiplier × H = 4 × 100 = 400.

qa.q: The rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks against government securities is the
qa.a: repo rate
qa.e: Repo is a repurchase agreement; the RBI lends and banks later repurchase the securities.

qa.q: The rate at which the RBI borrows from commercial banks is the
qa.a: reverse repo rate
qa.e: Under reverse repo, banks park surplus funds with the RBI.

qa.q: To increase money supply, the RBI should
qa.a: buy government securities in the open market
qa.e: Buying securities pays money to banks, raising their reserves and lending.

qa.q: A bank has deposits of ₹1,000 crore and the CRR is 4%. Cash it must keep with the RBI (₹ crore) is
qa.e: CRR amount = 4% of 1,000 = 40.

qa.q: SLR requires banks to keep a fraction of deposits in
qa.a: liquid assets such as cash, gold and approved government securities
qa.e: SLR assets are kept by the banks themselves in liquid forms.

qa.q: Which is a quantitative instrument of monetary policy?
qa.a: Cash reserve ratio
qa.e: CRR affects the total volume of credit; the others are qualitative.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A rise in the repo rate tends to reduce credit in the economy. Reason (R): A higher repo rate raises the cost of borrowing for banks, which pass it on as higher loan rates.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Costlier funds make banks charge more, so people borrow less.

qa.q: Assertion (A): When the RBI sells government securities, money supply increases. Reason (R): Open market operations involve buying and selling of government securities.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Selling securities takes money out of banks, so money supply falls; A is false and R is true.

qa.q: Which of these is a qualitative tool of monetary policy?
qa.a: Margin requirement
qa.e: Margins influence lending against particular securities, so they are selective (qualitative).

qa.q: Shares worth ₹2,00,000 are offered as collateral with a 25% margin requirement. The maximum loan (₹) is
Moral suasion refers to
qa.a: persuasion and advice by the RBI to banks
qa.e: It works through requests and advice rather than formal rules.

qa.q: To correct deficient demand, the RBI should
qa.a: lower the repo rate and buy government securities
qa.e: Cheaper and more abundant credit raises spending.

qa.q: Sterilisation by the RBI means
qa.a: neutralising the effect of foreign capital inflows on money supply, e.g. by selling government securities
qa.e: Selling bonds absorbs the extra rupees created when the RBI buys foreign exchange.

qa.q: During high inflation, which pair of actions would the RBI take?
qa.a: Raise CRR and sell securities
qa.e: Both actions reduce banks' ability to lend.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Raising margin requirements reduces credit for buying securities. Reason (R): A higher margin means the borrower must pay a larger part from own funds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The loan is the value minus the margin, so a higher margin reduces the loan.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sterilisation increases money supply to fight inflation. Reason (R): Large capital inflows can raise money supply when the RBI buys foreign exchange.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Sterilisation reduces (neutralises) the extra money supply, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Ex ante investment refers to
qa.a: planned investment
qa.e: Ex ante means intended or planned, before the event.

qa.q: A firm planned inventory investment of ₹40 crore, but actual inventory investment was ₹55 crore. Unplanned inventory accumulation (₹ crore) is
qa.e: Unplanned = actual − planned = 55 − 40 = 15.

qa.q: In a two-sector economy, aggregate demand consists of
qa.a: consumption expenditure and investment expenditure
qa.e: Two-sector means only households and firms, so AD = C + I.

qa.q: Autonomous investment is investment that
qa.a: does not depend on the level of income
qa.e: It is fixed at Ī, independent of income.

qa.q: A firm produced ₹300 crore of goods and sold ₹270 crore. Its planned inventory investment was ₹10 crore. Unplanned inventory change (₹ crore) is
qa.e: Actual inventory change = 300 − 270 = 30; unplanned = 30 − 10 = 20.

qa.q: Which expenditure is part of aggregate demand in an open economy with government?
qa.a: Net exports
qa.e: AD = C + I + G + (X − M).

qa.q: Assertion (A): Equilibrium income is determined by ex ante aggregate demand. Reason (R): Ex post saving always equals ex post investment.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true: plans decide equilibrium, and the actual values are always equal as an identity. But the ex post identity does not explain why planned AD decides equilibrium.

qa.q: Investment in the macroeconomic sense means
qa.a: addition to physical capital and inventories
qa.e: Only new physical capital and inventories count; buying existing assets is a transfer of ownership.

qa.q: When income rises from ₹1,000 crore to ₹1,500 crore, consumption rises from ₹800 crore to ₹1,150 crore. MPC is
With C = 200 + 0.6Y, consumption at Y = 1,000 is
With C = 200 + 0.6Y, APC at Y = 1,000 is
In C = C̄ + cY, the term C̄ stands for
qa.a: autonomous consumption
qa.e: C̄ is consumption when income is zero.

qa.q: The value of MPC usually lies
qa.a: between 0 and 1
qa.e: People spend part of any extra income and save the rest.

qa.q: Consumption is ₹480 crore at income ₹400 crore. APC is
qa.e: APC = 480/400 = 1.2; it exceeds 1 because spending is more than income.

qa.q: Assertion (A): APC falls as income rises in the consumption function C = C̄ + cY. Reason (R): C̄/Y gets smaller as income rises while c stays constant.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: APC = C̄/Y + c; the first part shrinks with income.

qa.q: MPC is 0.9 and income rises by ₹50 crore. Consumption rises by (₹ crore)
If MPC is 0.65, MPS is
The saving function corresponding to C = 120 + 0.7Y is
Income is ₹2,000 crore and consumption ₹1,700 crore. APS is
For S = −80 + 0.4Y, the break-even level of income is
Which relation always holds?
qa.a: APC + APS = 1
qa.e: Income is either consumed or saved, so the averages add to 1 (as do MPC and MPS).

qa.q: When income is ₹100 crore and consumption is ₹130 crore, APS is
Assertion (A): APS can be negative but MPS cannot be negative in the standard consumption function. Reason (R): At low incomes consumption exceeds income, while extra income is always partly saved.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Dissaving makes S and APS negative at low Y; but since 0 < c < 1, MPS = 1 − c is positive.

qa.q: Assertion (A): MPC + MPS can be greater than 1. Reason (R): Every increase in income is either consumed or saved.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Because extra income is split between consumption and saving, MPC + MPS = 1 exactly; A is false.

qa.q: Equilibrium income in the Keynesian model is determined where
qa.a: planned aggregate demand equals aggregate supply
qa.e: Equilibrium requires planned AD = AS (equivalently planned S = planned I).

qa.q: C̄ = 50, c = 0.75 and Ī = 50. Output is ₹500 crore. Aggregate demand (₹ crore) at this output is
Output is ₹500 crore but planned aggregate demand is only ₹475 crore. What happens next?
qa.a: Unplanned inventories pile up and output falls
qa.e: Unsold goods accumulate, so firms cut output.

qa.q: When planned investment exceeds planned saving, income will
qa.a: rise
qa.e: I > S means AD > AS, so output and income increase.

qa.q: Autonomous expenditure Ā in a two-sector model equals
qa.a: C̄ + Ī
qa.e: Ā is the part of AD that does not depend on income.

qa.q: With taxes, the consumption function becomes
qa.a: C = C̄ + c(Y − T)
qa.e: Households consume out of disposable income, Y − T.

qa.q: Assertion (A): When AD falls short of output, firms experience unplanned accumulation of inventories. Reason (R): Some of the goods produced remain unsold.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Unsold output piles up as unintended stock.

qa.q: Planned saving S = −40 + 0.25Y and planned investment I = 60. Equilibrium income is
C̄ = 80, Ī = 120 and MPC = 0.75. Equilibrium income is
In the Keynesian cross, the 45° line represents
qa.a: points where aggregate expenditure equals income (aggregate supply)
qa.e: Each point on it has equal values on both axes, so it stands for AS.

qa.q: Autonomous expenditure is ₹150 crore and MPS is 0.2. Equilibrium income (₹ crore) is
Autonomous expenditure is ₹100 crore, MPS = 0.25 and actual income is ₹300 crore. Is the economy in equilibrium?
qa.a: No; AD (₹325 crore) exceeds output, so income will rise
qa.e: AD = 100 + 0.75 × 300 = 325 > 300, so output rises towards Y* = 400.

qa.q: The fixed-price assumption of the short-run Keynesian model is justified when
qa.a: there are unemployed resources and unused capacity
qa.e: With idle capacity, output can rise without pushing up prices.

qa.q: The vertical intercept of the AD line in the two-sector model is
qa.a: C̄ + Ī
qa.e: AD = Ā + cY, so at Y = 0, AD = Ā = C̄ + Ī.

qa.q: Assertion (A): At equilibrium income, planned saving equals planned investment. Reason (R): At equilibrium, Y = C + I and Y = C + S.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Subtracting C from both gives S = I at equilibrium.

qa.q: With C = 50 + 0.9Y and I = 25, equilibrium income is
An increase in autonomous investment shifts the AD line
qa.a: upward and parallel
qa.e: Only the intercept changes, so the line moves up without changing slope.

qa.q: A rise in MPC causes the AD line to
qa.a: become steeper, swinging upward from the same intercept
qa.e: MPC is the slope of the AD line.

qa.q: Ā = 200 and MPC rises from 0.6 to 0.75. Equilibrium income rises from 500 to
Ā rises from 100 to 140 with MPC = 0.8. Equilibrium income rises by
A change in the slope of the AD curve is called a
qa.a: parametric shift in c (the MPC)
qa.e: Changing a parameter (here c) changes the curve itself.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A fall in autonomous consumption lowers equilibrium income by more than the fall itself. Reason (R): The multiplier effect magnifies a change in autonomous expenditure.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: ΔY = ΔĀ/(1 − c), which is larger than ΔĀ when 0 < c < 1.

qa.q: Which change would make the AD line flatter?
qa.a: A rise in MPS
qa.e: Higher MPS means lower MPC, i.e. a smaller slope.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A change in MPC shifts the AD line parallel. Reason (R): MPC determines the slope of the AD line.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Because MPC is the slope, a change in it swings the line instead of shifting it parallel; A is false.

qa.q: If MPS is 0.2, the investment multiplier is
The multiplier is 4 and investment rises by ₹250 crore. Income rises by (₹ crore)
Investment rises by ₹80 crore and income rises by ₹400 crore. MPC is
MPC = 0.75 and investment rises by ₹60 crore. Consumption rises by (₹ crore)
The value of the multiplier is 1 when
qa.a: MPC = 0
qa.e: k = 1/(1 − 0) = 1: no extra rounds of spending.

qa.q: The multiplier works through the process of
qa.a: successive rounds of induced consumption spending
qa.e: Each round's income is partly spent, creating income for others.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The higher the MPC, the higher the value of the investment multiplier. Reason (R): k = 1 / (1 − MPC).
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: As MPC rises, 1 − MPC falls, so k rises.

qa.q: The sum ΔI(1 + c + c² + c³ + ...) with 0 < c < 1 equals
qa.e: A geometric series with first term 1 and ratio c sums to 1/(1 − c).

qa.q: The paradox of thrift states that when all people try to save a larger share of income,
qa.a: total saving remains unchanged or falls while income falls
qa.e: Higher MPS lowers AD and income; equilibrium saving still equals the unchanged investment.

qa.q: C̄ = 20, Ī = 80. MPS rises from 0.2 to 0.25. Equilibrium income falls from 500 to
C̄ = 20, Ī = 80 and MPS = 0.25. Total saving at equilibrium is
qa.e: At equilibrium S = Ī = 80 (check: −20 + 0.25 × 400 = 80).

qa.q: Involuntary unemployment exists when
qa.a: people willing to work at the prevailing wage cannot find jobs
qa.e: It is unemployment despite willingness to work at the going wage.

qa.q: According to the principle of effective demand, in the short run with fixed prices, output is determined by
qa.a: aggregate demand
qa.e: Firms produce what is demanded when there is spare capacity.

qa.q: Full employment equilibrium means
qa.a: all those willing and able to work at the prevailing wage are employed
qa.e: Full employment is about those willing and able to work at the going wage.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A virtue for an individual (saving more) can become a problem for the whole economy. Reason (R): When everyone saves more, aggregate demand and income fall.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Lower spending cuts income, so the economy's saving does not rise.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Equilibrium output is always at full employment. Reason (R): Equilibrium is where planned AD equals output.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Equilibrium only requires AD = AS; that can happen below full employment, so A is false.

qa.q: Full-employment output is ₹2,000 crore and AD at that output is ₹2,150 crore. The inflationary gap (₹ crore) is
qa.e: Inflationary gap = AD − full-employment output = 2,150 − 2,000 = 150.

qa.q: Deficient demand leads to
qa.a: a fall in output and employment
qa.e: Unsold goods pile up and firms cut production and jobs.

qa.q: Excess demand at full employment mainly causes
qa.a: a rise in the price level
qa.e: Output cannot rise beyond full employment, so prices rise.

qa.q: Which is a fiscal measure to correct deficient demand?
qa.a: Increasing government expenditure
qa.e: Higher government spending directly raises AD.

qa.q: Which monetary measure is used to control excess demand?
qa.a: Raising the cash reserve ratio
qa.e: A higher CRR leaves banks with less to lend.

qa.q: Full-employment output is ₹600 crore, autonomous expenditure is ₹100 crore and MPC is 0.8. The economy faces
qa.a: deficient demand, since equilibrium income is ₹500 crore
qa.e: Y* = 100/0.2 = 500 < 600, so AD at full employment (100 + 0.8 × 600 = 580) is short by 20.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Excess demand creates an inflationary gap. Reason (R): At full employment, extra demand cannot be met by more output, so prices rise.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since resources are fully used, the excess demand raises prices.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Cutting the repo rate helps reduce excess demand. Reason (R): A lower repo rate makes credit cheaper.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Cheaper credit raises spending, worsening excess demand, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: The government budget is a statement of
qa.a: estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for a financial year
qa.e: It is an annual estimate of the government's receipts and spending.

qa.q: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution is the 'Annual Financial Statement' presented?
qa.a: Article 112
qa.e: Article 112 requires the Annual Financial Statement (the budget) to be laid before Parliament.

qa.q: A good is non-excludable when
qa.a: it is difficult to prevent non-payers from enjoying it
qa.e: Non-excludability means non-payers cannot easily be kept out.

qa.q: Why are public goods usually provided by the government?
qa.a: Because of the free-rider problem, private firms cannot collect enough payment
qa.e: People can use them without paying, so markets underprovide them.

qa.q: Which is an example of a public good?
qa.a: National defence
qa.e: Defence protects everyone at once and non-payers cannot be excluded.

qa.q: Providing public goods is the budget's
qa.a: allocation function
qa.e: Allocation of resources to public goods is the allocation function.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Markets fail to provide public goods in sufficient quantity. Reason (R): Public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable, so consumers can avoid paying.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Non-excludability creates free riders, so private provision is unprofitable.

qa.q: A good that is rivalrous and excludable is a
qa.a: private good
qa.e: Rival and excludable goods are private goods sold in markets.

qa.q: The redistribution function of the budget aims to
qa.a: make the distribution of income fairer through taxes and transfers
qa.e: Taxes on the rich and transfers to the poor make disposable income fairer.

qa.q: Raising government spending during a recession is an example of the
qa.a: stabilisation function
qa.e: It aims to smooth fluctuations in output and employment.

qa.q: The two parts of the government budget are
qa.a: revenue budget and capital budget
qa.e: The budget is divided into revenue and capital accounts.

qa.q: Which is a transfer payment used for redistribution?
qa.a: Unemployment allowance
qa.e: Transfers are payments without any service in return.

qa.q: Which objective is served when the government invests heavily in railways and power plants?
qa.a: Economic growth
qa.e: Capital spending raises productive capacity and growth.

qa.q: The use of government spending and taxes to influence the economy is called
qa.a: fiscal policy
qa.e: Fiscal policy works through the budget; monetary policy is run by the RBI.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Progressive income taxes help the redistribution function. Reason (R): Under progressive taxation, people with higher incomes pay a higher rate of tax.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Taking a larger share from the rich and spending on the poor reduces inequality.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Stabilisation means the government always increases its spending. Reason (R): Stabilisation aims to reduce fluctuations in output and employment.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: During inflation the government cuts spending or raises taxes, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Which is a direct tax?
qa.a: Corporation tax
qa.e: Corporation tax is paid by companies on profits and cannot be shifted.

qa.q: Which is a non-tax revenue receipt?
qa.a: Dividends received from public sector undertakings
qa.e: Dividends are non-tax revenue; borrowings and disinvestment are capital receipts.

qa.q: Revenue receipts are receipts that
qa.a: neither create liabilities nor reduce assets
qa.e: This is the defining test of a revenue receipt.

qa.q: A tax whose burden can be shifted to others is called
qa.a: an indirect tax
qa.e: Sellers pass indirect taxes like GST to buyers through prices.

qa.q: Progressive taxation helps reduce inequality because
qa.a: higher incomes are taxed at higher rates
qa.e: Higher rates on the rich reduce income gaps.

qa.q: Grants received by the government from an international organisation are a
qa.a: revenue receipt
qa.e: They create no liability and reduce no asset, so they are non-tax revenue receipts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): GST is an indirect tax. Reason (R): The burden of GST is passed on to the final consumer through prices.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since the burden is shifted, GST is indirect.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Interest received by the government on loans given to states is a capital receipt. Reason (R): Interest receipts do not create any liability for the government.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Since interest creates no liability and reduces no asset, it is a revenue (non-tax) receipt; A is false.

qa.q: Which is a capital expenditure?
qa.a: Repayment of a loan taken by the government
qa.e: Repayment reduces a liability, so it is capital expenditure.

qa.q: Interest payments by the government are
qa.a: revenue expenditure
qa.e: They neither create assets nor reduce liabilities.

qa.q: Grants given by the Centre to state governments are treated as
qa.a: revenue expenditure
qa.e: Grants create no asset for the Centre, even if states use them to build assets.

qa.q: Loans given by the Central Government to a state are
qa.a: capital expenditure
qa.e: A loan creates a financial asset (a claim on the state).

qa.q: Which is NOT revenue expenditure?
qa.a: Construction of a government college building
qa.e: A building is an asset, so it is capital expenditure.

qa.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the two types of expenditure?
qa.a: Capital expenditure creates assets or reduces liabilities; revenue expenditure does neither
qa.e: The asset/liability test separates them.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Purchase of shares of a public sector company by the government is capital expenditure. Reason (R): It creates a financial asset for the government.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Shares are assets, so buying them is capital expenditure.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Subsidies are capital expenditure. Reason (R): Subsidies neither create assets nor reduce liabilities.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: By the asset test, subsidies are revenue expenditure; A is false and R is true.

qa.q: Which is a capital receipt?
qa.a: Disinvestment proceeds
qa.e: Selling PSU shares reduces government assets.

qa.q: Which is a non-debt-creating capital receipt?
qa.a: Recovery of loans
qa.e: Recovery reduces an asset but creates no new debt.

qa.q: Borrowing by the government from the public is a capital receipt because it
qa.a: creates a liability
qa.e: Borrowings must be repaid, so they create a liability.

qa.q: Interest received on loans given to state governments is a
qa.a: revenue receipt
qa.e: It neither creates a liability nor reduces an asset.

qa.q: A government receives ₹300 crore from market loans, ₹80 crore from disinvestment and ₹20 crore as loan recoveries. Non-debt capital receipts (₹ crore) are
qa.e: Non-debt = disinvestment + recoveries = 80 + 20 = 100.

qa.q: Sale of shares of a public sector company to the public is called
qa.a: disinvestment
qa.e: Disinvestment reduces government's stake in PSUs.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Borrowings are capital receipts. Reason (R): Borrowings create a liability for the government.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The liability test makes borrowings capital receipts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Disinvestment proceeds are debt-creating capital receipts. Reason (R): Disinvestment reduces the government's assets.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Disinvestment creates no debt, so it is a non-debt capital receipt; A is false.

qa.q: Revenue expenditure is ₹4,500 crore and revenue receipts are ₹3,800 crore. Revenue deficit (₹ crore) is
Total expenditure ₹10,000 crore, revenue receipts ₹7,000 crore, non-debt capital receipts ₹500 crore. Fiscal deficit (₹ crore) is
Fiscal deficit is ₹2,500 crore and interest payments are ₹1,100 crore. Primary deficit (₹ crore) is
Fiscal deficit equals the government's
qa.a: total borrowing requirement
qa.e: The gap between spending and non-borrowed receipts must be borrowed.

qa.q: A zero primary deficit means
qa.a: the government borrows only to pay interest on past debt
qa.e: If FD = interest payments, all borrowing goes to interest.

qa.q: Revenue deficit ₹300 crore, capital expenditure ₹900 crore, non-debt capital receipts ₹200 crore. Fiscal deficit (₹ crore) is
qa.e: FD = RD + capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts = 300 + 900 − 200 = 1,000.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A revenue deficit implies dissaving by the government. Reason (R): The government borrows to finance its current consumption expenditure.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Using borrowings for current needs means it dissaves.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A budget in which expenditure exceeds receipts is a surplus budget. Reason (R): In a balanced budget, estimated receipts equal estimated expenditure.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Expenditure greater than receipts is a deficit budget; A is false and R is true.

qa.q: The FRBM Act was enacted in
qa.e: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act was passed in 2003.

qa.q: The main aim of the FRBM Act is to
qa.a: ensure fiscal discipline by reducing deficits
qa.e: It set targets to reduce fiscal and revenue deficits.

qa.q: Financing a deficit by borrowing from the RBI (deficit financing) tends to cause
qa.a: inflation
qa.e: Borrowing from the RBI creates new money, raising AD and prices.

qa.q: Fiscal deficit is ₹800 crore and revenue deficit is ₹560 crore. The share of revenue deficit in fiscal deficit (%) is
Crowding out means that
qa.a: heavy government borrowing reduces funds available for private investment
qa.e: Government borrowing can raise interest rates and reduce private investment.

qa.q: How is the fiscal deficit related to the revenue deficit?
qa.a: Fiscal deficit = revenue deficit + capital expenditure − non-debt capital receipts
qa.e: RD is one component of FD; the other is net capital spending not covered by non-debt receipts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A high fiscal deficit can lead to a debt trap. Reason (R): Borrowings increase future interest payments, which raise revenue expenditure.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Rising interest burdens need more borrowing, so debt keeps growing.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A fiscal deficit is always harmful for the economy. Reason (R): A fiscal deficit used for capital expenditure can raise productive capacity.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: If borrowing builds assets, it can support growth, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the three linkages of an open economy?
qa.a: Linkage through weather forecasts
qa.e: The three linkages are output, financial and labour markets.

qa.q: In the circular flow of an open economy, imports are
qa.a: a leakage
qa.e: Spending on imports goes out of the domestic flow.

qa.q: If the exchange rate is ₹84 per dollar, the rupee cost of a $25 book is
A rise in the exchange rate from ₹82/$ to ₹86/$ means
qa.a: the rupee has lost value against the dollar
qa.e: More rupees are needed per dollar, so the rupee is weaker.

qa.q: Exports are treated as an injection because
qa.a: they represent foreign spending on domestic output
qa.e: Foreigners' purchases add to demand for domestic goods.

qa.q: An Indian engineer moving to Germany for a job is an example of
qa.a: labour market linkage
qa.e: Movement of workers across countries is a labour market linkage.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Exchange rates matter in an open economy. Reason (R): People and firms need to convert one currency into another to trade and invest abroad.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Every international purchase needs currency conversion at the exchange rate.

qa.q: Buying shares of a US company by an Indian investor is an example of
qa.a: financial market linkage
qa.e: Trading in financial assets across countries is a financial linkage.

qa.q: Balance of trade refers to
qa.a: exports of goods minus imports of goods
qa.e: BoT covers only visible items (goods).

qa.q: Exports of goods are ₹800 crore and imports of goods are ₹1,050 crore. The balance of trade (₹ crore) is
qa.e: BoT = 800 − 1,050 = −250, a trade deficit.

qa.q: Which item is recorded in the current account?
qa.a: Remittances sent home by workers abroad
qa.e: Remittances are transfers, part of the current account; the others are capital or reserve items.

qa.q: BoT is −₹400 crore and net invisibles are +₹250 crore. Current account balance (₹ crore) is
qa.e: CA = BoT + net invisibles = −400 + 250 = −150.

qa.q: Which of these is an invisible item?
qa.a: Export of IT services
qa.e: Services are invisibles; goods are visibles.

qa.q: How does current account balance differ from balance of trade?
qa.a: It also includes services, income and transfers
qa.e: CA = BoT + net invisibles.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A country can have a trade deficit and a current account surplus at the same time. Reason (R): A large surplus on invisibles can more than offset a trade deficit.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: CA = BoT + net invisibles, so positive invisibles can outweigh a negative BoT.

qa.q: Interest received by Indians on bonds held abroad is recorded under
qa.a: income in the current account
qa.e: Investment income is an income flow in the current account.

qa.q: A country with a current account deficit is
qa.a: a net borrower from the rest of the world
qa.e: It spends more abroad than it earns and must finance the gap.

qa.q: Which is recorded in the capital account?
qa.a: Foreign direct investment
qa.e: FDI is a transaction in assets.

qa.q: An Indian company buying a factory in Vietnam is a
qa.a: debit in India's capital account
qa.e: Buying foreign assets is an outflow, a debit.

qa.q: Capital inflows of ₹900 crore and outflows of ₹650 crore give a capital account balance (₹ crore) of
qa.e: Balance = 900 − 650 = 250 (surplus).

qa.q: External assistance in the BoP refers to
qa.a: loans and aid received from foreign governments and international bodies
qa.e: It is a capital account item covering aid loans.

qa.q: When should a current account deficit cause the least concern?
qa.a: When it is financed by long-term investment that raises future output and exports
qa.e: Sustainable financing and productive use make a CAD less worrying.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Foreign portfolio investment is a capital account transaction. Reason (R): It involves buying and selling of financial assets such as shares and bonds.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Asset transactions are recorded in the capital account.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A current account surplus means the country is a net borrower. Reason (R): A current account surplus means receipts exceed payments on current items.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: With a surplus, the country lends abroad; it is a net lender, so A is false.

qa.q: Transactions undertaken for their own sake, like trade for profit, are called
qa.a: autonomous transactions
qa.e: Autonomous items happen independently of the BoP position.

qa.q: A BoP deficit means
qa.a: autonomous payments exceed autonomous receipts, so official reserves fall
qa.e: The gap in autonomous items is covered by drawing down reserves.

qa.q: The current account deficit is $25 billion and net capital inflows (excluding reserves) are $18 billion. Official reserves change by ($ billion)
qa.e: −25 + 18 = −7: reserves fall by $7 billion.

qa.q: The item that makes the BoP balance when some transactions are not recorded properly is
qa.a: errors and omissions
qa.e: It is the statistical balancing item.

qa.q: In BPM6, FDI and portfolio investment are recorded in the
qa.a: financial account
qa.e: BPM6 separates the financial account from the narrow capital account.

qa.q: Which is an accommodating transaction?
qa.a: The central bank selling foreign exchange from reserves to cover a gap
qa.e: Accommodating transactions cover the gap left by autonomous ones.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In an accounting sense, the balance of payments always balances. Reason (R): Any surplus or deficit in autonomous transactions is matched by official reserve transactions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Reserve changes (plus errors and omissions) close the gap so the total is zero.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A rise in a country's official reserves indicates a BoP deficit. Reason (R): Official reserves are used to finance a BoP deficit.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Reserves rise when there is a BoP surplus, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Which is a source of demand for foreign exchange in India?
qa.a: Indians travelling abroad on holiday
qa.e: Indians need foreign currency to spend abroad; the others supply foreign exchange.

qa.q: Why does the demand curve for foreign exchange slope downward?
qa.a: A higher exchange rate makes imports costlier in domestic currency
qa.e: As e rises, imports cost more rupees, so fewer dollars are demanded.

qa.q: Which is a source of supply of foreign exchange to India?
qa.a: Foreign direct investment into India
qa.e: Foreign investment brings dollars that are converted into rupees.

qa.q: The supply curve of foreign exchange slopes upward because
qa.a: a higher exchange rate makes domestic exports cheaper for foreigners
qa.e: With more rupees per dollar, foreigners can buy more Indian goods for each dollar.

qa.q: A $600 phone costs how much more in rupees when e rises from ₹82/$ to ₹84/$?
Who among these is a participant in the foreign exchange market?
qa.a: Authorised dealers such as commercial banks
qa.e: Banks, brokers, authorised dealers and the central bank trade currencies.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A rise in the exchange rate (₹ per $) increases the supply of dollars. Reason (R): Indian exports become cheaper for foreign buyers.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Cheaper Indian goods raise exports, bringing in more dollars.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Purchase of foreign assets by Indians increases the supply of foreign exchange in India. Reason (R): Indians need foreign currency to buy foreign assets.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Buying foreign assets creates demand for foreign exchange, not supply; A is false and R is true.

qa.q: Under a flexible exchange rate system, the exchange rate is determined by
qa.a: the demand for and supply of foreign exchange
qa.e: Market forces set the rate.

qa.q: The exchange rate changes from ₹84/$ to ₹82/$ due to market forces. This is
qa.a: appreciation of the rupee
qa.e: Fewer rupees per dollar means the rupee gained value through the market.

qa.q: A sharp rise in India's imports of electronics, other things equal, will
qa.a: raise the demand for dollars and depreciate the rupee
qa.e: Importers need more dollars; demand shifts right and e rises.

qa.q: The rupee depreciates from ₹80/$ to ₹88/$. The percentage rise in e is
Who gains most directly from depreciation of the rupee?
qa.a: Indian exporters
qa.e: Each dollar earned converts into more rupees.

qa.q: If interest rates in India rise relative to those abroad, the rupee tends to
qa.a: appreciate
qa.e: Higher returns attract foreign capital, raising the supply of dollars.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Depreciation of the domestic currency tends to increase exports. Reason (R): Domestic goods become cheaper for foreign buyers.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: A weaker rupee lowers the dollar price of Indian goods.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A rise in India's national income tends to appreciate the rupee. Reason (R): A rise in income raises the demand for imports.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: More imports raise demand for dollars, which depreciates the rupee; A is false and R is true.

qa.q: A basket costs ₹6,400 in India and $80 in the USA. The PPP exchange rate (₹ per $) is
According to PPP, if India has higher inflation than the USA, in the long run the rupee will
qa.a: depreciate
qa.e: Rising Indian prices mean more rupees are needed for the same basket, so e rises.

qa.q: The real exchange rate is defined as
qa.a: e × P_f / P
qa.e: It compares foreign prices (converted into rupees) with domestic prices.

qa.q: e = ₹84/$, a US basket costs $50 and the Indian basket costs ₹3,500. The real exchange rate is
Under the gold standard, exchange rates were
qa.a: fixed by the gold content of currencies
qa.e: Each currency had a fixed gold price, so rates were fixed.

qa.q: Under the gold standard, a country with a BoP deficit would experience
qa.a: an outflow of gold and a fall in money supply and prices
qa.e: Paying for the deficit drains gold, shrinking money supply and prices.

qa.q: Assertion (A): If purchasing power parity holds, the real exchange rate equals 1. Reason (R): Under PPP, e = P / P_f.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Substituting e = P/P_f into e × P_f / P gives exactly 1.

qa.q: The price-specie-flow mechanism corrects a trade deficit mainly through
qa.a: changes in domestic prices caused by gold flows
qa.e: Gold outflow reduces money and prices, making exports competitive.

qa.q: Devaluation of a currency refers to
qa.a: an official rise in the exchange rate (fall in currency value) under a fixed system
qa.e: Devaluation is a deliberate government decision under a fixed rate.

qa.q: Which is the key difference between devaluation and depreciation?
qa.a: Devaluation is an official act under a fixed rate; depreciation is due to market forces under a flexible rate
qa.e: Both mean a loss of value, but the cause and system differ.

qa.q: At the fixed rate ₹75/$, demand for dollars is $500 million and supply is $440 million. To hold the peg, the central bank must sell ($ million)
qa.e: Excess demand = 500 − 440 = 60; the central bank meets it from reserves.

qa.q: A major demerit of a fixed exchange rate system is that
qa.a: the central bank must hold large foreign exchange reserves
qa.e: To defend the peg, reserves must be large enough to meet excess demand.

qa.q: Revaluation means
qa.a: an official fall in the exchange rate, raising the currency's value
qa.e: Revaluation is the opposite of devaluation under a fixed system.

qa.q: The Bretton Woods system of fixed but adjustable exchange rates lasted from 1944 until
qa.e: It broke down in 1971 when US dollar convertibility into gold ended.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Under a fixed exchange rate, a black market for foreign exchange may develop. Reason (R): If the official rate keeps foreign exchange cheaper than its market value and reserves are short, people trade illegally at a higher rate.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Rationing at an artificial price pushes trade into an unofficial market.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Depreciation is a deliberate decision of the government. Reason (R): Under a fixed system, the government can officially change the exchange rate.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Depreciation is market-driven; the deliberate act is devaluation. A is false, R is true.

qa.q: Under managed floating, the exchange rate is
qa.a: mainly determined by the market, with central bank intervention to smooth large swings
qa.e: It is a mix of market determination and occasional intervention.

qa.q: Which is a merit of a flexible exchange rate system?
qa.a: BoP imbalances can be corrected automatically by exchange rate changes
qa.e: Market changes in e adjust exports and imports.

qa.q: Which is a demerit of a flexible exchange rate system?
qa.a: Uncertainty due to frequent changes in the exchange rate
qa.e: Volatility makes trade and investment riskier.

qa.q: With MPC = 0.75 and marginal propensity to import = 0.05, the open economy multiplier is
Why is the open economy multiplier smaller than the closed economy multiplier?
qa.a: Part of each round of extra spending leaks out as imports
qa.e: Imports are a leakage that reduces the induced domestic spending.

qa.q: c = 0.8, m = 0.2 and autonomous spending rises by ₹60 crore. The rise in income (₹ crore) is
Assertion (A): India follows a managed floating exchange rate regime. Reason (R): The RBI intervenes in the forex market to curb excessive volatility of the rupee.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: RBI intervention to smooth a market-determined rate is exactly managed floating.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A rise in domestic income increases net exports. Reason (R): Imports rise when domestic income rises.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Higher imports reduce NX = X − M, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: The main aim of the colonial government's economic policies in India was to
qa.a: make India a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods
qa.e: Policies served Britain's industrial interests.

qa.q: During the first half of the 20th century, India's per capita output grew at about
qa.a: 0.5% per year
qa.e: Aggregate output grew under 2%, per capita output only about 0.5% a year.

qa.q: Whose estimates of India's national income during the colonial period are considered very significant?
qa.a: V.K.R.V. Rao
qa.e: Rao's estimates are regarded as the most significant of that era.

qa.q: Muslin (malmal) of which place was famous worldwide before colonial rule?
qa.a: Dhaka
qa.e: Dhaka's fine muslin was famous internationally.

qa.q: India's aggregate real output in the first half of the 20th century grew at
qa.a: less than 2% per year
qa.e: Growth was slow, below 2% a year.

qa.q: Which of these economists did NOT estimate India's national income in the colonial period?
qa.a: Amartya Sen
qa.e: Naoroji, Digby, Shirras, Rao and Desai made colonial-era estimates; Sen's work came after independence.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's economy was stagnant under colonial rule. Reason (R): Colonial policies were designed to serve Britain's economic interests rather than India's development.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Policies focused on raw materials and markets for Britain, so India's own growth stalled.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Before colonial rule, India was known only for agriculture. Reason (R): India had a strong handicraft base in textiles, metal work and gem work.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: India was also famous for handicrafts, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: About what percentage of India's population depended on agriculture under colonial rule?
qa.e: About 85% of the population lived in villages and depended on agriculture.

qa.q: Under the zamindari system, the profits from agriculture went mainly to
qa.a: the zamindars
qa.e: Zamindars collected rent while cultivators got little.

qa.q: Which was a major cause of agricultural stagnation under colonial rule?
qa.a: Land settlement systems like zamindari
qa.e: The zamindari system and lack of investment held back productivity.

qa.q: Commercialisation of agriculture under colonial rule meant
qa.a: a shift towards cash crops needed by British industry
qa.e: Farmers were pushed to grow crops like indigo for Britain's industries.

qa.q: Zamindars were reluctant to improve agriculture mainly because
qa.a: they were interested only in collecting rent, and revenue terms were harsh
qa.e: Rent extraction and fixed revenue deadlines discouraged investment.

qa.q: Which of these was NOT a cause of low agricultural productivity under colonial rule?
qa.a: Large-scale use of high-yielding variety seeds
qa.e: HYV seeds came with the green revolution after independence.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indian agriculture remained stagnant under British rule. Reason (R): The area under cultivation expanded during this period.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but expansion of area does not explain stagnation; the causes were the land system, low technology and poor irrigation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Commercialisation of agriculture greatly improved farmers' conditions. Reason (R): Cash crops were grown mainly to feed British industries.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Cash crops served Britain, not farmers, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: De-industrialisation in colonial India refers to
qa.a: the decline of handicrafts without the growth of modern industry
qa.e: Handicrafts collapsed and modern industry did not grow enough to replace them.

qa.q: TISCO was incorporated in
qa.e: Tata Iron and Steel Company was incorporated in 1907.

qa.q: Jute mills in colonial India were mostly located in
qa.a: Bengal
qa.e: Jute mills were concentrated in Bengal and mainly foreign-owned.

qa.q: Cotton textile mills in colonial India were mostly owned by
qa.a: Indians
qa.e: Cotton mills in Maharashtra and Gujarat were largely Indian-owned.

qa.q: Which was a major weakness of Indian industry at independence?
qa.a: Almost no capital goods industry
qa.e: India had to import machines; industry's GDP share was small.

qa.q: The two-fold motive of colonial industrial policy was to make India
qa.a: a supplier of raw materials and a market for British finished goods
qa.e: These two aims explain de-industrialisation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India lacked a capital goods industry at independence. Reason (R): Colonial policy encouraged India to import machinery and finished goods from Britain.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Since India was treated as a market for British goods, machine-making did not develop.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sugar, cement and paper industries developed in India before the First World War. Reason (R): TISCO was incorporated in 1907.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: These industries came up after the Second World War, so A is false; TISCO's 1907 date is true.

qa.q: Under colonial rule, India mainly exported
qa.a: primary products such as raw cotton, jute and indigo
qa.e: India was a raw material exporter and a buyer of finished goods.

qa.q: More than half of India's foreign trade under colonial rule was with
qa.a: Britain
qa.e: Britain held monopoly control; the rest was with China, Ceylon and Persia.

qa.q: The Suez Canal was opened in
qa.e: It opened in 1869, sharply reducing transport costs.

qa.q: The term 'drain of wealth' refers to
qa.a: the use of India's export surplus to pay for British administration, wars and invisibles
qa.e: The export surplus did not come back to India as gold or silver.

qa.q: How did the opening of the Suez Canal affect India's trade?
qa.a: It reduced transport costs and strengthened British control over Indian trade
qa.e: A shorter route made it cheaper for Britain to trade with and control India.

qa.q: Which was a feature of India's foreign trade under colonial rule?
qa.a: A large export surplus
qa.e: Exports exceeded imports, but the surplus was drained.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's large export surplus did not lead to an inflow of gold or silver. Reason (R): The surplus was used to pay for Britain's administrative and war expenses and invisible imports.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The surplus was spent on colonial costs, so no precious metals came in.

qa.q: Which country was NOT among India's other trading partners (apart from Britain) in the colonial period, according to NCERT?
qa.a: USA
qa.e: NCERT names China, Ceylon and Persia as the other partners.

qa.q: The first official census of British India was held in
qa.e: The first census was in 1881; censuses followed every ten years.

qa.q: 1921 is called the year of the great divide because
qa.a: it marked the end of the first stage of demographic transition
qa.e: After 1921, India entered the second stage of demographic transition.

qa.q: Life expectancy in India at the time of independence was about
qa.a: 32 years
qa.e: Life expectancy was about 32 years.

qa.q: The infant mortality rate in colonial India was about
qa.e: It was alarmingly high at about 218 per 1,000.

qa.q: Overall literacy in colonial India was
qa.a: less than 16%
qa.e: Literacy was below 16%, female literacy only about 7%.

qa.q: Before 1921, India was in which stage of demographic transition?
qa.a: The first stage
qa.e: Both birth and death rates were high before 1921.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The death rate in colonial India was very high. Reason (R): Public health facilities were unavailable or inadequate, and diseases were widespread.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Poor health facilities and widespread diseases caused high mortality.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Female literacy in colonial India was about 50%. Reason (R): Overall literacy was less than 16%.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Female literacy was only about 7%, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: At independence, the share of the workforce in agriculture was about
qa.e: Agriculture employed about 70–75% of workers.

qa.q: The share of the workforce in manufacturing at independence was about
qa.e: Manufacturing employed only about 10% of workers.

qa.q: The share of the workforce in services at independence was about
qa.e: Services employed about 15–20% of workers.

qa.q: In which region did the dependence of the workforce on agriculture DECLINE during the colonial period?
qa.a: Madras Presidency
qa.e: Madras, Bombay and Bengal saw a shift towards manufacturing and services.

qa.q: Occupational structure refers to
qa.a: the distribution of the workforce among different occupations or sectors
qa.e: It shows how workers are spread across sectors.

qa.q: In which of these did the share of the workforce in agriculture INCREASE during the colonial period?
qa.a: Rajasthan
qa.e: Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab saw a rise in agricultural workforce share.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The occupational structure of colonial India showed little change over time. Reason (R): Agriculture continued to employ the largest share of workers.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: The heavy dependence on agriculture persisted, so the overall structure barely changed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Regional variation in occupational structure increased during the colonial period. Reason (R): In Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab the share of agriculture in the workforce fell.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: Regional variation did grow, but in Orissa, Rajasthan and Punjab agriculture's share rose, so R is false.

qa.q: Railways were introduced in India in
qa.e: NCERT dates the introduction of railways to 1850.

qa.q: The main motive behind colonial road building was
qa.a: moving the army and carrying raw materials to ports and railway stations
qa.e: Roads served administrative and export needs.

qa.q: Which was a harmful effect of colonial railways?
qa.a: They weakened the self-sufficiency of village economies through commercialisation
qa.e: Linking villages to export markets eroded village self-sufficiency.

qa.q: The Coast Canal mentioned by NCERT as an uneconomical waterway was on the coast of
qa.a: Orissa
qa.e: It was on the Orissa coast.

qa.q: Which was NOT a major economic challenge India faced at independence?
qa.a: A large surplus of capital goods
qa.e: India had almost no capital goods industry.

qa.q: The electric telegraph in colonial India mainly served to
qa.a: help maintain law and order
qa.e: The telegraph was used largely for administrative control.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Colonial railways helped Indians travel long distances. Reason (R): Railways were built mainly to serve British economic and administrative interests.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but the colonial motive does not explain why Indians could travel more; the travel benefit was a by-product.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's economy at independence was poised for rapid self-sustained growth. Reason (R): Agriculture was stagnant and industry lacked a capital goods base.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Given these weaknesses, A is false; R correctly describes the situation.

qa.q: India adopted which type of economic system after independence?
qa.a: Mixed economy
qa.e: India combined a strong public sector with a private sector.

qa.q: The Planning Commission was set up in
qa.e: It was set up in 1950; the First Plan began in 1951.

qa.q: Who was the chairperson of the Planning Commission?
qa.a: The Prime Minister
qa.e: The Prime Minister chaired the Planning Commission.

qa.q: Who is regarded as the architect of Indian planning?
qa.a: P.C. Mahalanobis
qa.e: Mahalanobis shaped the Second Five Year Plan.

qa.q: In a socialist economy, decisions about what and how to produce are taken by
qa.a: the government
qa.e: The state decides production according to society's needs.

qa.q: A perspective plan is a
qa.a: long-term plan, usually of about 20 years
qa.e: Long-term goals are set in a perspective plan; Five Year Plans work towards them.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India chose a mixed economy after independence. Reason (R): Leaders wanted a strong public sector along with a private sector, guided by planning.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Combining the state and the market is what a mixed economy means.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In a capitalist economy, the government decides what goods are produced. Reason (R): In a capitalist economy, goods are produced according to market demand and profits.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Market forces decide in capitalism, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: 'Growth' as a planning goal refers to
qa.a: an increase in the country's capacity to produce goods and services
qa.e: Growth is measured by a steady rise in GDP.

qa.q: Which goal of planning includes social changes such as equal rights for women?
qa.a: Modernisation
qa.e: NCERT treats modernisation as both new technology and social change.

qa.q: The goal of self-reliance mainly aimed to
qa.a: reduce dependence on imports, especially of food
qa.e: India wanted to avoid importing goods it could produce, particularly food.

qa.q: Equity as a planning goal means
qa.a: the benefits of growth should reach the poor sections of society
qa.e: Equity is about fair sharing of benefits and meeting basic needs.

qa.q: Which is an example of conflict between planning goals?
qa.a: Labour-saving modern machines raise growth but reduce employment
qa.e: Technology adoption can conflict with the aim of providing jobs.

qa.q: Unlike many developed countries, India's structural change after 1950 saw
qa.a: the service sector become the largest part of GDP while most workers stayed in agriculture
qa.e: India moved from agriculture to services in GDP without a large shift of workers to industry.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Planners stressed self-reliance in food production. Reason (R): Dependence on imported food could make the country vulnerable to foreign pressure.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Food imports could expose India to foreign interference, so food self-reliance was a priority.

qa.q: Assertion (A): All four goals of planning can always be achieved together without conflict. Reason (R): Growth, modernisation, self-reliance and equity were the goals of the Five Year Plans.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Goals can conflict, e.g. modern technology vs employment; A is false, R is true.

qa.q: The main objective of land ceiling legislation was to
qa.a: reduce concentration of land ownership in a few hands
qa.e: Ceilings fixed the maximum land one could own; surplus went to the landless.

qa.q: Abolition of intermediaries in agriculture meant
qa.a: removing zamindars so that tillers became owners
qa.e: Zamindari abolition gave ownership to cultivators.

qa.q: In which pair of states were land reforms relatively more successful?
qa.a: Kerala and West Bengal
qa.e: Committed governments in Kerala and West Bengal implemented 'land to the tiller'.

qa.q: How does ownership of land encourage higher output?
qa.a: Owners get the benefit of extra effort, so they invest more
qa.e: Incentives work when the tiller keeps the reward of improvement.

qa.q: Benami transfers helped landlords to
qa.a: avoid land ceilings by registering land in others' names
qa.e: Benami transfers hid ownership to escape the ceiling.

qa.q: Roughly how many tenants came into direct contact with the government after abolition of intermediaries?
qa.a: 200 lakh
qa.e: About 200 lakh tenants came into direct contact with the government.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Land ceiling laws were not fully effective. Reason (R): Big landlords used loopholes and benami transfers to keep surplus land.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Evasion through loopholes explains the limited success.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Land reforms were equally successful in all Indian states. Reason (R): Kerala and West Bengal had governments committed to land to the tiller.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: Success varied widely; only some states did well, so A is false; R is true.

qa.q: The green revolution refers to
qa.a: a large increase in foodgrain production using HYV seeds
qa.e: It was driven by HYV seeds with fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation.

qa.q: HYV seeds required
qa.a: regular water supply, fertilisers and pesticides in correct quantities
